text: Round Robin - Thermophysical Property Measurement

The key scientific objectives are: (a) Conducting baseline space ESL containerless property measurement experiments for two paired classes of levitation-based thermophysical properties:Density/Thermal Expansion, Viscosity/Surface Tension.
(b) Selecting materials compatible with both electrostatic levitation (ESL) and electromagnetic levitation (EML) to allow comparison between space facilities.
(c) Using modeling to evaluate theories used to predict the influence of gravity on propertymeasurement experiments.
(d) Actively encouraging collaboration with existing science teams using other facilities through organizing a Round Robin test consortium

The experimental approach involved inserting a sample carousel of 20 individual samples into the JAXA ISS-ELF facility, conditioning the test atmosphere, and conducting individual melt cycles on each sample.
The heating lasers were used to precondition the sample when the sample is heated to a desired pre-bake temperature.
Following the preconditioning period, the sample was charged by the electrodes and released to achieve stable positioning.
The lasers were then used to thermally cycle the sample.

The cycle starts by application of the highest laser heating power (activated by a control current setting in the ELF software measured in amps) until the sample is fully molten and achieved the maximum liquid superheat temperature.
The heater power was then turned down to maintain the desired isothermal hold.
Surface excitation was conducted using varying volage from the electrodes at this temperature.
Surface tension and viscosity was measured using the droplet oscillation behavior.
The laser power was then turned off to allow the molten sample to cool down.
Density and cp/ε evaluations are conducted during the free cooling without any influence from the laser.
Once recalescence occurred, the sample was then allowed to become fully solid at room temperature which marks the completion of a thermal cycle.
Overall, processing a single melt cycle can take up to 10 - 15 minutes excluding the pre-bake.
Following the cycle completion, the sample is retrieved back into the cartridge to end the test on this sample.
Using the described experimental approach several thermophysical properties were measured on a variety of metallic melts as described below:
Density –One high-speed video camera was used to monitor the sample size as a function of time during the free cooling phase.
Sample edge was detected using a custom algorithm for the density measurement.

The volume of the sample was calculated using a known calibration of pixels/mm3, which was subsequently correlated with temperature allowing calculation of density and thermal expansion coefficient (from the slope of the density curve).
Tracking of sample mass loss was accomplished post-mission using Langmuir’s equation of evaporation.
Surface tension – After melting, the heating laser is set to a reduced value such that the sample is held at constant temperature.
A sinusoidal modulation of the positioning voltage was applied to both electrodes to excite surface oscillations without changing sample position.
The resulting sample deformation was measured by the high-speed linear array.
A frequeny sweep was conducted to identify natural frequency.

Two method was applied to identify the natural frequency from the sweep: (1) Maximum amplitude method where maximum deformation is observed at the natural frequency and (2) Excitation crossover method where the natural frequency was observed at the linear intersections of the damped and free oscillations.
Natural frequencies identified using both methods were used to evaluate the surface tension.
Viscosity – In conjunction to surface tension, viscosity was measured from the damped oscillations at the identified natural frequency.
The characteristic exponential time decay from a sinusoidal fit was used to evaluate the viscosity.

Specific heat capacity and emissivity – The ratio of these two quantities was evaluated from the cooling curve as monitored by the IR pyrometer after correction for conductive mass losses to the gas environment.
Evaporation – Integration of the time-temperature profile allows calculation of evaporation assuming a known relationship using Langmuir’s equation for loss as a function of temperature.
Pre- and post- measurement of sample mass anchors these predictions.
Dynamic mass is crucial for tracking for density, surface tension and viscosity measurement.
The experimental hypothesis was that in microgravity environment in the absence of stirring, high quality thermophysical property would be measured compared to the ground-based levitation facility.
This was successfully observed for gold samples.

This research aids in dissemination of an baseline archived dataset allowing researchers to validate models accounting for gravity-induced systematic error in property measurement used for industrial welding, casting and additive manufacturing operations .
Industry will be better able to correlate ground and space results to expand the quantity and quality of available information without the requirement for access to space.
Advance the understanding of how to best allocate the scant resources available for space-based materials property measurement using levitation.

In the future this could lead to development of a model where fidelity and cost can be readily calculated for a given material classification and serve as the basis for prioritization of specific ground and space thermophysical property investigations.

Multi-Scale Modeling and Experimentation on Liquid Phase Sintering in Gravity and Microgravity Environments
In this study, the compositions start with W-Ni-Cu-Mn powder mixtures.
The solid-liquid ratio is adjusted via changes in the tungsten content from 70 to 90 wt %.
Most of the tungsten remains solid during sintering.
The liquid is formed from melting the mechanically alloyed Ni-Cu-Mn additive.
The liquid dissolves up to 28 wt % tungsten at the sintering temperature, giving the desired semisolid system.
In these experiments, changes are also made to the Ni:Cu ratio from 3:2 to 2:3 to slightly adjust the tungsten solubility.
Seven cartridges with seven samples each are processed in microgravity.
One cartridge is heated to the temperature where first significant densification occurs on Earth, 1180°C, and five of the cartridges are processed for progressively longer times at 1210°C.
A seventh cartridge is for backup in case of an aborted run, otherwise it provides a replicate at 34 min at 1210°C.
An early part of this research focused on developing a W-Ni-Cu-Mn alloy to allow lower sintering temperatures to accommodate downgraded furnace peak temperatures.
The new alloys are tested using ground proof runs to gather ground data.
Those results are contrasted with the microgravity data.
Extensive testing is documented to show the experimental platform; tests involved thermal overload, vibration, equipment proofing, evaporation, transient runaway, and temperature verification trials.
An early failure in the quartz ampoule led to redesign.
Subsequent ground runs were conducted without failure.
This report emphasizes the development of the experiments and details the densification and distortion data, and provides microstructure data.
Modeling ideas were established early and awaited samples for verification.

Much effort was directed to developing a time sequence whereby modeling data would be available for rheological variables associated with the solid-liquid-pore structures existing during sintering, namely extraction of the viscosity and strength variations during the 60 min of isothermal hold.
The model is implemented in finite element analysis where stress on the sintering body is assessed using variations in the composition, component size, and gravity.
The idea of removing distortion during liquid phase sintering has much appeal.
Loss of dimensional precision during sintering is a common industrial problem.
Forming technologies allow for precise green bodies (green is the term adopted to indicate the component after forming, but prior to sintering).
The body force due to gravity acts in the vertical direction and increases with height and density.

In these trials, components of 12 mm in height are processed and analyzed for features such as density, dimensional variation (distortion), microstructure, grain size distribution, and pore agglomeration after return to Earth.
Gravity normally produces sufficient substrate friction to locally resist shrinkage during sintering, giving an elephant foot geometry.
Microgravity trails examine if densification is possible without distortion, the benefit being net-shape processing.
For this research on gravity effects on distortion and densification during liquid phase sintering, the two primary metrics are nonuniform dimensional change and the elimination of pores.
Along these lines, isotropic right circular cylinders are fabricated for sintering.
Both the initial and sintered dimensions are measured over several locations to quantify densification (and shrinkage) and distortion.
Densification is measured using dimensional shrinkage (up to 15 %), relying on the change in porosity divided by the initial porosity (37 %).
The samples are initially 63 % dense.
Distortion is calculated using multiple dimensional measurements over closely spaced locations and is expressed as the coefficient of variation (standard deviation divided by the mean size).
For microstructure assessment to help explain the behavior, the samples are sectioned, mounted, and polished.
Optical microscopy, quantitative microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and energy dispersive analysis of X-rays provide information on the microstructure, especially the pore and grain structure.
Quantitative microstructure data include grain size, pore size, connectivity, and distributions for these features.
The results are compared to models to validate constitutive laws.
In prior research microgravity resulted in large pores, extensive distortion, and a low grain connectivity microstructure with smaller grains.
The idea of removing distortion during liquid phase sintering has much appeal.
Loss of dimensional precision during sintering is a common industrial problem.
Forming technologies allow for precise green bodies (green is the term adopted to indicate the component after forming, but prior to sintering).
The body force due to gravity acts in the vertical direction and increases with height and density.
The distortion problem is most evident in structures with protrusions and unsupported or cantilever features.

Accordingly, for some liquid phase sintered components a majority of the production expense is in correcting dimensional issues after sintering, by use of coining, straightening, grinding, or machining.
Many powder metallurgy components start with a green density of just 60 % of theoretical.
Shaping is possible using a variety of options - die pressing, injection molding, warm extrusion, cold isostatic pressing, or slurry casting.
High performance demands a high sintered density, often from 98 to 100 %.
The change from 60 to 98 % density comes with about 15 % shrinkage in each dimension.
However, as the component height increases gravity induces nonuniform shrinkage.
The friction force at the component bottom increases.
This friction force resists densification on the bottom surface, resulting in nonuniform dimensions, effectively distorting the green body.
The economic attraction for sintering technologies is the delivery of net-shapes, avoiding post-sintering machining if possible.
Unfortunately, it is easy to lose dimensional control, necessitating secondary operations that add greatly to the fabrication expense.
In the ideal, tooling design would anticipate sintering shrinkage, even nonuniform shrinkage, enabling sintering to directly deliver final size.
This would be possible with computer tools to design the tooling in anticipation of shrinkage and distortion.
Our initial conjecture suggested that liquid phase sintering in microgravity would remove distortion, since shrinkage and microstructure should be uniform.
Sintering is a heat treatment applied to powders with the intent of bonding the particles into a solid structure.
It is widely applied to forming complex shapes for automotive, computer, metal cutting, oil and gas drilling, hand tools, firearms, and hardware.
Tools is designed to shape the powder into a shape that is oversized to allow for shrinkage.
With sufficiently high temperature, heat induces atomic motion and repositioning of solid to form bonds between the particles that strengthen the body.
Usually that occurs via diffusion along interfaces such as grain boundary liquid films.
In industrial production, the powder is shaped prior to sintering, such as by die compaction or injection molding, with subsequent sintering to produce a complex shape.
Accordingly, sintering is frequently applied to high performance materials and is applied in practice over a wide range of products and industries from bricks to rocket engines.
It is especially useful for high temperature materials, such as the refractory metals, including tungsten.
If densification can be acheived without distortion, considerable expense is avoided by net-shape fabrication.
In this sense, tremendous industrial benefit is possible using liquid phase sintering with densifcation but no distortion.
In the US sintering technologies are responsible for about 60 kg of each automobile, and dozens of parts in each computer and cell phone.
Liquid phase sintering is a desirable option, where in an alloy some liquid forms during the heating cycle (between the liquidus and solidus temperatures for the alloy).

The idea of liquid phase sintering gained significance attention during the 1920s as a means to consolidate hard powders, such as cemented carbides (WC-Co), into high performance engineering structures, such as metal cutting tools, wire drawing dies, and oil-less bearings.
The tungsten heavy alloys emerged at the same time.
It is the latter system selected to demonstrate processing gains or losses associated with gravity.

NASA Research Under Project Quasi-crystalline Undercooled Alloys for Space Investigation (QUASI) and ESA-Based Investigations, THERMOLAB-ISS and ICOPROSOL
The primary objectives are:
Investigations of nucleation of crystal phases from supercooled (metastable) liquids as a function of stirring (fluid-flow) conditions.
Systematic studies of this under terrestrial conditions are not possible due to the presence of convective flow in the liquid.
Measurements of thermophysical properties of metallic liquids under microgravity conditions, including the specific heat, viscosity, surface tension.
These are then compared with measurements made under terrestrial conditions, when possible.

These data are important for the analysis of the nucleation data, fluid flow calculations; additionally they are important for understanding fundamental connections between liquid dynamics and structure.
Measurements of the supercooling are made under controlled stirring conditions.
The nucleation rates are derived from the distribution of maximum supercooling following the approach developed by Skripov.

By systematically changing the fluid-flow rates by applying controlled voltages to the heater/positioner coils in the ESA electromagnetic levitation facility on the ISS (ISS-EML), the nucleation rates can be studied as function of stirring, allowing the hypothesis to be examined.
When the composition of the nucleating crystal phase is different from that of the liquid, long range diffusion can become important for the nucleation process.
The potential impact on the nucleation rate depends on the ratio of the attachment rates to the nucleating cluster and the time required for long-range diffusion.
This can be investigated by nucleation measurements made as a function of stirring, since fluid-flow can decrease the impact of long-range diffusion.
Realistic modeling approaches have the potential to greatly improve the efficiency of materials development.
However, progress is frequently hampered by the lack of relevant thermophysical property data needed for the modeling.
Further, key processes such as crystal nucleation from the liquid or other phase transitions within the liquid, are often poorly understood, making it difficult to realistically model them.

In many cases, the experimental data and a deeper understanding of some processes cannot be obtained from terrestrial experiments due to interactions with sample containers at the temperatures of interest.
The combination of the containerless based terrestrial methods and the ISS-EML enables these measurements.

In addition to their relevance for processes such as additive manufacturing on earth, where nucleation in highly stirred conditions is important, measurements in two different gravitational fields will be important for designing additive manufacturing in space and on the Moon.

Flow Boiling and Condensation Experiment Flow Boiling Module

The proposed research aims to develop an integrated two-phase flow boiling/condensation facility for the International Space Station (ISS) to serve as a primary platform for obtaining two-phase flow and heat transfer data in microgravity.

By comparing the microgravity data against those obtained in Earth’s gravity, it will be possible to ascertain the influence of body force on two-phase transport phenomena in pursuit of mechanistic models as well as correlations, and to help determine the minimum flow criteria to ensure gravity independent flow boiling and condensation.
This research is a joint effort between the Purdue University Boiling and Two-Phase Flow Laboratory (PU-BTPFL) and the NASA Glenn Research Center.
Personnel from the two organizations combine extensive experience in research and development of both flow boiling and condensation systems, and in conducting microgravity experiments.
The objectives of the Flow Boiling and the Flow Condensation Experiment (FBCE) in the long duration microgravity environment of the ISS are to:

Develop experimentally validated, mechanistic model for microgravity flow boiling critical heat flux (CHF) and dimensionless criteria to predict minimum flow velocity required to ensure gravity independent CHF.

Develop experimentally validated, mechanistic model for microgravity annular condensation and dimensionless criteria to predict minimum flow velocity required to ensure gravity independent annular condensation.
Also, develop correlations for other condensation regimes in microgravity.

Obtain flow boiling data (heat flux, flow visualization, the wall temperature difference) in long duration microgravity environments for a well characterized heating surface as functions of liquid inlet mass velocity and subcooling.

Obtain flow condensation data (heat flux, flow visualization, the wall temperature difference) in long duration microgravity environments for a well-characterized condensing surface as functions of inlet quality and flow rate of condensing vapor.
Specific tasks for the study will be as follows.
The approach used in this project is to perform the following sequential series of tasks:
Provide detailed design and instrumentation requirements for the Flow Boiling Module (FBM).
Provide design and instrumentation requirements for the entire flow loop.
Generate test matrix for operating conditions of the study.
Perform initial validation tests in both terrestrial gravity and parabolic flight.
Perform tests on board the ISS.
Based on both the ISS and terrestrial data, develop a series of predictive tools, including empirical correlations as well as theoretical, computational, and machine learning models.
In literature spanning many decades, body force in terrestrial gravity is identified as having a profound influence on two-phase transport behavior.
This behavior is drastically altered In the absence of gravity, wherein flow fluid and heat transfer are dictated by flow inertia and surface tension.
This implies predictive tools from terrestrial gravity studies are inapplicable for design of NASA's reduced gravity systems.
This limitation points to a need for performing two-phase flow and heat transfer experiments on board the ISS as basis for formulating relevant reduced gravity predictive tools.
The proposed research will lay the foundation for development of advanced high power to weight ratio thermal management systems for NASA's future space vehicles and planetary bases.

Purdue University research has also shown tremendous value in findings from this projects to numerous other applications including ultra-fast charging of electric vehicles, fusion reactors, hydrogen storage, avionics, high-Mach turbine engines, and advanced electronics in laser, microwave, and radar systems.

Plasma Kristall 4

PK-4 is not an apparatus dedicated for specific experiments but rather a laboratory which shall offer the possibility to perform a large variety of experiments with complex plasmas and to react to new developments in this field in a manner as flexible as possible.

The main interest lies in the investigation of the liquid phase and flow phenomena of complex plasmas for which PK-4 is especially suited thanks to a DC-discharge and its geometry (elongated glass tube with a large observational access).
The experiments for PK-4 can be divided into research in three classes of fundamental questions:

Microscopic properties of complex plasmas This category comprises the charging of the particles, the external forces on the particles (e.g. ion drag), the fundamental interactions between the particles, agglomeration, and particle growth.

Macroscopic properties of complex plasmas In this category belong hydrodynamics (e.g. viscosity), thermodynamics (e.g. equation of state), and non-equilibriums aspects (e.g. lane formation, self-organisation) of complex plasmas.

Generic properties of classical many-body systems Complex plasmas are ideal model systems for studying various problems of strongly coupled many-body systems in solid state physics, fluid physics, plasma physics, nano-technology and even nuclear physics because complex plasmas can easily be produced and observed in real time on the microscopic and kinetic level.
Hence dynamical processes can be investigated on the level of single particles which is not possible in most systems.
Therefore new insights in the dynamics of those processes can be provided.
Typical examples are crystallization and melting, phonons in plasma crystals, dust waves, Mach cones, nozzles, turbulence, and nano-fluidics.

The basic experimental protocol starts with an evacuation of the plasma chamber for several hours (a minimum of 20 hours; base pressure: less than 10-3 Pa) to guarantee good plasma conditions, e.g. no striations.
Then neon or argon gas is filled in with a gas flow of typically 2 sccm reaching pressures between 5 and 250 Pa.
Afterwards the plasma is ignited by the high-voltage (about 1000 V) of the DC electrodes corresponding to a DC current of the order of 1 mA and a longitudinal electric field of about 2 V/cm.
Then the micro-particles are injected.
They get quickly charged in the plasma and drift from the cathode to the anode with a typical velocity between 1 and 10 cm/s.
In addition, the electric fields from the two RF coils/electrodes or the fast polarity switching can be used to manipulate the particles, e.g. to capture and confine them.

Gas flow, modulation of the DC and RF fields, the powerful manipulation laser, the thermal manipulator, and the EM electrode can also be used to manipulate the particles, e.g. to accelerate them or to introduce oscillations.
A sketch of the PK-4 experiment is shown in Figure 1.
The micro-particles are made visible by illumination with a laser beam, which is widened into a sheet by a cylindrical lens.
The scattered light is recorded by one or two CCD cameras (e.g. up to 200 frames per second, with a maximum resolution of about e.g.10 microns/pixel).
The light emission (“plasma glow”) from the plasma will be measured using the narrow band IF-filters.

The basic measurements comprise the positions of the particles, their velocities (extracted from the track length of the particles or from their positions in consecutive images), and correlations between the particles.
These quantities are determined from the images by using a dedicated IDL program or other methods for image analysis.
At the end of each experiment run the particles will be removed by gas flow before the plasma is switched off in order to avoid the contamination of the glass walls
PK-4 enables fundamental investigation of flows and related instabilities, by mimicking molecular mechanisms at a scale which allows for real time in-situ optical observations.
This requires on-orbit experiments to be undertaken in order to observe the processes at work, which are obviously disturbed by the influence of gravity on Earth.

Even though PK-4 is principally a fundamental experiment, understanding the processes at work and understanding how complex plasmas can be influenced by varying research parameters gives a better understanding of how improvements can be made in areas and industries where plasmas are used.
Understanding how dusty plasmas behave in microgravity could shed light on plasma phenomena in space, which could lead to new research methods or improved spacecraft designs.

Foam Optics and Mechanics

The objective is to take advantage of microgravity to eliminate drainage and to use imaging and multiple light scattering diagnostics in order to non-invasively measure and elucidate the time evolution of key features of the bubble-packing structure of wet foams – namely, the bubble size distribution and bubble rearrangement dynamics – and how they are affected by degree of wetness by systematically increasing the liquid content for sequences of otherwise identical foams.
FOAM is divided into two experiments: FOAM Coarsening and FOAM Stability.
Experiment Cells The FOAM-C experimental set-up comprises five segments with a total of 20 small test cells containing a variety of liquid mixtures.

The Fluid Science Laboratory on the ISS Columbus module will automatically shake and analyze these mixtures using complex laser optics, highly sensitive photodiodes and high-resolution cameras that can take up to 10,000 images per second.
Each test cell weighs only 20 grams and contains less than 2 cm³ of the liquid mixture, while each segment comprises four test cells and weighs a total of 320 grams.
Diagnostics - Overview video, - Multiple light scattering spectroscopies (SVS - Speckle Variance Spectroscopy and/or DWS - Diffusing-Wave Spectroscopy)
Example of Protocols - First, the foam is made at the time T0.
Then the foam is left to age while optical diagnostics measure its dynamics during aging (up to 24 hours foam age).
These cycles can be repeated several times.

Another cell with a different composition (liquid fraction, concentration) is then subject of a new series of experiments. - Granular matter samples of defined volume concentration shall be agitated until a steady state is reached.
Consequently, optical diagnostics measure the grains dynamics in the steady state and after turning the agitation off.
Experiment Protocol For each foam sample, there are different sets of measurements that are to be repeated in sequence, for the total run duration.
The maximum experiment duration shall be assumed with 24h per experiment run for each sample.
At the beginning of a science campaign on orbit replaceable units shall be exchanged (if necessary) and the EC is installed in FSL by the Crew.
Each run starts with the foaming process.
Data acquisition shall start just at the end of the foaming process.
After a run, either the same sample can be processed again, or another sample can be processed.
After a run, data post processing and downlink of results can occur.
The results can influence the experiment procedure of subsequent runs, and the possibility to change experiment parameters through telecommand shall be provided.
At the end of a science campaign selected scientific data is downlinked and then the EC is uninstalled by the Crew.
Runs Repetition Each sample shall be tested 3 times (one just needs to “re-foam” the sample after its first period of coarsening).
Experiment Duration and amount of Data The measurements (alternatively SVS, DWS, DTS, Camera) shall be performed during the whole run duration.
In the following the measurement time is a requirement.
On the opposite, the resulting amount of data is based on the required scientific measurements and the specific data production of the instrument, it is an indication but not a requirement.

This experiment might provide useful insights for the manufacture, use and ageing behavior of foams, which are utilized in a wide range of areas, including in cosmetics and personal-hygiene products, in the food industry, in cleaning products, sealing products and for firefighting.

Particle Stabilized Emulsions and Foams

The work proposed in the PASTA project follows the line from characterizing the surface properties of particles via a complex analysis of the properties of layers at liquid/gas and liquid/liquid interfaces to studying the behaviour of liquid films and finally to model real foams and emulsions.
The work comprises the application of available knowledge to the preparation and characterization of particle stabilized emulsions, produced by adapting to the Soft Matter Dynamics instrument.
The role of gravity on quiescent wet foams can be captured in 2 key questions:
Is the growth law for average bubble size R~√ time, such that R dR/dt is a constant?
If so, what is the liquid-fraction dependence of this rate?
How do the rate and the nature of the bubble rearrangement dynamics change as the liquid fraction is increased to the point of un-jamming (transition solid-like to liquid-like)?
PASTA will address the SPECIFIC OBJECTIVES:
Evaluate the characteristic time for the droplet coalescence as a function of the formulation Identify and investigate specific dynamic regimes for droplets dynamics (for example Brownian vs.
Capillarydriven) during emulsion destabilization.
Test and develop models for emulsion stability/destabilization prognosis.
The PArticle STAbilised emulsions experiment (PASTA) is placed inside the Fluid Science Rack (FSL) in the European Columbus module of the ISS.
Each PASTA sample cell is fitted with a piston that allows to agitate the mixture within the cell at various frequencies and durations to emulsify the mixture.
The sample cells are grouped 4-by-4 in sample cell units that can be fitted on a carousel inside SMD.

This carousel allows for placing each individual sample cell in the diagnostics position of SMD, where it can be observed with the SMD sensors and several diagnostic tools, like the overview camera that takes microscope image sequences in black and white of the sample cell.

Emulsions have large relevance for applications in a wide spectrum of technologies, processes, and products in different fields including oil and gas, specialty materials, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and foods.
Both stable and unstable emulsions are needs that are shared across a variety of applications.

For example, efficient de-emulsifiers are needed to facilitate the process of phase separation (breaking) in the crude oil emulsions extracted from the wells, while high stability oil-in-water emulsions are required in the final stage of production of the same well or to facilitate pumping high-viscosity oils through pipelines.
In the food industry, many products based on emulsified fats or oils (condiments, sauces, frozen confections, and others) require long term stability.
However, destabilizing emulsions are key to processing raw food materials such as milk and vegetable oils.

Characterization of Biofilm Formation, Growth and Gene Expression on Different Materials and Environmental Conditions in Microgravity

To use microbial strains that are relevant to human spaceflight, and nosocomial infections that have also occurred in spaceflight, and substrata materials that are relevant to (i) spacecraft structures and surfaces, (ii) life support systems, (iii) space biology research hardware, and (iv) medical instrumentation.

We are meeting this objective by the use of the same fungal strain that was isolated from a bio-damaged Mir window (Penicillium rubens), and an uropathogenic bacterial strain (Pseudomonas aeruginosa).
To culture the selected microbial strains in a way that enables biofilm formation, during an up- to-6-month experiment.
To achieve this goal, we used BioServe’s already spaceflight- proven hardware and conducted preliminary testing during the first year of the experiment.

To quantify potential changes on biofilm mass, thickness, and overall morphology (including the formation of the “column-and-canopy structures) on the spaceflight cultures with respect to matched ground controls.
This was achieved by acquiring post-flight (samples fixed in paraformaldehyde) morphological data through confocal laser scanning microscopy.
To elucidate the molecular mechanisms behind the observed morphological changes.

This was done with the bacterial samples by acquiring post-flight transcriptomic data (samples fixed with RNA Later II) and conducting differential gene expression analyses between spaceflight cultures and matched ground controls.
To assess differential expression of genes associated with conferring microbes with oxidative, acidity, and antimicrobial resistance.
This was done through RNA Sequencing and comparative gene analysis.
To determine physical mechanisms of material/microorganisms interaction in biofilms and their associated molecular basis.

The morphological and transcriptomic data was utilized to identify potential correlation in between the differential gene expression and altered material/microorganism interaction in space, with respect to matched ground controls.
Different topographic structures were assessed to provide further insight into this aspect (topographical patters with periodicities, same size, as the microbial size).

The Space Biofilms project, performed at the International Space Station, contributes to the understanding of microbial communities in space by characterizing the morphology and gene expression of bacterial and fungal biofilms formed in microgravity with respect to ground controls.
The project has two big branches, the bacterial and the fungal side.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa was used as model organism for the bacterial side and both morphology and transcriptomic (selected samples) studies were performed with bacterial samples, while Penicillium rubens was used as model organism for the fungal side and a morphology study was performed for fungal samples.

Bacterial biofilm formation was characterized at one, two, and three days of incubation (37°C) over six different materials: stainless steel 316, passivated stainless steel 316, a lubricant impregnated surface (LIS), catheter grade silicone with and without a linear microtopography, and cellulose membrane.

Fungal biofilm formation (mold) was characterized at 10, 15, and 20 days of incubation (25°C) over seven different materials: stainless steel 316, aluminum alloy (Al6061), titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V), quartz, catheter grade silicone, carbon fiber, and a superhydrophobic surface “nanograss”.
Bacterial samples: 144 flight and 144 ground samples were prepared for the Space Biofilms bacterial experiment.

The experiment independent variables were two gravitational regimes (Earth gravity and microgravity), three incubation times (1, 2, and 3 days), six material-media combinations (LBK media was used for samples grown over SS316, pSS316, and LIS; while mAUMg-hi Pi media was used for samples grown over cellulose, silicone, and silicone DLIP), two types of fixative/preservative (PFA and RNAlater), and replicates (four).
To provide the necessary levels of containment, each sample was prepared in a Fluid Processing Apparatus (FPA) and eight FPAs were integrated into a Group Activation Pack (GAP).
Once in microgravity, samples were activated by introducing the bacterial inoculum into the sterile medium and placing the samples at 37°C for the corresponding incubation time.
After the incubation time the samples were terminated by introducing the fixative (for morphology samples) or the preservative (for transcriptomic samples).
The morphology samples were stained (one dye for lipids and one dye for nucleic acids) and imaged with a confocal microscope.
The resulting 3D images of the biofilms (.nd2 files) were processed and analyzed using the COMSTAT2 software to quantify biofilm mass, biofilm thickness, and biofilm surface area coverage.
The transcriptomic samples had their RNA extracted and sequenced.
The resulting transcriptomic data files (fastq files) were processed and used for gene expression analysis using DeSeq2.

For more information on the bacterial sample preparation see section 4, and for information about the experiment performance in space see section 5 of the following paper: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actaastro.2022.07.015 For more information on the bacterial morphology and transcriptomic analyses see the Methods section of the following paper: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41526-023-00316-w Fungal samples: 288 flight and 288 ground samples were prepared for the Space Biofilms fungal experiment.

The experiment independent variables were two gravitational regimes (Earth gravity and microgravity), three incubation times (10, 15, and 20 days), seven material substratum (stainless steel 316, aluminum alloy Al6061, titanium alloy Ti-6Al-4V, quartz, catheter grade silicone, carbon fiber, and a superhydrophobic surface “nanograss”), two types of fixative/preservative (PFA and RNAlater), and replicates (6-12 depending on the specific set).
To provide the necessary levels of containment, each sample was prepared in a well of a 24-well plate and sealed with a gas permeable membrane.
Additionally, four 24-well plates were integrated into a Plate Habitat (PHAB).
Once in microgravity, samples were activated by wetting pads inside the PHAB to increase the environment humidity and by placing the samples at 25°C for the corresponding incubation time.

After the incubation time the samples were terminated by introducing the fixative (for morphology samples) or the preservative (for transcriptomic samples)*. *The transcriptomic samples were not analyzed as part of this project.
The morphology samples were stained (one dye for chitin and one dye for extracellular matrix proteins) and imaged with a confocal microscope.
The resulting 3D images of the biofilms (.nd2 files) were processed and analyzed using the COMSTAT2 software to quantify biofilm mass, biofilm thickness, and biofilm surface area coverage.

For more information on the bacterial sample preparation, the experiment performance in space, and the fungal morphology analyses see section 2 of the following paper:- https://doi.org/10.3390/life13041001

It is hypothesized that, in comparison to matched ground controls: a) Biofilm mass and thickness in microgravity will be increased for all bacterial and fungal species, growth medium, and substratum material; b) Gene expression will vary as a function of growth medium, substratum material, and gravitational regime; c) A systematic increase in expression of the genes that confer microorganisms with oxidative, acidity, and antimicrobial resistance will be observed in space (becoming more pronounced with time in space); and d) The formation of the “column-and- canopy” bacterial biofilm architecture and the material/microorganism interaction mechanisms in space will vary from one microbial species and material to the other, and will be associated with the differential expression of specific genes.

Furthermore, due to our proposed approach, the knowledge derived from this project may be translatable to biofilm-associated illnesses on Earth.

Electrically Driven Liquid Film Flow Boiling in the Absence of Gravity

a-Provide fundamental understanding of the combined electrically driven (based on EHD conduction phenomenon) liquid film flow and dielectroporetic vapor extraction mechanism in the presence of phase change (liquid to vapor) in the absence of gravity.

b-Provide a phenomenological foundation for the future development of electric field based two phase thermal management systems, leveraging EHD engineering advantages to develop systems of arbitrary mass flow requirements and geometries.
As vapor bubbles cover the surface and grow or coalesce, the modes of heat transfer will be limited to conduction and possibly radiation.
To avoid this and to enable boiling to take place, EHD-driven liquid film will be fed from the condenser section towards the heater.
The inertia of liquid film flow along with DEP extraction force will repel vapor bubbles that have formed on the heater surface.
In order to study the competing effects of flow inertia/DEP extraction force vs. bubble behavior in zero gravity, one needs to understand EHD generated liquid film flow and the DEP mechanism.
The flow inertia is a function of applied EHD potential, electrode design, liquid film thickness and working fluid properties.
The DEP extraction force is also a function of its corresponding electrode design, the spacing between its electrode and heated surface, and the applied potential for a given working fluid.

Thus, the controlling parameters for this study are applied EHD conduction pumping potential, applied DEP potential, heat flux, and liquid film height for the selected working fluid and electrode designs.
The electrode designs for EHD conduction pumping and DEP mechanism are based on our previous numerical and experimental work.
Therefore, the electrode dimensions, design or distance from the heater surface will not need to be varied during this study.

Boiling is not acceptable in the absence of gravity unless the generated vapor bubbles can be expelled from the boiling surface and fresh liquid can be pumped onto the hot surface through some mechanism.

EHD conduction pumping has the capability of pumping thin liquid films toward the heat source where the boiling takes place, with sufficient inertia to begin expelling bubbles from the heated surface at low heat fluxes.
Furthermore, applying an EHD Dielectrophoretic (DEP) extraction force near the boiling surface guarantees the repulsion of vapor bubbles away from the heated surface even at high heat fluxes.
Finally, the combined EHD driven liquid film flow boiling and DEP extraction force are expected to sustain and enhance the critical heat flux in the absence of gravity.
Combining EHD conduction and DEP effects is therefore critical to the success of the ISS experiment.

This multi-physics proposal will provide basic scientific understanding about competing physical phenomena of flow inertia and bubble dynamics in electrically driven liquid film flow boiling in the presence of electric bubble extraction force (i.e., dielectrophoretic force) in microgravity.

The electrically driven liquid film flow boiling data aboard ISS will determine the critical heat flux, onset of boiling, absence of hysteresis, and bubble characteristics in the absence of gravity.There are a number of potential terrestrial and space applications for this electrohydrodynamic (EHD) driven two-phase heat transport device in all scales (from macro-scale to truly micro-scales).
For example, this device can be used to effectively remove heat from electronics in micro- and zero-gravity environment for NASA's future space stations and long term missions.

It can also be used in satellites (e.g., embedded system into satellite's multi-functional structure).Terrestrially, it can be used in high intensity electronics cooling as well as in various phase change devices.

To achieve these applications, the basic scientific understanding about competing physical phenomena of flow inertia and bubble dynamics in electrically driven liquid film flow boiling in the presence of electric bubble extraction force (i.e.,dielectrophoretic force) in microgravity is needed.

Growth of Large, Perfect Protein Crystals for Neutron Crystallography
The Perfect Crystals investigation uses microgravity environment on the International Space Station to grow crystals of human manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD).
This sheds light on how the antioxidant protein helps protect the human body from oxidizing radiation and oxides created as a byproduct of metabolism.
For best results, the analysis technique requires large crystals with minimal imperfections, which are more easily produced in the microgravity environment of the space station.

The Growth of Large, Perfect Protein Crystals for Neutron Crystallography investigation grows perfect, large-volume crystal suitable for neutron macromolecular crystallography of large unit cell protein crystals in microgravity.

The protein of study in this investigation is human manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD or SOD2), which has an enzymatic mechanism that relies on a proton shuttling pattern that has yet to be fully elucidated.

Neutron macromolecular crystallography allows for visualization of protons that cannot be achieved by XRay Diffraction or Cryo-EM, but requires large-volume crystals minimal imperfection for best results.
Gravity has been implicated as a cause of defects in crystals grown on Earth.

The marriage of the liquid-liquid capillary diffusion crystal growth technique to the microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) allows for the growth of multiple greater than 1 mm3 crystals with very few defects.
Please refer to AccessingPerfectCrystalData.pdf under the Science Documents section.
In 2001, the Borgstahl laboratory successfully grew large crystals of SOD using microgravity conditions on the International Space Station (ISS).

Using existing crystallization hardware that uses the Granada Crystallization Boxes (GCB) for capillary counter diffusion protocols will be used to achieve microgravity crystallization results for SOD.

The principal outcome will be to identify the role of hydrogen atoms in enzymatic activity, discern superoxide from peroxide, and water from hydroxide ion by their protonation state and decipher a structure-based mechanism for human MnSOD more precisely than from previous X-ray crystallographic models determined from Earth-grown crystals.
Manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) is implicated in a number of human diseases, including non-Hodgkins lymphoma, lung cancer and colorectal cancer.
Understanding how it works is an important step toward developing better prevention and treatment methods for such diseases.
In space application, MnSOD could help researchers protect astronauts on future long-term missions.
Astronauts receive significantly more exposure to oxidizing radiation than people on Earth, and on long journeys such as to Mars may receive dangerous doses that create Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS).
These can damage DNA and other biomolecules, causing diseases such as cancer.
The manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) enzyme converts ROS into molecular oxygen and hydrogen peroxide, which other enzymes can then break down.
Studies on MnSOD can help researchers can develop artificial techniques to reduce ROS and help protect astronauts on future long-term missions.

Advanced Colloids Experiment- Microscopy
The ACE-M1 investigation aims to study the behavior of microscopic particles in colloidal mixtures such as gels and creams.
Objectives include the study of the physics of colloidal coarsening and the role of polydispersity (variation in particle size) in determining the stability of colloidal systems.
Previous Earth-based experiments show that polydispersity dramatically affects the time it takes for these gels to collapse.
The imaging goal was to observe crystallites and resolve particle centroid positions with less than 20% error.
The ACE-M1 investigation utilized a Sample Cartridge disk with 10 Sample Wells for 10 samples.
Samples were colloidal fluids of small and large particles in varying concentration over .5 to 2.0 mg/ml.
Protocols included Homogenization and microscopic Observation and Imaging.
A crew member used magnetic stir bars embedded in the sample well to homogenized each sample.

Fluorescent microscopy and Imaging of the colloidal crystallites in each well as they developed over time allowed observation of particle movements and interactions to characterize and quantify rates of growth of structures formed.
Polydispersity significantly affects the time scale and dynamics of coarsening.

It is believed that polydispersity can lead to a substantial difference in the collapse time of weak gels, and understanding this effect in a microgravity environment can provide critical insights into product design and stability.
Space Benefits: By conducting colloidal research in microgravity, the ACE-M1 experiment can obtain clearer data on the dynamics of liquid mixtures, free from the effects of gravitational forces.
This research can improve the manufacturing processes for creating new, longer-lasting products for use both in space and on Earth.
Earth Benefits: Understanding the behavior of colloidal mixtures and the coarsening process can help materials scientists design products with longer shelf lives.

This has significant implications for a wide range of products, including food, medicine, cosmetics, gels, and cleaning solutions, potentially leading to reduced waste and enhanced product performance​.

Advanced Colloids Experiment-Microscopy 2 Reflight
Sometimes its hard to tell a gas from a liquid.
ACE-M2R observes the microscopic behavior of liquids and gases separating from each other.

The investigation examines the behavior of model (colloid rich) liquids and model (colloid poor) gases near the critical point, or the point at which there is no distinct boundary between the two phases.
ACE-M2R uses a new microscope to record micro-scale events on short time scales, while previous experiments observed large-scale behavior over many weeks.

Liquids and gases of the same material usually have different densities, so they would behave differently under the influence of gravity, making the microgravity environment of the International Space Station ideal for these experiments.
This investigation is a re-flight of the original ACE-M2 with the intent to resolve issues from the original flight.
The ACE-M2 investigation utilized 2 Sample Modules (1 is duplicate for back-up) with 15 Sample Wells each for a total of 30 samples, 15 flight and 15 slight identical for back-up.
Samples were colloidal fluids varying concentrations of two different types of fluorescent dye and particle size; large and small.
Magnetic stir bars embedded in each sample well were used to homogenized each sample.

Fluorescent microscopy and Imaging of the colloidal crystallites in each well as they developed over time allowed observation of particle movements and interactions to characterize and quantify rates of growth of structures formed.
Near the critical point, variations in density and effective temperature will significantly influence particle interactions, leading to observable changes in phase stability and transition behavior.
These changes are expected to reveal underlying mechanisms governing critical phenomena in colloidal systems, enhancing the predictability of particle dynamics in similar environments.

Space Applications: On Earth, gravity plays a big role in how liquids and gases interact: The heavier liquid phase settles beneath a lighter gas phase, and these differences in density enable easy separation.
But the flow and behavior of complex fluids and phase separation where there is little or no gravity is not well understood.
A greater understanding of liquid-gas interaction in microgravity could benefit a wide range of fluid storage, transport and processing systems for future spacecraft.

Earth Applications: Particle separation and behavior in liquids, gels, and creams is important for developing consumer and household products, which are worth billions of dollars annually to the U.S. economy.

Many consumer products are complex fluids, combining microscopic particles in gel or liquid, which are similar to the model colloidal system used in the ACE investigations which give insight into product formulations that could be used to maximize stability and shelf life.

Advanced Colloids Experiment - Temperature 1

The ACE-T1 investigation seeks to answer fundamental questions about behaviors of colloids, helping scientists to understand how to control, change, and even reverse interactions between tiny particles.
The objective is to build a fundamental understanding of the behavior of antisotropic (directionally dependent) Janus particles and their 3D self-assembly in microgravity.

For decades, important advances have been reported in the literature regarding the effects of directionally dependent particles, both the chemical and morphological aspects, that provide the potential to extend the complexity of the self-assembled structures.
The ACE-T1 investigation was executed in 2 phases and utilized 3 Sample Modules (SM), each having 3 temperature controlled capillary cells with 20 ml sample fluid each.

The scanner allowed 30 frames per second of confocal images to be taken by the CCD camera.
A sample’s 3D crystal structure was reconstructed by assembling individual slices with an image analysis program, from which colloidal growth, structure, and dynamics can be observed and measured.
To obtain statistically meaningful data, at least ten colloidal structures in one capillary cell was imaged, at least ~400 minutes of observation on each capillary.
Fundamental science and colloidal engineering can be pursued and understood directly at a particle level.

Microscopy enables scientists to directly observe what is happening at a colloid particle level - one no longer requires a theoretical model to hope to connect macroscopic experimental observations to microscopic ones (as when observing experiments at the size scale seen with a photograph taken of a BCAT or PCS sample).
SPACE APPLICATIONS Observing colloidal interactions without the influence of gravity provides new insight into how unhindered particles form network and structures.
Results from ACE-T1 lay a foundation for understanding this mechanism.
Very small scale self-assembly of materials can be an efficient method to build new materials and equipment in space.

This knowledge is crucial for developing self-assembling, self-moving, and self-replicating technologies for use on Earth.
It is anticipated that this novel fabrication approach can be applied to produce novel functional material in various applications such as self-assembly, photonics, diagnostics, and drug-delivery.

Advanced Colloids Experiment - Temperature 6
ACE-T6 studies the microscopic behavior of colloids in gels and creams.
Consumer products are often required to be ‘structured’ by colloidal gels to prevent instability - or bulk separation of dispersed benefit actives.
Benefit actives are generally dispersed as micron-size drops in liquid products to impart a consumer benefit, such as fabric softness.

This leads to a fundamental challenge- how do you preventing bulk separation of the actives (i.e. maintain shelf life) while at the same time maintaining the relative ease-of-flow characteristics of the products.

The objective of ACE-T6 is to use confocal microscopy to study the 3D behavior of microscopic particles in gels and creams, to advance knowledge of the fundamental physics associated with gel coarsening to improve the shelf-life stability of products.
The microgravity environment on ISS was required to detach phase separation from coarsening.
The ACE-T6 investigation utilized a single Sample Module (SM) having 3 temperature controlled capillary cells with 20 ml colloidal sample fluid and each having differing particle concentration.
The capillary cells were situated on the temperature gradient stage (typical range: 20 – 60 °C, 10 °C temperature differential over the full length).
The experiment employed confocal microscopy, which uses a 532-nm frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser, a confocal scanner, and an 8- to 12-bit digital CCD camera.
The scanner allowed 30 frames per second of confocal images to be taken by the CCD camera.
A sample’s 3D crystal structure was reconstructed by assembling individual slices with an image analysis program, from which colloidal growth, structure, and dynamics can be observed and measured.
To obtain statistically meaningful data, at least ten colloidal structures in each capillary was imaged, for at least ~400 minutes of observation on each capillary.
ACE-T6 addresses the effect of polydispersity on coarsening in colloidal systems.
It is hypothesized that polydispersity in the polymer makes order-of-magnitude differences in the time scale of collapse of weak gels.
The investigation attempts to make benchmark microgravity measurements and advance theories that allow a more comprehensive understanding of the role of polydispersity in the coarsening process.
This research will have significant impact in two areas.
First, in the scientific community, there is a large disconnect between microscopic structure and dynamics of these mixtures to the macroscopic changes in the structure which lead to collapse.
This work will significantly enhance the knowledge necessary to advance this important area of science.

Second, understanding this relationship should enable us to anticipate instability in products, directly impacting the development of multi-billion dollar products and initiatives which improve the lives of 4.8 billion people on Earth per day from products originating from Procter and Gamble alone.
Understanding the behavior of mixtures and coarsening can help materials scientists to make colloidal mixtures with longer shelf lives.
This has great potentials in creating a wide range of products from food, medicine, cosmetics, gels, and cleaning solutions which do not expire quickly.

Advanced Colloids Experiment - Temperature 7
The ACE-T7 experiment involves the design and assembly of complex 3D structures from small particles suspended within a fluid medium.
These so-called “self-assembled colloidal structures”, are vital to the design of advanced optical materials and active devices.

The objective of ACE-T7 was to utilize confocal microscopy for time- and space-resolved, 3D imaging of non-spherical colloids whose phases can be controlled by adding depletants and/or adjusting spatial temperature changes around a particular location.
The research goal is to produce cubic colloidal structures, and study the dynamics of crystal nucleation and growth.
ACE-T7 varied the size of the depletant in different samples with the goal of seeing the effect on crystallization.
The imaging goal was to observe crystallites and resolve particle centroid positions with less than 20% error.
The ACE-T7 experiment used the Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) and the Light Microscopy Module (LMM) with enhancements.

ACE-T7 utilized two sample cartridges, each having three temperature-controlled capillaries for a total of six samples; each capillary volume has 50 mm length, 2.0 mm ID width, and 0.2 mm ID height, with automated mixing capabilities using magnetic stir bars embedded in the capillaries.
Each sample volume was about 20 μl.
Each cartridge could be heated or cooled uniformly via Peltier temperature control.

The concentrations of hollow silica microcubes and silica nanoparticle depletants are varied to study the effect that each of these parameters have on the dynamics of crystal nucleation and growth in microgravity.
In total, six capillaries are prepared, numbered C1-C6.

In capillaries C1-C4, the depletant concentration is kept constant at a concentration that produces cubic crystals in a timely manner on Earth (within 1 hour), while the concentration of hollow silica cubes is varied.
In capillaries C5 and C6, the depletant concentration is increased and two different concentration of hollow silica cubes are used.
After homogenization of each sample using the magnetic stirrer, the particles are left undisturbed to crystallize.
Samples were preliminarily observed with a 2.5X objective, followed by measurements with 10X, 63X (air), 63X (oil), and 100X (oil) objectives.
It is hypothesized that under certain conditions, the particles should self-organize into crystals with simple cubic symmetry, which is set by the size of the nano-size depletant.
Increasing particle number density using a temperature gradient, i.e., thermophoresis, is expected to induce formation of crystallites.
Three-dimensional structures that are impossible to create or reform on earth due to sedimentation issues (high density contrast between particles and fluid) should be observed in microgravity.
Future space exploration may use self-assembly and self-replication to make materials and devices that can repair themselves.

Self-assembly and evolutionarily optimized functional units are key to long-duration space voyages which will require use self-assembly and self-replication to make materials and devices that can repair themselves.

Such materials might include photonic crystals with programmed distributions of defects.
Optical technology utilizing such materials may offer intriguing solutions to unavoidable heat generation and bandwidth limitations facing the computer industry.
The beginning of this process is understanding the basic interactions between micro- and nanoscale particles, and how to control them using external sources such as temperature and light.

Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator
The BRE flight program seeks to establish the burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity ambient in terms of material properties.
The specific flight objectives are as follows.
Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter.
Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures.
NASA - considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen.
Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels.
Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired).
Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.
To accomplish the above objectives, flight experiments are proposed.
Additionally, preliminary flight tests will be performed to verify the experiment operations and for comparison with ground-based tests.
For each test, conditions will be established for the chamber contents, namely choice of diluent, oxygen concentration, and pressure.
Fuel flow will commence followed by ignition.
The flames will initially be observed without varying the fuel flow rate.
Because burner surface temperature and heat flux will vary, this will allow a broad range of conditions to be observed during a single test.
As the surface temperature of the burner increases, and the flame remains steady, a continuous set of data is produced for the flammability map.
Eventually either the flame will extinguish, the surface temperature of the burner will equilibrate, or the temperature limit of the heat flux sensor will be reached.
At this time the fuel flow will be terminated.
So a test should terminate for a given flow rate at extinction, and for continued burning when the burner surface temperature has steadied or the temperature limit of the heat flux sensor is neared.
The extinction limit could be found once the burner temperature has steadied, and the heat flux sensor has not exceeded its limit.
At that state, the flow rate can be reduced in small increments, until extinction is observed and the flow rate shut off.
Again, in this process, new data is being produced for the flammability map.
Ignition limit tests are not proposed for microgravity, but we will explore these under normal gravity.
We believe there is better control on Earth-based ignition testing and that these results should carry over to microgravity conditions.
In addition to the flight experiments, in normal gravity testing will continue.
These tests will involve gaseous, liquid, and solid fuels.
These experiments will further establish the validation of the BRE for 1-g applications and show its usefulness to establish 1-g ignition and extinction limits.
As available, drop facility testing will be used to refine procedures, test instrumentation, and help to establish viable flow conditions.
We will also pursue a CFD model for the quiescent microgravity burning.
This will also guide us in the flight experiments, and potentially provide a predictive methodology.
The BRE investigation hypothesizes that there can exist a regime of quasi-steady burning in microgravity as a function of materials properties.
Steady burning may never be achieved, and only slowly changing unsteady flames are possible.
The proposed tests aboard the ISS aims to query this hypothesis by establishing a range of quasi-steady burning conditions for condensed fuels in the microgravity environment.

It is hypothesized that BRE can determine a range of burning conditions in microgravity as a function of heat of gasification, reradiation heat flux, applied radiant heat flux, heat of combustion and smoke point.
This could enable the Cone Calorimeter (NASA Test 2) test as a basis for establishing flammability maps for real materials.
The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in an inert matrix).
Thus achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity.
Other than a candle flame, this has not been shown before.
BRE yielded important data relevant to spacecraft fire safety.

Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires.

While BRE’s results are still preliminary, they suggest that NASA may want to increase use of its alternative flammability Test 2, with the cone calorimeter, where that test can measure material properties corresponding to the microgravity flames observed with the BRE burner.

In order to provide the experimental data needed to allow rigorous testing of computational models at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum, we have the following objectives: A) Characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, lift-off heights, temperatures and extinction limits.

B) Characterize the sooting tendencies of diffusion flames with long residence times, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, gas temperatures in the soot-free portion of the flame, soot luminosity, soot temperatures, and soot volume fractions.

ACME CLD Flame project goals include the generation of improved computational models with improved soot sub-models that are effective for both dilute flames and sooting flames that vary from low to high soot loading levels.
The enhanced time and spatial scales in a microgravity environment will be important for achieving both goals.
Experimentally, we plan to study methane and ethylene diffusion flames over a wide range of test conditions.
For the more dilute flames, measurements will be made of flame chemiluminesence of OH* and CH* to observe variations in lift-off height and flame shape as extinction limits are approached.
The sooting tendencies of the more fuel-rich flames will be investigated using soot luminosity and laser extinction measurements to determine soot temperatures and soot volume fractions.
Flame temperatures in non-sooting regions will be measured using thin-filament pyrometry.
Based on observations, modifications can be made to the kinetics and soot model to match better the experimental results.

If the overall agreement of the measurements and computations is good, the results of the computations can be “mined” to provide insight on species (and hence chemical processes) that cannot be measured directly using the diagnostics available for the proposed experiment.

Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices.

The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in such systems is critical in the modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which soot formation and radiative transfer take place.
In addition, an understanding of those factors that affect flame extinction in diffusion flames is critical in the suppression of fires and in improving engine efficiency.

While normal gravity combustion studies can provide important information on combustion processes, the effects of gravitational forces often complicate the interpretation of both computational and experimental results.
Momentum effects dominate most practical combustion devices, but the contribution of buoyancy forces is hard to eliminate in normal gravity.
A goal of the study will be to apply sophisticated numerical tools and quantitative diagnostic techniques to the study of hydrocarbon diffusion flames in a microgravity environment.
This will lead to a more detailed understanding of the interaction of convection, diffusion and chemistry under momentum-dominated conditions.

Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames

The objective of this investigation is to better understand the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current, analyze the dynamic response of flames to electric field changes, evaluate soot formation, and characterize stabilized near-limit lifted flames.
The E-FIELD flames experiment investigates how electric fields influence the behavior of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity.
This unique environment is ideal for isolating electric field effects from buoyancy forces.
The experiment is conducted with gas-fueled flames, both with and without a coflow of air.
In the former case, the tests are conducted using the same coflow burner used by the Coflow Laminar Diffusion (CLD) Flame experiment.
An electric field is generated by creating a high voltage (up to 10 kV) differential between the burner and a flat circular mesh suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner.
Measurements, as a function of the field strength and fuel, are taken of the ion current through the flame and the flame’s response time to electric forcing.

The gas-jet burner is used to create a small, focused flame for detailed ion-driven convection studies while the coflow burner surrounds the fuel jet with a weak synthetic air flow to enable flame stability and soot behavior analysis.
A high-voltage copper mesh electrode positioned above the burner tip generated an electric field with controlled polarity and strength.
The electric field interacts with ions generated through chemi-ionization during combustion, driving ion-driving convection and influencing flame behavior.
Methane and ethylene were used as fuels and diluted with nitrogen to control flame strength.
Dilution levels were varied to explore a range of combustion dynamics, from highly stable to near-extinction flames.
Voltage-current curves were recorded to assess the relationship between electric field strength and chemi-ion current, revealing ion-driven convection effects.
High-resolution cameras captured flame shape, luminosity, and soot distribution.
Spectral imaging with filters measures chemiluminescent emissions and soot volume fraction.
There were thermopile detectors to measure flame radiant emissions.
All experiments were conducted in the combustion integrated rack (CIR).
Tests were administered with Glenn Research Center (GRC) directing astronaut actions.
Parameters such as fuel flow rate, coflow velocity, and field polarity are were varied to isolate specific effects on ion production, flame stability, and soot behavior.

The application of electric fields in microgravity environments will significantly influence laminar diffusion flames by enabling precise manipulation of flame stability, soot behavior, and combustion dynamics through ion-driven convection and chemi-ionization processes.

The E-FIELD Flames research is not being conducted to serve any space applications, but it is possible that its findings could aid the development of future space-based combustion devices (e.g., for solid waste processing).
The use of electric fields to control flames can reduce the production of harmful pollutants in practical terrestrial combustion.
The combustion of fossil fuel is the primary human source of greenhouse gas and acid rain and furthermore creates soot, which can be beneficial but is also a health hazard.
Combustion using electrical fields may also allow for more efficient combustion, reducing fuel consumption in addition to unwanted emissions.

A series of experiments is proposed with the following specific objectives, in both soot-free and sooty flames, to compare with detailed computational simulation to assess transport properties and detailed chemical kinetics (including chemiluminescence): Objective A.

Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species distribution) of diffusion flames established at initially non-steady, spherical flame structures for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates.
Objective B.

Determine the quasi-steady convective/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (low system Damköhler numbers) and radiative/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (high system Damköhler numbers) for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty).
Objective C.

Determine the existence (for different Zeldovich number, Ze), onset (as a function Da), and nature (i.e. mode, frequency, amplitude) of pulsating instabilities theoretically predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number.

A series of experiments is proposed in which mixtures of various gaseous fuels and diluents will be issued into an oxidizing environment through a spherical porous burner and ignited to obtain, nominally, a spherical, one-dimensional stabilized flame.

Synchronized measurements are to be made including spectrally resolved images, flame and burner temperatures, radiative flux measurements, and system operating conditions (including reactant flow rates, ambient temperatures, pressures and acceleration levels, etc.).
These data are to be used for comparisons of flame behavior and structure with detailed numerical simulations of the flames.
Conventional gaseous fuels including hydrogen, methane, and ethylene will be used.
Hydrogen is the simplest fuel and its reaction mechanism is also reasonably established.
Methane is the simplest hydrocarbon and extensive studies have been conducted on its combustion chemistry.
Ethylene is a typical sooty fuel and is also an important intermediate for the oxidation of higher hydrocarbons.
Diluents mixed with fuel are to include nitrogen and helium to adjust mixture diffusivities, and carbon dioxide to influence flame radiation characteristics.
The transient numerical simulation of spherical flames developed as part of this program includes detailed chemistry and transport models, especially radiation mechanisms.

Each description of the flames obtained from the experiment, including measurements of aspects of the flame structure, growth or flame front velocities, and the specific test conditions where steady state flames, flame extinctions, flame front instabilities, soot suppression limits, etc., comprise a rigorous test of the detailed model.
Together they provide a measure of the comprehensiveness of the chemical kinetic and transport models.

The numerical simulation is also being used as a predictive tool to develop the science requirements for this experiment, especially the collection of test conditions and most aspects of the measurement systems.

Due to time and g-jitter limitations, little of the planned test matrix can be adequately explored in the ground based test facilities, and the flight experiment definition will rely on the best effort in the modeling work.
The impact of this work consists of both practical and fundamental aspects.

Practically, with diffusion flame burning as the basis in many combustion engines and devices, understanding the underlying dynamics and chemistry of diffusion flames is important in improving performance in terms of power, efficiency, pollutant emissions, and reliability.

Fundamentally, the unique buoyancy-free environment offered by microgravity affords simple aerodynamic flow fields to acquire diffusion flame data of high fidelity, with the prospect of understanding unit thermochemical processes as well as quantifying the associated physico-chemical parameters.

The three primary science objectives are to measure the initial on-orbit thermal performance, to measure long duration thermal performance, and to assess any lifetime degradation.
Flight data will be used to validate microgravity portions of an OHP operating limits model recently published by members of the team.
Returned flight experiment hardware will be subjected to post-flight testing to assess the presence of any non-condensable gas that may have formed on orbit.

Microgravity influence on fluid flow, especially two-phase flow, is significantly different than in a terrestrial environment.

Potentially shift the way NASA designs its future deep space craft and extraterrestrial human habitats, providing safer, more reliable temperature regulation for the human occupants and the sensitive technology housed inside Cooling electronics.

BASS-II results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth.

1) Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity.
