To summarize, BASS-II's approach, microgravity combustion tests were performed aboard the International Space Station.
Active crew support for real-time “lab partner” operations.
The wind tunnel was installed in the Microgravity Science Glovebox which supplied power, imaging, and a level of containment.
Fuel samples were mounted inside a small wind tunnel which could impose airflow speeds up to 40 cm/s.
Main variables are airflow speed and oxygen concentration (oxygen varied below 21% by adding nitrogen).
Flame appearance, flame growth, and spread rates were determined in both the opposed and concurrent flow.

BASS–II tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, O2 concentration, temperature, etc.).

NASA tests and controls materials from a flammability perspective using an upward burning test in normal gravity, which is considered to be the worst-case geometry for flammability of the material on Earth.

Testing at constant O2 mole fractions permits studying flame spread and extinction at low and high flow speed.
We are interested in finding the fundamental limit for a given material.
A primary goal of BASS-II is improved spacecraft fire safety, improved understanding of combustion in space and how to avoid it.
If you’re on a mission far from Earth, a fire can be catastrophic.
BASS-II helps engineers select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods on future space missions.

This simpler combustion process enables researchers to evaluate computer models of fuel burning.

The two main objectives for BASS are to:
1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity.
The relation between these can be investigated by observing flames burning for the longer times available in flight.

Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).
2.) Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow.
The experiment was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Glove Box (MSG).
Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) measuring were used as a fuel source as well as Nomex fabric and Ultem.
A Kanthal wire (29-gage)igniter was used to initiate combustion at one end of the fabric.
Airflow was controlled using a variable speed fan, with airflow speeds reaching as high as 40 cm/s.
The airflow was directed along the fuel surface in either the opposed or concurrent direction.
This investigation explored two primary air flow configurations; concurrent-flow and opposed-flow.
With concurrent-flow air flows in the same direction as the flame spread and in opposed-flow air flows in the opposite direction of flame spread.
Flames were observed in the top and edge profiles and data was collected on flame size, shape, color, spread rate, and potential flame quenching.
The samples were placed in a small flow duct (76 mm x 76 mm cross section) that allowed for airflow across the fabric.
Other sample shapes were utilized as well including spheres and cylinders.

BASS experiments were based on the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature, etc.) To test this hypothesis with any but the thinnest materials requires extended microgravity time – longer than available in drop towers or parabolic aircraft.
Current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on a standard test method (NASA–STD–6001 Test 1) that segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects.
A critical element of this understanding is the radiative heat emission from the flame.

These results are used in first order models and predictions of heat release in spacecraft fires and as a means to extend heat release data from tests like the NASA cone calorimeter test (NASA–STD–6001 Test 2) to a performance-based material selection process.
Using nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques.
BASS results provide essential guidance to ground-based microgravity combustion research efforts.
Detailed combustion models are validated using the simpler flow environment afforded by tests in microgravity.
Once validated, they can be used to build more complex combustion models needed to capture the important details of flames burning in normal gravity.
These models have wide applicability to the general understanding of many terrestrial combustion problems and will guide novel spacecraft design and ensure the safety of future crewed missions.

Binary Colloidal Alloy Test - 3

The BCAT-3 investigation aimed to exploit the long range ordered structures formed using the self-assembly of colloidal particles and demonstrate the use of colloid engineering to synthesize new materials with novel properties.

The goal was to use a mixture of two different materials or binary alloys to greatly increase the flexibility of the resultant colloidal structures and qualitatively study the phase behavior and crystallization properties of these binary alloys.

In addition, the investigation proposed to study the properties of mixtures of colloids and polymers where the addition of the polymer induces weak attractive interactions between the colloidal particles by the depletion mechanism, leading to a rich phase behavior for the colloidal particles.
BCAT-3 is implemented in a bench-top investigation which is set up on the Maintenance Work Area (MWA) on ISS.
The samples are contained within a Fluids Module (FM) which held 10 samples in couvettes in individual wells.
The ten samples in BCAT-3 were selected as part of three separate experiments examining different physical processes: critical point, binary alloys, and surface crystallization.
The samples were manually homogenized using a stir-bar (a Teflon coated mixing magnet) inside each couvette.
Samples are mixed, examined and imaged using a digital EarthKAM camera, to document the separation of colloid and liquid components and the formation of colloidal crystals over time.

Colloidal particles would exhibit behaviors analogous to atoms, allowing the study of phase transitions, crystallization, and self-organization without the interference of sedimentation and convection present on Earth.

This investigation hypothesizes that by taking advantage of microgravity and avoiding sedimentation binary alloys with very different materials and sizes and by addition of polymers particles to induce attractive forces can lead to exciting and promising form of colloidal engineering to synthesize a new class of materials.

Self-assembly of micron and submicron colloidal particles into highly ordered three-dimensional structures offers an alternative to traditional lithographic techniques, which are often limited to surface-level patterning.

These ordered arrays of particles can exhibit novel optical properties, such as redirecting light via diffraction or altering local photon densities, enabling the creation of advanced optical filters, switches, and sensors.
Moreover, these structures can serve as templates for macroporous materials, which have diverse chemical applications, including catalysis, separation media, and biomaterials.

Precision macroporous ceramics and polymers can also be used as lightweight insulators, chromatographic materials, and catalytic supports, offering transformative solutions across industries such as energy, manufacturing, and medicine.

Cold Atom Lab - Microgravity Dynamics of Bubble-Geometry Bose-Einstein Condensates

Microgravity Dynamics of Bubble-geometry Bose-Einstein Condensates (Cold Atom Lab - BEC Bubble Dynamics) aims to study Bose-Einstein Condensates (BECs) and degenerate Fermi gases (DFGs) confined to a the surface of an experimentally-controlled topologically-connected ''bubble.'' The limitations of gravitational sag have prevented terrestrial exploration of a quantum gas confined to such as surface.
This investigation aims to test fundamental ideas in quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics, and strongly-correlated many-body physics in condensed matter.
Studying the behavior of quantum gas bubbles could provide insights for next-generation quantum sensors and simulators.
This investigation uses rubidium (87 Rb) and potassium (39K and 41K) samples in the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) aboard the International Space Station (ISS).
The approach for the investigation comprises two main aspects: the creation of ultracold atomic gases and the subsequent manipulation and probing of these gases to study systematic mitigations.

Creation of Ultracold Atomic Gas: Laser Cooling: Atoms are released into a vacuum chamber and collected into a magneto-optical trap (MOT), where they are initially cooled using laser cooling techniques.

This technique cools the sample by essentially ‘pushing’ the laser against the motion of the atoms effectively lowering the momentum, and therefore the velocity, kinetic energy, and temperature, of the sample.
This is followed by a brief stage of “optical molasses” during which the quadrupole magnetic field is turned off and the laser frequency is further detuned.
State Preparation: The sample is optically pumped to a low magnetic field-seeking quantum state.

The state is then subjected to an intermediate quadrupole magnetic field which allows for the transferred from the MOT, located at the bottom of the science region, to an atom-chip-based trap, located at the top of the science region.
Evaporative Cooling: The atoms undergo evaporative cooling to below the critical temperature, leading to the formation of a Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC).
Evaporative cooling cools the sample by removing the highest-energy atom from the trap so that the remaining atoms re-thermalize at progressively lower temperatures.
Decompression and Release: The atom trap is slightly relaxed to further cool the atoms, eventually releasing them completely to allow free expansion.
At this point, investigators can search for the primary signatures of a BECs for confirmation that one was formed.

Formation of a BEC is typically associated with the behavior of the velocity distribution, such as the presence of a narrow peak centered at near zero velocity and the low velocity peak growing (greater fraction of atoms in this domain) as the temperature decreases.
Manipulation and Probing: Probing Techniques: The ultracold gas is probed using laser, radiofrequency, and/or microwave pulses.
These techniques are designed to investigate the pairwise interactions and molecular dynamics crucial for mitigating systematics in high-precision measurements.
Time-of-Flight Imaging: After a predetermined time of flight, the sample is imaged using absorption imaging techniques.
This process involves taking two images: one of the sample and a reference image post-destruction of the sample.
As implied, this is the end of the experimental cycle for this specific BEC as the measurement process destroys the sample.
The manipulation and probing aspect is particularly important for this specific investigation as the ultracold atomic gas must be treated with certain fields to achieve the bubble topology.

To do this, a locally harmonic spin-dependent trapping potential originating from inside an applied magnetic field is combined with a near-resonance oscillatory magnetic field with a certain radiofrequency.
Together these two magnetic fields produce atoms in spatially dependent dressed atomic states that experience dressed or adiabatic dressed potentials.
These potentials can then be manipulated via tuning the radiofrequency field so that the atoms take on an ellipsoid or bubble-like geometry.

This investigation hypothesizes that radiofrequency dressing can be used to create a trap formed by a spherical or ellipsoidal shell structure capable of confining quantum gases to a “bubble” topology.

Due to gravitational sag and trap distortion present in terrestrial experiments this trap topology has not been explored, and further, it is only able to be explored in the microgravity environment unique to the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL).
The low-energy excitations of such systems, as well as various theories on the physics of phase transitions will be investigated using this bubble-geometry.

This work, while focused on the fundamental physics of ultracold atoms and not directly connected to human life, has a similar impact to life on Earth as that of all fundamental physics; it broadens our understanding of the physical world and helps us further cement our collective picture of quantum mechanics as ''the way the world works.'' It explores the limits of how large Bose-Einstein condensates can be made, and to what extent the gravity-well of terrestrial labs render certain investigations difficult or impossible.

The observations made aboard CAL through this project are a clear demonstration that physical insight can sometimes require microgravity facilities to be fully developed, and that space borne atomic physics experiments can be valuable contributions to our collective scientific efforts.
Additionally, insight into fundamental laws of quantum mechanics can have many applications in many on Earth.

Quantum computers continue to exponentially accelerate as a field of study and in industry, and research into these fundamentals can support scientific workforce development, public science outreach and research and development.

The Consortium for Ultracold Atoms in Space (CUAS), led by Nicholas Bigelow, conducted groundbreaking experiments in atomic clocks, atom interferometry, and quantum gases, with a strong focus on the application of these quantum technologies in space environments.

The consortium's research was guided by the objectives outlined in the National Research Council (NRC) report and NASA's Research Announcement (NRA), particularly in precision measurement and quantum gas studies.

The Consortium fostered a collaborative approach, bringing together scientists from top institutions like MIT, Stanford, Berkeley, and Harvard, as well as international partners such as those from the DLR (German Space Agency).
This collaboration allowed the group to pool expertise, regularly refine their goals, and push forward only the most promising space experiments.
The procedure for the creation of an ultracold gas is fairly standardized.
The atoms are released into a vacuum chamber, collected into a magneto-optical trap (MOT), and cooled via laser cooling.
The sample is then optically pumped to a low magnetic field seeking quantum state and transfer from the MOT to an atom-chip based trap.
The atoms are then evaporatively cooled to below the critical temperature so that a Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC) begins to form.
The atom trap is slightly relaxed to further cool the atoms, and eventually the atoms are completely released from the trap and allowed to expand freely.
At this point, the ultracold gas is probed using laser, radiofrequency, and/or microwave pulses.
After a prespecified time of flight, the sample is imaged using absorption imaging techniques.
This is the end of the experimental cycle for this specific BEC because the measurement process destroys the sample.
A total of two images are taken, the first being an image of the sample and the second being a reference image that is taken after the destructive absorption imaging process.
This general process was followed by the Consortium for experiments requiring the production or probing of ultracold quantum gases.
In their work on atom interferometry, the Consortium conducted experiments to detect dark-energy scalar fields with unprecedented sensitivity.
The team also focused on measuring the fine structure constant with high accuracy, which involved overcoming systematic effects that could be amplified in the space environment.

Collaborations with the Bose-Einstein Condensate and Cold Atom Laboratory (BECCAL) science definition team and other international partners were essential for demonstrating long coherence times in microgravity, testing the equivalence principle, and searching for dark-energy candidates.

These experiments were conducted with a focus on utilizing the microgravity conditions available aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and other space-based platforms, which provided a unique environment to achieve results unattainable on Earth.

In the realm of atomic clocks and quantum sensors, the Consortium developed new configurations for optical lattice clocks and achieved precision at the 19th decimal place, setting a new record for stable laser performance with a linewidth of 10 mHz.
These experiments were designed to improve the accuracy of space-based timekeeping and navigation systems, which are critical for the success of space missions.
The Consortium also explored innovative cooling methods, such as direct optical cooling to achieve Bose-Einstein condensation, which simplified the setup for quantum experiments in space.
These methods were tested and refined in microgravity environments, demonstrating their potential to enhance the performance of quantum technologies in space.

Overall, the Consortium’s approach to conducting experiments was characterized by a strong emphasis on leveraging the unique conditions of space, particularly microgravity, to achieve results that would be impossible on Earth.

Their collaborative efforts, cutting-edge experimental designs, and focus on precision allowed them to make significant contributions to the field of quantum technologies in space, laying the groundwork for future space missions and advancing our understanding of fundamental physics.

This consortium aims to provide a space for the world’s experts on Bose-Einstein Condensates (BEC), atom optics, atom interferometry, and related quantum realms to push the current boundaries of quantum gas and atomic physics space experiments.

It is hypothesized that with the realization of a space atom laser and precision atomic interferometry there is potential for significant scientific advancement by testing the equivalence principle with quantum test masses and pushing the limits of the standard model.
A space atom laser is expected to provide truly novel investigations of the wave-like nature of matter.

Varied experiments and manipulation of quantum gases (both single-species and dual-species) including deep cooling, condensate mixture phases, and precision motional control are hypothesized to mature the technology of quantum gases and provide first of its kind opportunity to investigate interacting quantum gases in space.
Significant progress has been made on atomic interferometry and atomic clocks in terrestrial experiments.
The work has long-term impact for fundamental science, navigation technologies, and global clock synchronization.
Clocks are vital to navigation, communication, and security.
ATOM INTERFEROMETRY We have pushed atom interferometry for space applications forward in many ways:
We have shown that atom interferometry can detect dark-energy scalar fields with unprecedented sensitivity.
There is a chance to cover all the relevant parameter space so as to detect them or to rule them out once and for all.
This work has been published in Science, Nature Physics, and Physical Review D.
We have demonstrated a theoretically predicted, but never observed, attractive force on atoms from blackbody radiation.
It is an important limitation that has to be taken into account in the design of atomic-physics space missions.

We have pushed forward the accuracy of atom interferometry for measuring the fine structure constant, which has resulted in a measurement of this constant with an accuracy about three times better than the best previous one.
The agreement of this measurement with others sets very strong constraints on hypothesized particles from the dark sector, such as dark photons.
We have developed atom interferometry with lithium atoms, opening up the possibility to do interferometry with a much wider class of atoms than available previously.
We will continue to develop atom interferometry for demonstrating the gravitational Aharonov-Bohm effect, and measuring fundamental constants very precisely.
We will also work with the Bose-Einstein Condensate Cold Atom Laboratory (BECCAL) science definition team and other teams to identify future targets for spaceborne fundamental physics.
The interferometry work has several main thrusts.
In the first thrust, we have been investigating how spaceborne atom interferometry can probe models for dark matter and dark energy.
This has resulted in experimental demonstrations of such tests for so-called chameleon and symmetron models, and theoretical studies on how to make detailed predictions of the putative signals.
In the second thrust, we have developed strategies to overcome systematic effects in atom interferometers that use Bragg diffraction, as the one planned for the Cold Atom lab.
In the third, we have developed specific plans for spaceborne atom interferometry.
We have collaborated with the German team Document for atom interferometry on the Cold Atom Lab and BECCAL.
Plans include demonstrating long coherence times thanks to microgravity, tests of the equivalence principle, and searches for dark-energy candidates.

They have also collaborated with Nan Yu (Jet Propulsion Laboratory-JPL) on a concept study QTEST (Quantum test of the Equivalence Principle and Spacer-Time) for testing the equivalence principle in space.
CLOCKS AND QUANTUM SENSORS TECHNOLOGIES We have demonstrated the first direct optical cooling to Bose-Einstein condensation, without any evaporative cooling.
This has promising impact of simplifying spaceborne experiments.
The Bose-Einstein condensation by direct optical cooling was achieved for small ensembles of ~1000 atom.
We will attempt to make substantially larger condensates with the same method by using a more powerful trapping laser.
We have been working on spin squeezing in the optical-transition clock with trapped ytterbium atoms.

By implementing both frequency and intensity feedback loops for the magical wavelength trap inside an optical cavity, we have now lengthened the trap lifetime for the Yb sample from 200 ms to 2 seconds.
We have also started non-destructive state-dependent measurements for spin squeezing by observing the light transmitted through the cavity, and we can already more than resolve the shot-noise limit.
In the Rb experiment, we are working towards using Rydberg states for increasing the light-atom interaction in cavity QED.
We have frequency-stabilized the control laser coupling the P state to high-lying Rydberg states.
We have demonstrated a new optical lattice clock configuration using a three-dimensional optical lattice, leading to measurement precision in the 19th decimal place.
We have also demonstrated another record-breaking performance on stable lasers, with the narrowest laser linewidth at 10 mHz.

This technique, already demonstrated on the ground, should work better in space and could be useful for future space navigation systems.

This investigation utilizes the atom interferometry equipment aboard the CAL instrument for precision measurement experiments.
The BEC formed according to the steps laid out in the Creation of Ultracold Atomic Gases section is split using an off resonance standing wave laser.
The split waves packets will travel different trajectories, and then recombine after a secondary laser beam is applied.
After the recombination, the atomic interference pattern can be collected.
The flight-based results can be compared to theoretical investigations and ground studies done at JPL, enabling comprehensive understanding and development of systematic mitigation techniques.

This investigation hypothesizes that, combined with the current atomic cooling techniques, the implementation of expansion cooling will produce atoms with temperatures on the order of a trillionth of a degree above absolute zero (10^-12 K).
With the unique settings provided by Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) the maximum expansion and low temperature limits are able to be probed.

Atomic interferometry can be used to measure the acceleration of cold atoms relative to the International Space Station, allowing investigators to explore using ultracold atoms as part of an inertial navigation system.
The development of precision inertial sensing techniques is useful for Earth-based as well as space-based navigation.

Besides using direct sensing for inertial navigation, rotation sensing can also be useful for north-finding while gravity sensing can be used to tabulate local gravity variations and form a type of three-dimensional map for navigating.
These techniques also have many applications in geophysics.
Gravity sensing can be used for oil and mineral exploration, while rotation sensing can detect dynamics in the Earth's core.
Gravity sensing also has defense applications such as locating underground tunnels and potential screening cargo for high-density contraband or weapons.
Other precision measurement applications have less direct impact, but advance scientific knowledge.
For instance, precision tune-out spectroscopy measurements of atomic matrix elements can be used to improve the interpretation of atomic parity violation experiments.
These in turn impact our understanding of the standard model of particle physics and thus the nature of our universe.
Direct benefits of such understanding can be hard to trace, but in general the continued advance of technological applications builds on advances in our fundamental knowledge.

Cold Atom Lab - Fundamental Interactions for Atom Interferometry with Ultracold Quantum Gases in a Microgravity Environment
Precision atom interferometers (AI) in space promise exciting technical capabilities with diverse applications of interest to NASA.

These quantum sensors are particularly relevant for fundamental physics research, with proposals including unprecedented tests of the validity of the weak equivalence principle, precision measurements of the fine structure and gravitational constants, and detection of gravity waves and dark matter/dark energy.

This investigation will utilize the capabilities of NASA's multi-user Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL), in the microgravity environment onboard the International Space Station (ISS), to study mitigation schemes for the leading-order systematics expected to limit future high-precision measurements of fundamental physics with AIs in microgravity.

The flight experiments, supported by theoretical investigations and ground studies at Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), will concentrate on the physics of pairwise interactions and molecular dynamics in ultracold quantum gases as a means to overcome uncontrolled AI shifts associated with the gravity gradient and few-particle collisions.

A space-based dual-species AI will be further developed and used, which is planned as an on-orbit upgrade to the CAL science module after approximately a year of science investigations, for proof-of-principle tests of systematic mitigations and phase-readout techniques for use in the next-generation of precision metrology experiments based on AIs in microgravity.
The proposed studies require the effective position invariance, long free fall times, and extremely low temperature samples uniquely available with the CAL apparatus.
It is anticipated that these studies can lead to the unprecedented level of control and accuracy necessary for AIs to explore some of the most fundamental physical concepts in nature.
Investigation comprises two main aspects: the creation of ultracold atomic gases and the subsequent manipulation and probing of these gases to study systematic mitigations.
For dual-species operations the process is slightly more complicated, especially with the addition of a sympathetic cooling step, however, the general process is fairly standardized.
Creation of Ultracold Atomic Gas:
-Laser Cooling: Atoms are released into a vacuum chamber and collected into a magneto-optical trap (MOT), where they are initially cooled using laser cooling techniques.

This technique cools the sample by essentially ‘pushing’ the laser against the motion of the atoms effectively lowering the momentum, and therefore the velocity, kinetic energy, and temperature, of the sample.

This is followed by brief stages of “compressed MOT”, in which the trapping force of the MOT is increased to compress the gas, and then an “optical molasses” stage, during which the quadrupole magnetic field is turned off and the laser frequency is further detuned to minimize the temperature of the gases.
-State Preparation: The sample is optically pumped to a low magnetic field-seeking quantum state.

The atoms in this state are then subjected to an intermediate quadrupole magnetic field which traps the atoms from the MOT and allows for the transfer from the MOT, located at the bottom of the science region, to an atom-chip-based trap, located at the top of the science region.

-Evaporative Cooling: The atoms undergo forced evaporative cooling, using frequency sweeps of either RF or microwave fields, to bring the gases below the critical temperature, leading to the formation of a Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC).
Evaporative cooling cools the sample by removing the highest-energy atom from the trap so that the remaining atoms re-thermalize at progressively lower temperatures.
-Decompression and Release: The tightness of the atom trap is adiabatically relaxed to further cool the atoms via decompression colling.
After a short hold time in the relaxed trap, the atoms are released by rapidly turning the atom-chip and bias coil currents to zero to allow the atoms to expand in freefall.
At this point, investigators can search for the primary signatures of a BECs for confirmation that one was formed.

Formation of a BEC is typically associated with the behavior of the velocity distribution, such as the presence of a narrow peak centered at near zero velocity and the low velocity peak growing (greater fraction of atoms in this domain) as the temperature decreases.
Manipulation and Probing:
-Probing Techniques: The ultracold gas is probed in freefall using laser, magnetic field, radiofrequency, and/or microwave pulses.

These techniques are designed to establish atoms in the proper state, perform atom interferometry, or establish and investigate the pairwise interactions and molecular dynamics crucial for mitigating systematics in high-precision measurements.
-Time-of-Flight Imaging: After a predetermined time of flight, the sample is imaged using absorption imaging techniques.

This process involves shining resonant light on the atoms and taking two images, per atomic species, of the shadow cast in the light: one of the sample and a reference image post-destruction of the sample.
As implied, this is the end of the experimental cycle for this specific BEC as the measurement process destroys the sample.
This approach is particularly suited for studying mitigation schemes for leading-order systematics that can affect future high-precision measurements with atom interferometers (AIs) in microgravity.

By leveraging the unique microgravity environment provided by NASA’s Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) on the International Space Station, this investigation aims to achieve the level of control and accuracy required for groundbreaking tests of fundamental physics principles, such as the weak equivalence principle, and precision measurements of the fine structure and gravitational constants.
The integration of theoretical investigations and ground studies at JPL supports these flight experiments, enabling comprehensive understanding and development of systematic mitigation techniques.

This investigation hypothesizes that the control of interactions and association/dissociation of weakly-bound molecules in ultracold quantum gases can overcome uncontrolled Atomic Interference (AI) shifts in space which are caused by the gravity gradient and few-particle collisions.
Investigators will interrogate this hypothesis by conducting tests using ultracold quantum gases and exploring Feshbach resonances at new energy regimes.

Investigators expect unprecedented levels of control and accuracy in the AI that will enable exploration of some of the most fundamental physical concepts in nature and open up venues for exploration of novel quantum phases in exotic dynamical regimes.
Our studies are designed to achieve technological advances in precision metrology that can only be realized in the microgravity environment of the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL).

The tools of ultracold atomic and molecular physics are utilized (namely Feshbach resonances) for exquisite control of the differential center-of-mass distributions of the dual-species quantum gases and on methods to use the fundamentals of few-body interactions to maintain coherence in atomic ensembles for enhanced precision sensor capabilities.
Subsequent proof-of-principle studies with the dual-species atom interferometer on CAL will further advance the state of the art for precision interferometry with ultracold matter waves.

The impact of such research to the field of metrology can be seen through its potential to increase precision for atom-interferometry and also the possibility of engineering highly efficient system-specific devices based on the fundamental nature of few-body interactions.

The microgravity environment of the CAL facility strongly favors such explorations and allow for the possibility of uncovering novel effects and quantum phases of matter, a major goal in ultracold quantum gases and other disciplines of fundamental physics.

These studies can benefit life on Earth by providing both fundamental understanding of nature in previously inaccessible environments and energy regimes, and by enhancing the tools available for scientific exploration at the highest precision.

Cold Atom Lab - Zero-G Studies of Few Body and Many-Body Physics
Zero-G Studies of Few-Body and Many-Body Physics (Cold Atom Lab - Few-Body Physics) investigates the dynamics of interacting ultracold atoms under varying conditions.

The dynamics of few-body systems comprised of just three or four atoms can strongly influence the collective behavior of quantum gases and play an important role in development of quantum gas applications.
Modern laser cooling techniques are used to chill atoms to near absolute zero temperatures.
At these temperatures, atoms behave like matter waves, according to the laws of quantum mechanics.
Fully automated data runs, each lasting about one minute, acquire images of ultracold atom clouds under varying conditions.
The acquired data fills a critical need for the development of detailed and precise atomic physics models.
The development of these models is performed in theoretical studies accompanying the data gathering campaigns with the CAL instrument.
Studying the behavior and interaction of few atoms in microgravity could provide important data for developing a precise theory describing quantum gases on a microscopic level.
The knowledge gained in this study also aids in the development of future quantum technologies for which a detailed microscopic understanding of few-body physics is essential.
Examples of future quantum technologies include, among others, atom interferometers for inertial navigation or precision measurements of gravity and sensitive Terahertz (THz) detectors for astronomy.

The Zero-G Studies of Few-Body and Many-Body Physics investigation uses rubidium (87Rb) and potassium (39K and 41K) samples in the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) aboard the International Space Station (ISS).

The approach for the investigation comprises two main aspects: the creation of ultracold atomic gases and the subsequent manipulation and probing of these gases to study few-body physics and exotic quantum states.
Modern laser-cooling techniques are used to cool atoms to near absolute zero temperatures.
At these temperatures, atoms behave like matter waves, according to the laws of quantum mechanics.
Fully automated data runs, each lasting about one minute, acquire images of ultracold atom clouds under varying conditions.

Creation of Ultracold Atomic Gas: • Laser Cooling: Atoms are released into a vacuum chamber and collected into a magneto-optical trap (MOT), where they are initially cooled using laser cooling techniques.
This technique is based on the rapid scattering of light off atoms and can cool a cloud of atoms to temperatures below 1x10-3 K.
An additional magnetic field applied in conjunction with the lasers concentrates the cold atoms in a specific region of the vacuum apparatus, called the source chamber.

The MOT is the starting point for further cooling and experimental preparation. • State Preparation: Using further laser manipulations, the atoms are then prepared in a state that seeks to occupy regions of low magnetic fields.

By applying a suitable magnetic field geometry with a moving magnetic minimum, the cloud of atoms is transported to a so-called “science region.” Magnetic fields generated by a chip with current-carrying traces provide a trap for the atoms in the science region. • Evaporative Cooling: With the atoms trapped in the science region, evaporative cooling is performed by selectively removing the hottest rubidium atoms from the cloud.
The remaining atoms then rethermalize at a lower temperature.
The selective removal of the hottest rubidium atoms is achieved by applying suitably tuned radiofrequency radiation.
Potassium atoms are cooled by being in thermal contact with the actively cooled rubidium atoms, in a process called sympathetic cooling, where rubidium atoms act as a cold bath of atoms.
With sufficient evaporative cooling, the clouds of rubidium and potassium atoms can undergo a phase transition to a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC), providing a macroscopic, quantum mechanical object.

However, pronounced quantum mechanical effects can already be observed before reaching this phase transition. • Further sample preparation: After the preparation of the ultracold sample, further preparation steps are employed for the proposed studies.
These steps include changes to the trapping strength, changes of the internal states of the atoms, and the application of suitable homogeneous magnetic fields.
Manipulation and Detection: • Manipulation Techniques: The ultracold gas is manipulated using laser, radiofrequency, and/or microwave pulses.
In addition, homogeneous magnetic fields are used to shift internal energy levels of the atoms.

These techniques are designed to adjust the pairwise interactions as needed for the preparation of exotic quantum states. • Time-of-Flight Imaging: After a predetermined time-of-flight during which the cloud is released from the trap and can expand freely, the sample is imaged using absorption imaging techniques.
For this, a short laser pulse is flashed onto the atoms, and the shadow cast by the atoms is imaged on a CCD camera using a custom microscope setup.
This imaging process typically destroys the “quantumness” of the sample and concludes an experimental cycle.
The apparatus then starts over with the preparation of a new sample.
Many cycles are performed during a typical data-taking campaign, with a time scale of approximately one minute per run.
Ultracold atoms in microgravity provide a unique environment for the study of complex few-body phenomena.

One of the surprising predictions for quantum mechanical few-body systems is the existence of universality, i.e. the idea that highly intricate phenomena can be governed by underlying principles that are agnostic to specific microscopic realizations.
As a concrete example, Efimov physics predicts the emergence of an infinite series of exotic three-body bound states when the interactions between the atoms are made stronger and stronger.
It is predicted that these Efimov states are connected by universal scaling relations governing their energy and their size.
Our experiments aim to provide essential benchmark data to test this universality hypothesis.
By measuring two members of this infinite series, scaling relations can be probed and can be compared to some of the most advanced few-body theories to date.

This will be a steppingstone towards the investigation of a plethora of associated few-body phenomena, with the ultimate goal of significantly advancing the boundary of our understanding and paving the way for the development of new quantum technologies.

Physics is the discipline that provides understanding of biology and chemistry at the most microscopic level, and the area within physics most relevant to chemistry and biology is “few-body physics.” It is an often neglected portion of physics, because it is so difficult to do.

An important way to make progress is to simplify, simplify, simplify: to come up with model systems in which we can make progress that can later be applied to human-centric disciplines like biology, and develop exotic and useful new materials.
A promising way to simplify is to study matter at lower temperature, and lower densities.

The Cold-Atom Lab (CAL) flying in the International Space Station (ISS) is where we will reach the lowest possible temperatures, and low densities, to perform studies of simple, yet intricate (think “snowflakes”) clusters of three or four atoms.

Ultracold atomic gases are a key platform for a broad range of future quantum technologies, including ultraprecise sensing and timekeeping, novel medical imaging methods, secure communication schemes, high-performance computing, and development of exotic materials.
A precise knowledge of few-body physics is necessary to fully realize the potential of quantum technologies.

This project supports development of a detailed understanding of quantum mechanical few-body physics at the microscopic level, which may open new avenues for quantum gas applications in future space exploration.
Such applications include inertial navigation and precision measurements using atom interferometry, or calibration standards for detectors used in astronomy.

Capillary Flow Experiment - 2
Liquids behave differently in space than they do on Earth, so containers that can process, hold or transport them must be designed carefully to work in microgravity.

The Capillary Flow Experiment-2 furthers research on wetting, which is a liquid’s ability to spread across a surface, and its impact over large length scales in strange container shapes in microgravity environments.

This work will improve our capabilities to quickly and accurately predict how related processes occur, and allow us to design better systems to process liquids aboard spacecraft (i.e., liquid fuel tanks, thermals fluids, and water processing for life support).
Wetting describes how well a liquid is attracted to a solid surface.

Understanding the impact of wetting over large length scales in microgravity is important for a wide variety of engineering systems being developed for human spaceflight.Studies from CFE-2 may serve to demonstrate how liquids can be efficiently and passively separated from gases in the absence of gravity.
This is a key operation in fluid systems aboard spacecraft such as water purification systems for life support.
This research hypothesizes that capillary flows in microgravity are strongly influenced by container geometry, particularly interior corners and gaps.
For vane gaps, a critical wetting condition, dependent on gap size and vane design, is expected.

In interior corners, imbibition rates, phase separation, and bubble dynamics should be highly sensitive to 3D geometry, with long-duration microgravity being crucial for observing subtle, slow processes.
Experiments are designed to quantify these relationships and validate theoretical models.

The Capillary Flow Experiments demonstrate how capillary forces work in space, how differently shaped containers change the wicking behavior of a wetting fluid, and how such can be used to passively separate liquids and gases.

Understanding how microgravity amplifies these behaviors could improve the reliability of such key processes as water purification fuel storage and supply, and general liquid transport aboard spacecraft.
On Earth capillary action allows small amounts of liquid to flow up and into tight spaces despite the effects of gravity.
New miniature medical devices, known as lab-on-a-chip technologies, exploit this phenomenon to draw blood or other fluids into essentially miniature l diagnostic systems.
CFE-2 improves our understanding of how capillary forces work in a variety of system geometries including the open spaces within porous materials such as sand and soil, wicks and sponges.

Capillary Flow Experiment

The primary objective of the CL unit experiments is to identify the extent the role of the boundary condition at the contact line plays in the natural dynamic response of a large capillary interface to a variety of disturbances.

The primary objective of the ICF units is to experimentally determine secondary imbibition rates in complex containers due to spontaneous large length scale capillary flows along interior corners in weakly 3-dimensional containers.

Secondary objectives of the experiments are to quantify such flows in closed loop cycles, and to identify the passive phase separation characteristics of certain capillary driven multiphase-flows (e.g. bubbly flow) along interior corners.
The primary objective of the VG units is to determine equilibrium interface configurations and critical wetting conditions for interfaces between interior corners separated by a gap.
A secondary objective is to validate numerical predictions of the large length scale discontinuous or nearly discontinuous wetting phenomena.

Without gravity, it is more difficult to control the flow of fluids and this is a challenge for designing spacecraft systems such as liquid propellants/cryogens, thermal control systems, wastewater management and recycling.Capillary forces (the interaction of liquid with solid that can draw a fluid up a narrow tube) continue to act in the absence of gravity and can be exploited to control fluid orientation so that fluid systems on spacecraft perform predictably.CFE uses the low-gravity environment provided by the International Space Station to understand the special dynamics of capillary flow and will aid in the design of fluid transport systems on future spacecraft.

The CFE investigations operate under the hypothesis that capillary phenomena in microgravity, specifically contact line dynamics, interior corner flows, and vane-gap wetting, deviate significantly from idealized theoretical predictions based on simplified geometries and boundary conditions.

This deviation is anticipated to manifest as measurable differences in dynamic interface response (frequency and damping) for varying contact line conditions, geometry-dependent secondary imbibition rates in complex containers, and distinct critical wetting conditions in vane-wall gaps influenced by gap size and wettability.

The CFE experiments are designed to quantify these deviations, providing empirical data to refine existing theoretical models and enhance the predictive capabilities for low-gravity fluid management systems.

The knowledge gained from this payload has the potential to be instrumental in the design of future fluid systems for spacecraft-impacting fluid bearing containers such as propellant and cryogenic fluids tanks, thermal control system coolant reservoirs, water storage and management systems, liquid state low-gravity materials processing equipment, and biofluids handling instruments for inflight human health systems.
By performing this experiment, researchers will gain information that will lead to improvements in system reliability with reductions in system mass and complexity.
These applications of CFE are in direct support of NASA's mission to develop safe, reliable, and affordable spacecraft to pursue the greater exploration of our solar system and universe.

The results of the flight experiments are also expected to provide insights into terrestrial interfacial phenomena and may lead to models predicting fluid flows in porous media (i.e. ground water transport), complex capillary structures (i.e. high performance wicks for heat pipes employed in electronics cooling), and Lab-On-Chip technologies (i.e., microscale biofluids processing).

Cool Flames Investigation
The objectives of this investigation are to:
1) Examine the combustion behavior of n-dodecane and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane at pressures ranging from 0.25 atm to 5 atm.
2) Analyze the effects of helium dilution on cool flame behavior.
3) Examine the behavior of combustion characteristics.
4) Investigate the relationship between droplet size, pressure, and flame extinction, and (5) understand the consequence of soot formation during cool flame combustion.
The Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) contains the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) which facilitates the controlled combustion of fuel droplets.
A system of gas bottles and fuel syringes delivers the desired gas mixture to the combustion chamber ranging from 0.25 to 0.5 atm.
Droplets of fuel are dispensed and suspended between hypodermic needles or tethered using silicon-carbide fibers.
A hot-wire igniter is positioned near the droplet for ignition.
After ignition the wire is retracted.
Fuels observed include n-dodecane, farnesane, and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane.
Fuels diluted with molecular oxygen, atomic nitrogen, and helium to study the influence on flame extinction and dynamics.
Flames were observed with a black-and-white camera for droplet size measurements.
A UV camera was used for capturing the OH* radical emissions and flame size.
Other high resolution cameras were used for monitoring and documentation.
Narrow-band and wide-band radiometers for analyzed flame radiation.

Flame combustion of liquid hydrocarbon fuels such as n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures, and faresane in microgravity can provide insights into low-temperature chemical kinetics, revealing critical parameters like droplet extinction diameters and flame dynamics that are not observable on Earth.
A basic understanding of cool flames is important for understanding ignition phenomena of practical fuels and fuel additives.
Cool flames play a key role in the development and selection of new fuels and the design of advanced engines such as clean, high-efficiency Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) engines.

The research will also help combustion chemists to develop new computational models to compute combustion performance in for many practical applications on earth, including an understanding of how cool flame reactivity determines octane and cetane number for fuels in spark ignition and diesel engines.

Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) will provide critical validation for complex chemical kinetic mechanisms, advance the understanding of flame dynamics and instabilities in low-temperature combustion, and support the design of safer spacecraft systems by refining knowledge of combustion in microgravity environments.

Coarsening in Solid Liquid Mixtures-2

The objective of the CSLM-2 investigation was essentially the same as the original CSLM investigation with the addition of higher solid volume percent samples requiring longer times to reach steady state coarsening rates.
The CSLM-2 approach and hardware was identical to the predecessor CSLM investigation.
The solid volume fraction of the 4 samples for CSLM-2 were 0.3.

The theory of coarsening has been described by Lifshitz, Slyozov and Wagner (LSW) predicts that for the limit of zero volume fraction particles grow with time as the cube root of the average radius, and the particle size distribution becomes independent of time.

The investigation hypothesizes that finding a system which satisfies all the constraints of LSW theory such as particles are infinitely separated and there is no diffusional interaction between them is prohibitive for ground-based laboratory condition due to effects of particle sedimentation and buoyancy-induced convection and therefore the theory can only be tested by performing experiments in a microgravity environment, For CSLM-2 it is hypothesized that for large volume fraction solid samples the transient coarsening process will be longer and steady state will be reached much later compared to low volume fraction solid particles.
Coarsening occurs on Earth during the processing of any metal alloy and thus the coarsening process affects a large spectrum of products from dental fillings to turbine blades.
Since the properties of an alloy are linked to the size of the particles within the solid, coarsening can be used to strengthen materials.
This is the case with the majority of aluminum alloys used commercially today.
Conversely, if the coarsening process proceeds too long the material can weaken.
This occurs in jet turbine blades and is one of the reasons why turbine blades must be replaced after a certain number of hours of service.
Thus developing accurate models of the coarsening process is central to creating a wide range of new materials encompassing those used in automobiles to those used in space applications.

Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures
The objective of this investigation was to study dendritic coarsening in solid-liquid mixtures at low volume fractions of solid.
Specific interest was in examining dendritic structure close to the dendrite tip.
Additional objectives included measuring the rate at which topological singularities occur when a secondary dendrite arm separates from the main dendrite stem or when two arms fuse together.
The CSLM-3 approach and hardware was essentially identical to the predecessor CSLM and CSLM-2 investigations.
The solid volume fraction of the 4 Pb-Sn samples for CSLM-3 were 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4.
Isothermal holding times between 10 minutes and 48 hours were employed.
After the requisite holding times the samples were quenched using pressurized gas.
Upon receipt of the samples they were analyzed using three-dimensional reconstructions of the microstructure.
The 3D reconstructions was used to determine the interfacial curvatures, the genus and the spatial distribution of curvature in the system.
The experimentally measured structures were used to compare phase field simulations and experiment.
The fundamental questions that this investigation attempts to answer are as follows: Does the Interface Shape Distribution (ISD) vary with position from the tip of the dendrite?
If so, as is likely the case, does the ISD scale with time, as is usually the case during coarsening?
How important is the spatial distribution of curvature in setting the evolution of the structure?
How do diffusional interactions between the secondary, and perhaps tertiary, arms on different dendrites affect the evolution of the system?
How does the ISD evolve when there are multiple dendrites in the system?
Does scaling exist?

Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures
The primary objective of the microgravity experiment was to measure the temporal evolution of the average size-scale of a solid-liquid mixture during solidification.
Specifically, the objective was to measure the average intercept length and the average section area of the solid particles at various times and for various volume fractions of solid.
Using this data the amplitude of the temporal power law for the average section area. and intercept length was to be determined.

Once the amplitude of the temporal power law is known, the objective is to compare the result to the theoretical predictions on the dependence of the amplitude of the power law on the volume fraction of the coarsening phase.
The objective was also to determine the steady-state particle size distribution by measuring the distribution of section area of of the particles in a plane and the intercept length distribution.
The sample holder in the Sample Processing Unit (SPU) contained four Lead-Tin samples of 12 mm diameter and 6 mm thickness for various volume fractions of Tin.
The SPU heated the samples up to 185 degree C in less than 9.5 min, held the temperature for a predetermined time at 185 ± 0.1 degree C ranging from 0.25 to 48hrs (coarsening phase).

The heating system consists of two disc resistance heaters and one ring heater to insure uniform heating with four resistance temperature devices (RTD) installed mid-way between the discs 1 to measure temperature of the samples.
Subsequent to the predetermined coarsening time the samples were quenched using pressurized air to nearly room temperature in approximately 1 minute.
Once the samples were returned to earth they were sectioned and the measurements of particle size and distribution was performed.

The theory of coarsening has been described by Lifshitz, Slyozov and Wagner (LSW) predicts that for the limit of zero volume fraction particles grow with time as the cube root of the average radius, and the particle size distribution becomes independent of time.

The investigation hypothesizes that finding a system which satisfies all the constraints of LSW theory such as particles are infinitely separated and there is no diffusional interaction between them is prohibitive for ground-based laboratory condition due to effects of particle sedimentation and buoyancy-induced convection and therefore the theory can only be tested by performing experiments in a microgravity environment.

The importance of coarsening from a commercial perspective arises from the major effect that coarsening has on the properties of materials, for example materials can become stronger while undergoing coarsening.
The CSLM experiment will assess the validity of the theory of coarsening that has been used to design materials.
The result will be a more rational design of materials using a first-principles approach, reduced development cost for the production of new materials and better materials properties.
Such a first-principles design of materials will enable NASA and industry to create materials in a rapid cost-efficient manner with the superior properties that are needed for space exploration.

Constrained Vapor Bubble-2

The primary objective of CVB-2 is to determine the overall interfacial stability, characterize the hydrodynamics, measure heat transfer coefficients, and determine the overall conductance of a complex fluid (94% Pentane/6% Isohexane) in a microgravity environment.

The Constrained Vapor Bubble (CVB) Experiment was conducted on the International Space Station (ISS) and the temperature data have been used to analyze the heat transfer mechanisms operating within the quartz cuvette for 40 mm and 30 mm modules.
Even with the large millimeter dimensions of the CVB, interfacial forces dominate in these exceedingly small Bond Number systems with small viscous losses.

A comparison of the modeling results obtained using a simple one-dimensional analysis of the temperature fields found with the dry and partially liquid pentane filled cuvettes allowed the phase change and radiation fields to be determined in both microgravity and earth gravity.
Unique visual observation of the shape of the liquid flow field through a microscope enhanced the understanding of the temperature and vapor pressure [1],[2] measurements.
The internal heat transfer processes were very complicated, multidimensional, and the length of the closed system strongly affected the average internal heat transfer processes.
Internal radiation was shown to be more significant than originally anticipated as well as the effect of Marangoni convection.

The competing processes of capillary flow driving liquid from the cold to the hot end and Marangoni flow driving liquid from the hot end to the cold end resulted in the formation of a central drop and a pinch point in the film thickness profile.
The results also indicate that the study of the constrained vapor bubble in an open loop heat pipe configuration would allow the passive bubble more freedom to respond.

In microgravity environments, the introduction of a higher boiling point, higher surface tension component into a low-boiling-point fluid within a constrained vapor bubble suppresses temperature-induced Marangoni convection, thereby enhancing heat transfer performance and system stability.
Most liquids have a surface tension that decreases as temperature rises.
This causes fluid to flow in the direction of higher surface tension, a phenomenon known as Marangoni flow.
This reduces the effectiveness of a heat pipe, because liquid cannot return to the hot end.
CVB-2 investigates whether a mixture of two fuels (pentane and isohexane) that can reduce Marangoni flow and improve the efficiency of the CVB system on the International Space Station.
In addition, the investigation provides insight into how heat transfer functions in microgravity.
Most satellites use heat pipes to keep critical parts cool, and improved understanding of fluid mixtures could enable future heat pipes that are smaller, lighter and less expensive to launch.
A wide range of high-performance devices must be perpetually cooled in order to function, from supercomputers to personal laptops and LED light bulbs.
Fluid mixtures circulating through heat pipes can passively dissipate heat, using less energy than fans or cooling systems.
But heat pipe transport systems are sensitive to small differences in temperature, pressure, and gravity.
Studying how fluid mixtures and heat pipes function in microgravity provides insight into the fundamental principles of thermodynamics.
This also provides insight into how mixtures of fluids behave during boiling, condensation, evaporation, distillation, and stripping.
These processes are used in a variety of industries and environmental cleanup.

Constrained Vapor Bubble

The immediate macroscopic objectives are to determine the overall stability, the fluid flow characteristics, the average heat transfer coefficient in the evaporator, and the heat conductance of the CVB as a function of vapor volume and heat flow rate.

On the microscopic scale, the scientific objective is to evaluate the local details of the Kelvin-Clapeyron model of change-of-phase heat transfer under microgravity conditions where the extended Young-Laplace equation predominates.
The CVB-1 investigation used a variety of methods to study the behavior of the constrained vapor bubble (CVB) in a microgravity environment.
This approach involved conducting experiments, creating mathematical models, and using insights from past CVB experiments to analyze the findings after the flight.
Experimental Design and Testing: -Customized CVB Cells: Five CVB cells were fabricated from quartz.
Each cell featured a square cross-section (3 x 3 mm) and varying lengths to achieve specific liquid-to-vapor volume ratios.
One cell was a ''dry'' cell, evacuated to 5 torr, to establish baseline thermal behavior.
The remaining four cells were filled with either pentane (a completely wetting fluid) or ethanol (a partially wetting fluid) before launch.

Three cells utilized pentane at different volume ratios, while one was intended for ethanol. -Controlled Thermal Environment: The CVB cells were integrated into a system that allowed for precise control of heat input at the evaporator end and heat rejection at the condenser end.

The system maintained a stable and uniform thermal environment for the cells. -Microgravity Environment: The CVB experiments were conducted on the International Space Station (ISS) to provide the necessary microgravity conditions.

Data Acquisition: -Macroscopic Measurements: Throughout the experiment, macroscopic data were recorded, including temperature profiles along the cell, vapor pressure, heat input and rejection rates, and visual observations of the vapor bubble.

These observations were used to assess the overall performance and stability of the CVB system. -Microscopic Measurements: The investigation utilized an Image Analyzing Interferometer (IAI) to acquire detailed, microscopic measurements of the liquid film profile.
These measurements included curvature profiles, film thickness profiles, and adsorbed film thickness.

These data were crucial for understanding the local transport processes within the CVB. -Acceleration Measurements: The system monitored residual accelerations to assess their potential impact on the CVB's stability and behavior.
Time Correlation: All acquired data were meticulously time-correlated to ensure accurate analysis and interpretation.

Mathematical Modeling and Analysis: - Extended Young-Laplace Equation: This equation, incorporating both capillary and van der Waals forces, was employed to model the equilibrium shape of the liquid-vapor interface.
Kelvin-Clapeyron Transport Model: This model was used to analyze the non-equilibrium behavior of the CVB.
It incorporated conservation equations for mass, momentum, and energy, along with the extended Young-Laplace equation.

The model was considered for refinement to account for internal radiative heat transfer, observed in previous experiments. -Numerical Modeling: Two- and three-dimensional numerical thermal modeling were considered to evaluate and refine the Kelvin-Clapeyron model, particularly to capture the complex interplay between capillary and Marangoni convection. -Internal Heat Analysis: Temperature data were analyzed to quantify the contributions of conduction, external radiation, and internal radiation to the overall heat transfer within the CVB system.
This analysis built upon previous ground-based studies and included a detailed examination of the role of Marangoni convection.

Comparison with Ground-Based Studies: -Equilibrium Studies: The microgravity equilibrium data, including film thickness and curvature profiles, were compared with ground-based measurements to confirm the validity of the extended Young-Laplace equation under these conditions. -Non-Equilibrium Studies: Comparison of microgravity non-equilibrium data with results from ground-based studies illuminated the influence of gravity on CVB behavior.
Specifically, this comparison focused on the differences in flow field symmetry and the magnitude of heat transfer.

Stability Analysis: -Macroscopic Stability: The investigation evaluated the overall stability of the CVB system, considering the occurrence of dryout, oscillations, and cavitation, as a function of heat flux, liquid-to-vapor volume ratio, and working fluid. -Microscopic Stability: A stability analysis was performed, leveraging experimental observations and mathematical modeling, to understand the conditions and mechanisms that lead to instability within the thin liquid film.

Post-Flight Analysis: -Reflectivity and Image Data: Detailed analysis of the raw reflectivity and image data was conducted to extract information about the adsorbed film thickness and its influence on CVB behavior.

It is hypothesized that the isothermal equilibrium liquid film shape depends on the gravitational field and the intermolecular force field which changes rapidly in the vicinity of the liquid-vapor and liquid-solid interfaces.
This equilibrium shape in a particular gravitational field can be controlled by fixing the container shape, the liquid-substrate system, and the relative volume of the liquid to that of the vapor.
It is further hypothesized that the extended Young-Laplace equation can describe this shape over a large range of conditions.
Under non-equilibrium conditions resulting from an imposed temperature gradient, fluid flow and change-of-phase heat transfer are a function of further changes in the shape of the liquid volume.

It is postulated that these non-equilibrium effects can be analyzed using a Kelvin-Clapeyron transport model that includes the use of the conservation of heat, mass and momentum and the extended Young-Laplace equation.
CVB has performed ground-based studies in a thermal vacuum chamber to determine the efficiency of the heater and cooler configuration.
Large thermal response times that have been experimentally observed in space-based experiments cannot be obtained from these ground-based studies.
Space-based experimentation is the only method available to ascertain internal low-gravity fluid mechanics within a heat pipe.

The project aims to achieve an improved understanding of microscale heat transfer, improved designs for wickless heat pipes, and an increased efficiency in heat transfer devices for cooling critical components.
Targeted users are existing microelectronics industry and perhaps military applications.
New designs should be able to be developed several months following the analysis and presentation of the results from the experiment.

Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2
The focus of DAFT / DAFT-2 was to mitigate the risk for the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME).

SAME relied on a commercially available condensate nuclei counter, the TSI P-Trak, to quantify smoke aerosols in a microgravity environment, however there were concerns that th P-Trak would not be reliable in microgravity as it relies on gravity to recycle isopropyl alcohol used in the measurement process.
DAFT / DAFT-2 tests that a modified P-Trak particulate counter would be accurate in microgravity.
Summarized objectives include:
1) Demonstrate the Functionality of the Modified TSI P-Trak in Microgravity
2) Compare the TSI P-Trak Performance against the DustTrak control
3) Create and Analyze Aerosol Standards in Microgravity
4) Ensure the reliability of future aerosol experiments
The experimental approach consists of the following components:

1) Modification of Instrumentation: TSI P-Trak was modified for use in microgravity by redesigning the condenser tube to use capillary forces for recycling isopropyl alcohol and removing the mercury switch responsible for detecting instrument orientation.
2) Aerosol Generation: Arizona Red Dust (ARD) was chosen as an aerosol standard due to its ease of dispersion.
The ARD was aerosolized with GN2 to create particle samples.
The aerosol was contained within 15-liter Mylar bags.
3) On-Orbit Testing: The modified P-Trak gathered data from counting aerosol particles and these data were compared to the DustTrak CNC specifically designed to work in microgravity.
The TSI P-Trak operates by condensing isopropanol around aerosol particulates that are subsequently laser counted.
It was hypothesized that the P-Trak would not work in microgravity due to two potential failure modes that exist.
1) the system would clog or become obscured by isopropanol, and 2) the internal air-flow dynamics of the optics chamber of the device will cause an over counting of particulates.
The TSI P-Trak was modified for microgravity use via using capillary action to recycle the isopropanol.
Therefore, there are two basic hypotheses:
1) that the P-Trak, as modified for use in SAME, would function normally in microgravity.
2) that the aerosol created and filtered per the experiment design would be within the measurement capabilities of the test devices.
Extended duration space flight missions with larger vessels will require fire detection systems with increased reliability and sensitivity.
This research will impact the development of novel fire and smoke detection systems for the International Space Station and future spacecrafts.

Additionally, the successful adaptation of the TSI P-Trak for microgravity can inform the design of instruments for use in other challenging Earth environments, such as submarines or underwater laboratories where accurate detection of smoke can save lives.

The main objective of the DSI-R investigation was to quantitatively establish the fundamental physics controlling the spatiotemporal organization of the secondary sidebranch structure and its interaction with the array structure of primary branches under directional solidification conditions.

This investigation particularly focused on the origin of sidebranches that occur when columnar solidification patterns transform from cellular to dendritic as a function of thermal gradient and solidification velocity and study the potential for the formation of an intermediate multiplet pattern.
The dynamics and stability of cellular and dendritic growth patterns, and the relationship between the tip geometry and growth pattern were also to be investigated as well.
This intent of this investigation was to directly address outstanding issues that remain open in the understanding of complex dendritic microstructures.
The DSI-R investigation utilized a Bridgman type furnace and an experimental cartridge containing the organic transparent alloy of succinonitrile (SCN) - camphor.
The nominal concentration was 0.46 wt% camphor.
A single crystalline solid seed with a 100 direction parallel to the pulling axial direction is kept unmelted during all experiments.
Solidification is performed by pulling the experimental cartridge containing the alloy inside a thermal gradient G at a pulling rate V.
The G and V were the primary variable for each experimental run.
Images obtained by the direct axial observation, providing top-view interface images, and transverse observations, providing side-view interface images, were analyzed.
Bridgman solidification of transparent binary alloys in a diffusion controlled growth regime can yield benchmark data required for establishing the detailed dynamics of interface pattern selection.

The ''SPAtiotemporal evolution of three-dimensional DEndritic array Structures'' (SPADES) investigation conducted during the reflight of the Directional Solidification Insert (DSI-R) campaign targeted the columnar dendritic growth regime to quantitatively establish the fundamental physics controlling the spatiotemporal organization of the secondary sidebranch structure and its interaction with the array structure of primary branches under directional solidification conditions.
SPADES focused on the origin of sidebranches that occur when columnar solidification patterns transform from cellular to dendritic as a function of thermal gradient and solidification velocity.

The “Effects of Curvature and Unsteady Dynamics on Alloy Solidification Patterns” (CUSP) investigation extended the DSIP and SPADES project into a new direction that addressed the critical effects of the macroscopic curvature of the solidification front and the unsteady dynamics that occurs in response to changes of growth conditions or that is associated with side-branching.
A weak macroscopic interface curvature can have a major effect on both the array pattern evolution and grain structure.
The convex and concave interfaces lead to a continuous increase and decrease of the average primary spacing, respectively, and it only attains a stationary value for a flat interface.

By providing a reduced gravity environment where fluid convection is suppressed, space enables the direct experimental observation of the solid-liquid interface dynamics during the solidification process under long-duration and purely diffusive conditions.

The acquired benchmark data will make it uniquely possible to critically test computational models of alloy microstructures by quantitative comparisons of modeling predictions and experimental observations, thereby contributing to the development of Integrated Computational Materials and Engineering (ICME) tools for both space and earth applications.
Those tools are expected to “shorten development time, optimize designs and reduce costs relative to more traditional strategies involving building prototypes, testing and redesigning philosophies.

In addition, understanding alloy solidification in the microgravity environment of space is important to improve in-space processing (manufacturing, joining, and welding) of structural materials that will be used for future space exploration.

Development and Verification of a 3D Nucleate Pool Boiling Simulation Model Using PSI Data
The primary objective of this investigation was to develop and validate a numerical model for further investigation of nucleate pool boiling problems under microgravity conditions.
The moment-of-fluid (MOF) procedure is employed to reconstruct the interfaces of any number of material interfaces in a computational cell.

The salient features of the overall approach includes: (i) Multi-material interfaces are represented by the piecewise linear moment-of-fluid (MOF) reconstruction, (ii) the time derivative part of the heat equation is discretized using the backward Euler method which is a discrete maximum principle preserving time discretization scheme, (iii) the spatial derivatives part of the heat equation is discretized using the finite volume method, (iv) the temperature field is discretized on a multi-material “supermesh” in which there is just one temperature variable per material per cell, (v) the discrete location for a given variable is at the materials' centroid, (vi) “connected centroid” method is used in order to approximate fluxes, (vii) at Dirichlet or Neumann embedded interfaces, a linear exact correction term is prescribed so that the method approximates the temperature gradient with second order accuracy.

It is hypothesized that the developed model will have the following advantages which can lead to a more accurate prediction: (1) the method can better resolve thermal boundary layers (away from triple points) using adaptive mesh refinement, (2) a novel Moment of Fluid multiphase flow algorithm will straightforwardly prescribe a microlayer model in 3D general geometries, (3) the moment of fluid interface capturing algorithm will enable better handling of 3D problems such as bubble merging, (4) the modeling method can better conserve the boiling mass flow rate by directly exploiting the moment-of-fluid (sharp) interface reconstruction for approximating the interface heat flux in the vicinity of multiple (greater than 2) materials.
The verified model can be used to further study scenarios not investigated on ISS such as vapor bubble departure and collapse.
It can also be used to identify optimal heated surface configuration for better heat transfer characteristics.
In addition, the model can be used to study other problems under microgravity such as packed bed reactors.

The development of nucleate pool boiling simulation tool in microgravity based on the Navier-Stokes equations from this proposed work can be used to study other boiling problems in Earth gravity such as engine cooling and cooling in electronic devices.
