Capillary Channel Flow - Critical Velocities Experiment Unit 1
The investigation aims to characterize and quantify critical flow dynamics in open capillary channels of parallel plate and groove geometries.
A primary objective is determining the critical flow rates at which free surface destabilization (''choking'') and gas ingestion occur, emphasizing the capillary-inertial regime.
The investigation will examine the relationship between critical flow rate and channel length for complete and half-channel configurations.
Controlled, low-frequency flow oscillations will be introduced to probe instability onset sensitivity across geometries and lengths.

High-fidelity data on free surface shapes and critical velocities will be acquired to validate theoretical models and assess underlying assumptions, refining predictive capabilities for capillary flows relevant to spacecraft fluid management.
The CCF experiment was operated on the ISS in the MSG.
The CCF hardware consists of two experiment units, experiment unit number #1 for the parallel plate and groove geometry, and experiment unit number #2 for the wedge geometry.
Initally, one experiment campaign for each experiment unit was planned.
Due to the great success of the first two runs, two more additional runs were performed.
The challenge for these runs was the commissioning of the fluid loop.
The original design of the hardware did not foresee a commissioning from an undefined state, as it was the case after the first operation of each module.
The fluid management technology builtinto the CCF hardware - however - was able to recover from an undefined fluid distribution state and allowed additional runs.
The primary hypothesis guiding CCF-CV EU1 is that a limiting flow rate, or 'choking' phenomenon, exists in open capillary channels with parallel plate and groove geometries.
A relationship between the fluid velocity, the channel geometry, and the fluid properties governs this limit.

Furthermore, it is hypothesized that the introduction of wave oscillations within the flow will impact the critical flow rate, with the amplitude and frequency of these oscillations playing a significant role in the flow behavior and the onset of choking.
The knowledge of liquid management in space is important for any device which contain liquid and gas, and have one or many free liquid surfaces.

The requirements for the device which experiences different acceleration levels down to fully compensated gravity conditions (weightlessness) during its operation may include the phase separation of liquid from gas, gas from liquid, and the transport of liquid through liquid acquisition devices.

The results from the CCF experiments may help to design subsystems of future spacecrafts, such as the propulsion subsystem, the thermal control subsystem and the life support subsystem for crewed exploration.
The data can be used to build mathematical models which can be applied to real fluids and real dimensions.

The data can be used as well to validate computational fluid dynamics software packages which are state-of-the-art tools the design of spacecrafts.
Capillary forces on Earth are masked by gravity, but may become dominant in small scales.

It may be a wanted - as in the case of cleaning - or an unwanted - as in buildings - effect.
In a wider sense the CCF experiments contribute to this topic.

The objectives are to quantify phase separation efficiency in wedge channels as a function of flow parameters, bubble characteristics, and channel geometry; determine the influence of bubble size and injection frequency on separation efficiency; and optimize wedge geometry for passive phase separation.

Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets
This ground investigation sought to increase understanding of the issues that control the large discrepancy between soot formation in 1g and in 0g flames.

The objective of this investigation was to integrate computational and experimental methods to derive temperature distributions and soot volume fractions from the Smoke Point in Coflow Experiment (SPICE) data available in PSI.

By analyzing over 1600 raw DSLR images and incorporating advanced soot models, the study sought to improve understanding of soot formation, oxidation, radiative re-absorption, and aggregate growth in heavily sooting flames.

The work further aimed to reconcile microgravity and normal gravity flame behavior, identify key physical and chemical processes influencing smoke point development, and provide a framework for evaluating model parameter sensitivity.
The approach was to combine image processing, experimental diagnostics, and detailed soot modeling.
Raw Nikon NEF images were decoded into three color channels and analyzed using color-ratio pyrometry to extract soot temperature fields.
Absolute light calibration from SPICE was then used to calculate soot volume fractions.
For computational modeling, a coupled flow–species–soot system was implemented, modified to include radiation re-absorption and discrete-sectional aggregate formation.
Simulations were performed for both Yale and ACME burner configurations under normal and microgravity conditions.

Comparisons between experimental data and computed results guided sensitivity analyses of soot evolution parameters, including the effects of radiation, scattering, boundary conditions, and heat transfer to the burner structure.

Microgravity conditions would produce longer, more diffuse flames with lower temperatures and increased soot concentrations compared to normal gravity, and that careful integration of experimental temperature fields into the simulations would reduce discrepancies between measured and predicted soot distributions.

This study sought to enhance understanding of soot formation, flame structure, and radiative transport under microgravity and normal gravity, improving predictive models for combustion in both spacecraft and terrestrial systems.
For space applications, the results support safer fire detection, suppression, and cleaner combustion technologies critical for long-duration missions.
On Earth, the insights help reduce pollutant emissions, optimize combustion efficiency, and inform the design of cleaner energy and industrial systems.

Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography
The objective of this research was to develop and validate new flamelet generated manifold (FGM) modeling techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity.

Concurrent flame spread presented one of the greatest modeling challenges in combustion science due to the intricate coupling between heat transfer, mass transport, and chemical kinetics near the solid-vapor interface.
Traditional modeling strategies often relied on hybridized turbulence and chemistry models that were not fully consistent and failed to capture important intermediate reaction pathways.

To overcome these shortcomings, this PSI grant advanced the use of an unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) framework that reduced the complexity of reacting systems by mapping them into lower-dimensional manifolds.

The research aimed to leverage this methodology to simulate solid fuel combustion processes with high fidelity, using the NASA Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II) experiments as benchmarks.

Ultimately, the long-term goal was to enable accurate prediction of flammability limits for spacecraft materials and to provide a tool that could also serve as a subgrid-scale model in large-eddy simulations of fires, supporting spacecraft safety and hazard mitigation.
The approach combined high-resolution computational modeling with experimental validation to study concurrent flame spread in microgravity.
A previously developed computational framework was employed to run fully coupled simulations of fluid–solid responses, focusing on materials subject to charring and ablation.

Within this framework, the unsteady FGM method was implemented and tested on various BASS geometries, including flat sheets, spheres, and rod-shaped polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) samples, as well as wax cylinders.

Experimental imagery found in PSI from the BASS and BASS-II investigations was post-processed using newly developed two-color tomography methods with DSLR cameras, enabling 3D reconstructions of soot and temperature fields for direct comparison to model predictions.

The evaluation metrics included flame geometry, temperature distribution, soot volume fraction, and flame spread rate, with special emphasis on reproducing the “Goldilocks” flammability zone reported by Olson and Ferkul.

Comparative analyses were also carried out with a parallel NSF-supported terrestrial flame spread project, ensuring that the predictive capabilities of the UFGM approach were assessed across both microgravity and normal-gravity conditions.

The unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) approach was believed to be able to accurately reproduce concurrent flame spread in microgravity, including phenomena such as the “Goldilocks” flammability zone, by coupling near-wall thermal, mass transport, and chemical processes with far-field flow dynamics.
This research provides predictive tools for screening new materials’ flammability limits, which can lead to the design of safer spacecrafts.

The development of Large Eddy Simulation subgrid models is expected to improve hazard assessment capabilities critical for managing fire risks during long-duration space missions and within confined spacecraft habitats.
On Earth, these advancements could improve combustion modeling by deepening our understanding of coupled thermal, chemical, and flow processes, which betters fire safety standards.

The computational methods being refined have the potential to enable more effective fire prevention and mitigation strategies and foster innovations in diagnostics and simulations applicable across a variety of combustion scenarios.
Overall, this research can contribute significantly to safer human exploration in space and improvements to fire safety protocols on Earth.

Experiments were performed within the Directional Solidification Insert (DSI) of the Device for the study of Critical LIquids and Crystallization (DECLIC) aboard the International Space Station.
Homogeneous 3D cylindrical samples in a classical Bridgman setup was processed with various pulling velocities V and temperature gradients G.

This complex dynamical process selects a small range of wavelengths, from an unstable spectrum of wavelengths, to form a periodic array of cells.
From the technological viewpoint, the importance of cellular and dendritic microstructures is quite clear since these structures are exhibited in all important commercial solidification techniques.

Dynamic Response of Particle-Filled Polymeric Fluids in Flows with Complex Lagrangian Time Histories

The primary objective of this ground investigation is to exploit the unique flight data from the Shear History Extensional Rheology (SHERE, SHERE-II, SHERE-R) investigations to better understand the dynamic rheology of particle-filled polymeric fluids in complex flows.

These fluids, encountered in manufacturing processes such as fiber spinning, hydraulic fracturing, and roll-to-roll film production, experience alternating regimes of shear and extension in a Lagrangian frame.

By using SHERE’s microgravity dataset, the study seeks to isolate the interplay between polymer stresses, particle orientation, and flow disturbances—effects that cannot be cleanly separated in Earth’s gravity.

The overarching goal is to develop quantitative predictions and mechanistic insights into how particles alter extensional flow responses, strain hardening, and energy dissipation in viscoelastic suspensions.
The investigation combines numerical simulations, theoretical modeling, and SHERE flight data validation.

The SHERE experiments measured transient extensional responses of dilute particle suspensions in Boger fluids at moderate extension rates—regimes inaccessible on Earth due to sedimentation and buoyancy.

To interpret these data, the project applies finite-difference methods in spheroidal coordinates to resolve inertia-less viscoelastic flows around suspended particles, capturing strong local stress gradients near particle surfaces.
Semi-analytical theories are also employed to predict rheology in the limit of small polymer concentrations, allowing parameter sweeps that are computationally prohibitive in full simulations.

Three flow classes are studied: (1) sphere suspensions in transient extension with/without pre-shear to directly compare with SHERE data; (2) spheroidal particle suspensions transitioning between shear and extension to mimic fiber-film processing; and (3) alternating shear/extension flows modeling turbulent drag reduction.
Together, this multi-method approach bridges PSI experimental data with first-principles rheological predictions.

The central hypothesis is that particle-polymer interactions fundamentally alter the transient extensional rheology of polymer solutions in ways that cannot be predicted by simple additive models of particle and polymer stresses.

Specifically, the particle-induced velocity disturbances are expected to modify local polymer stress distributions, suppress strain hardening at large deformations, and alter stress development depending on flow history (e.g., pre-shear orientation effects).
Furthermore, anisotropic particles such as spheroids will introduce orientation-dependent rheological signatures, leading to different stress responses under alternating shear and extension.

By validating these predictions with SHERE microgravity data, the study tests whether advanced numerical and theoretical models can accurately capture the coupled dynamics of particles and polymers across relevant industrial flow regimes.

In-Space Benefits: For space exploration and on-orbit manufacturing, understanding the rheology of particle-laden polymeric fluids is crucial for the design of efficient life-support systems, in-space fabrication, and thermal management technologies.
Microgravity eliminates sedimentation, enabling stable suspensions and novel material processing methods, such as fiber spinning and advanced coatings.
Insights from SHERE-based models improve predictability of fluid performance in spacecraft systems where multiphase, particle-laden fluids may be used.
Earth Benefits: On Earth, particle-polymer suspensions underpin industries such as hydraulic fracturing, fiber spinning, extrusion molding, roll-to-roll manufacturing, and enhanced oil recovery.
Adding particles imparts tailored mechanical or conductive properties but also increases energy demands due to altered rheology.

This project provides mechanistic predictions for how particle orientation and polymer stress coupling influence flow resistance, helping optimize industrial processes, reduce energy consumption, and enable development of high-performance materials.
By combining SHERE microgravity data with advanced modeling, this work addresses gaps in extensional rheology knowledge that hinder efficient design of complex fluid processing systems.

Enhancement and Verification of Quantitative Phase-Field Crystal Modeling using NASA-PSI Coarsening in Solid- Liquid Mixtures Experiments Data

The key objectives of this investigation were to develop 1) a binary Molecular Dynamics (MD) interatomic potential for Pb-Sn system, 2) Phase Field Crystal (PFC) models for coarsening of solid-liquid mixtures; 3) a highly-parallel semi-implicit spectral and operator splitting numerical algorithm to use on high performance computing facilities that will enable the necessary large-scale PFC simulations (comparable to CSLM data length-scale); (4) Data mining of NASA-PSI Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures (CSLM), CSLM-2, CSLM-2R, and CSLM-3 experiments and using them in series of simulations in the developed computational tool for enhancement and verification of the proposed modeling framework.
The proposed multi-scale modeling framework is established around two atomistic computational material model of phase-field crystals (PFC) and molecular dynamics (MD).

PFC is a unique computational model at diffusive time scale with the capability of simulating solid-liquid processes with atomistic resolutions while MD acts on the time scale of atomistic vibrations.
A novel approach of modified-embedded-atom (MEAM) interatomic potential was adopted to obtain reliable interatomic potentials for Pb-Sn binary systems near or at the melting point (MP).

The potentials were used to calculate relevant properties such as latent heat, expansion in melting, liquid structure factor, solid-liquid interface stiffness, solidus and liquidus lines, and solid-liquid interfacial free energy.
The kinetics of coarsening in solid-liquid mixtures (Ostwald ripening of solid domains in the liquid phase) was simulated using a one mode phase field crystal (1PFC) model.
The simulation results were compared to experimental data previously obtained in a microgravity environment.
Simulations were carried out as a function of the difference in chemical potential between Pb and Sn.
Please the data layout document (DLD) describing the data organization in folders for each delta chemical potential and underlying files as per temperature of simulation and each time step.
Modified-embedded-atom (MEAM) interatomic potential and a one mode phase field crystal (1PFC) model can be utilized to simulate the kinetics of coarsening of solid phases in solid-liquid mixtures.

The proposed computational tool verified/quantified based on CSLM data will establish a virtual laboratory that can be used to study coarsening as well as other material processing phenomena on Earth involving with solid-liquid coexistence; e.g., rapid solidification and grain growth.
Since computational models are highly repeatable at lower cost, the proposed modeling framework will result in accelerated material process development and certification.
Solid-liquid coexistence is the initial step in many manufacturing technologies such as casting, liquid infiltration, and additive manufacturing.

Hence, this modeling framework can be used to investigate the relations between these manufacturing processes and the material properties in order to optimize/control the manufacturing processes parameters.
In addition, the results of this research will be disseminated to the public in forms of peer-reviewed articles, scientific reports, a project-specific website, and data uploaded to NASA-PSI website.

Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2

The primary goal of the FLEX-2 flight experiments is to extend the results of FLEX-1 to fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustor conditions, as well as, provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions in order to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models.
Detailed experimental objectives can be further itemized as:
Investigate the role of liquid-phase mixing on the burning characteristics of bi-component fuel droplets.
Examine the steady and unsteady liquid and gas-phase phenomena in pure fuel combustion.
Study flame extinction mechanisms and their boundaries.
Analyze the soot formation process, including soot volume fraction soot-shell dynamics.
Determine the influence of droplet interactions on the flammability limits and extinction behavior of droplet arrays.
Validate theoretical models of droplet combustion through comprehensive experimental data collection in microgravity environments.

The chamber was filled with the appropriate atmosphere, which was varied in pressure between 0.5 atm to 3.0 atm and O2 concentration between 0.1 to 0.4 mole fraction with the diluent gas making up the balance.
A settling time of approximately 2 minutes elapsed prior to initiating the test in order to ensure that the temperature and pressure of the chamber gases have stabilized.

This settling time was followed by the dispensing of a predetermined amount of fuel (based on the target droplet size) onto the support fiber for those tests in which the droplet is not freely deployed.

When sufficient fuel has been dispensed the dispensing needles were retracted and a dwell period of at least 10 seconds was allowed for the droplet internal fluid motion induced by deployment to subside.
This was then followed by initiating power to the ignitor for a selectable amount of time ranging from 1 second to 5 seconds after which the ignitor was retracted from the field of view.
If the flow field is to be generated by translating the droplet then droplet motion would commence at the same time that the ignitor is retracted.
A near real-time download of the color camera video was employed in order to verify successful droplet deployment, ignition, and overall progress of the experiment.
Pressure and temperature data of the chamber environment was also recorded in near real time.
The overall investigation approach can be summarized as:
Test parameters are determined, including pressure, temperature, fuel mixture, and humidity.
Fill the combustion chamber with the selected gas mixtures.
Deploy the droplet(s) carefully controlling the droplet diameter.
Allow the droplet to stabilize in the microgravity environment.
Ignite the droplet in a uniform and controlled fashion.
Monitor combustions and track flame evolution using high speed photography.
Monitor and adjust experimental conditions as needed.
Analyze data.

The independently varied experimental parameters during FLEX-2 experiments were 1) Fuel type 2) Ambient gas composition 3) Ambient Pressure 4) Droplet initial diameter 5) Droplet translation velocity (and acceleration) 6) Droplet spacing and initial size in a binary linear array.

Fairly sophisticated numerical simulations of convective droplet combustion have been developed in the last decade where the key contribution is the inclusion of full Navier-Stokes equations for the gas-phase flow field.
However, due to the inherent complexity of the problem, varying degrees of approximations have been made in treating the chemistry, radiation, and the coupling between the gas and liquid phases.
The validity of the assumptions or the hypothesis used in these simulation have not been confirmed by using benchmark data.

By conducting these experiments in a microgravity environment, the effects of buoyancy are minimized, and the droplet can be characterized only as a function of thermocapillary or solutalcapillary stresses allowing for a clear observation of the fundamental combustion processes, The present FLEX-2 experiments using bi-component mixtures.
In addition, the microgravity environment allows study of such phenomena as the transitions between radiative and diffusive extension of the flame.

The primary goal of the flight experiments is to provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions that could be used to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models.
The combustion of liquid fuels is the overwhelming energy source in the transportation sector.
Insights gained from these studies can lead to more efficient and cleaner combustion technologies which are crucial for reducing pollution and greenhouse gas emissions.
By improving fuel efficiency and developing better fuels, these experiments can contribute to:
1) More sustainable energy production.
2) Future combustor designs with minimal carbon footprint, maximum fuel efficiency and less pollutant emissions.
3) Allow quantitative evaluation of the performance of future fuels in combustors through the development of surrogates (mixtures of pure fuels that simulate the behavior of real fuels).
4) Validation of jet engine models by engine manufacturers with support from prior droplet results.

Flame Extinguishment Experiment

The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions.

The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests.

Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations.
These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions.
The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets.
A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI .
The basic outline of the procedure to construct this diagram is as follows:
Select the test pressure (0.5 − 1.5 atm) for the LOI tests.
Select a smaller droplet size (≈ 3 mm)
Select an ambient oxygen mole fraction that, based on ground-based testing, will support droplets burning to completion (as opposed to extinguishing at a finite droplet size).
Perform a droplet combustion test.
Increase the droplet size or repeat the test (if finite extinction diameter at flame extinction observed).
Continue steps 4 and 5 until flame exists for only a short time after ignition (radiative extinction).
Continue steps 4 thru 6 at a decreased ambient oxygen mole fraction.
Continue step 7 to an ambient oxygen mole fraction where the droplet does not ignite.
There were ambient conditions where the extinction droplet sizes at all ambient oxygen mole fractions were too small to either be observed or measured with the available diagnostics.
In this case, the determination of the LOI is similar, but more iterative.

Instead of observing flame extinction, however, the procedure involved an iterative sequence of tests (burn to completion followed by a no ignition test) with progressively smaller increments in ambient oxygen mole fraction to determine the LOI .

For the slow flow tests (in the flight experiment), the configuration of the flight hardware did not allow for adequate diagnostics over the entire test for a droplet in a uniform, steady convective flow.
In these tests, the procedure will be to duplicate tests above which yield finite-sized extinction droplet diameters.
Near the end of the tests, prior to flame extinction, the droplet will be subjected to a small, sub-buoyant, convective flow (imparted by translating the droplet at a slow, uniform speed).
The goal of the experiment is then to see how the presence of this flow influences the extinction process.
Note, a large number of the tests involve free droplets (as opposed to fiber-supported droplets) and a number of these tests will have droplets with a slow drift velocity.
Data gathered from these tests to examine the influences of a small, sub-buoyant flow on both the burning and extinction process.

The primary hypothesis of the FLEX mission is that microgravity conditions fundamentally alter the combustion and extinction characteristics of liquid fuel droplets due to changes in species and energy transport dynamics, radiative heat loss, and chemical kinetics.

Specifically, the hypothesis posits that the lack of buoyant convection in microgravity will lead to significant differences in the flammability limits and suppression efficacy of various fire suppressant agents compared to normal gravity conditions.

This hypothesis underpins the design of the FLEX experiments, which aim to map flammability boundaries, quantify suppressant efficacy, and develop predictive models to improve fire safety in space environments.
The research impacts and Earth benefits of the FLEX mission are significant and multifaceted.

By enhancing our understanding of microgravity combustion, the mission directly contributes to improved fire safety protocols for future space missions, ensuring the safety of crew members in environments where traditional fire suppression methods may be ineffective.
On Earth, the insights gained from these experiments have the potential to advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft.

The mission's findings on the effectiveness of various fire suppressants, including CO2, He, and SF6, in microgravity can lead to the development of more efficient and less harmful fire suppression systems, reducing the risk of toxic byproducts during fire events.

Additionally, the study of ''cool flames'' and low-temperature combustion processes observed in microgravity can inform the design of advanced combustion engines, leading to improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions in automotive and industrial applications.
Overall, the FLEX mission's contributions to combustion science have the potential to enhance both space exploration safety and terrestrial fire safety technologies.

Gradient Driven Fluctuation Experiment
The primary objectives of the GRADFLEX investigation can be summarized as follows:

To investigate non-equilibrium fluctuations in microgravity by studying the behavior of gradient-driven fluctuations in a microgravity environment, where the stabilizing influence of gravity is significantly reduced.
To measure the divergence of large-size fluctuations by observing and quantifying this divergence up to the limits imposed by the sample size.

To quantify the amplitude and spatial extent of fluctuations by precisely measuring the mean-squared amplitude of the fluctuations as a function of both wave vector (spatial extent) and frequency (temporal dynamics).

The investigation aims to rigorously test existing theoretical models of non-equilibrium fluctuations including comparing the measured amplitude and q-dependence of S(q) with predictions, both on Earth and in microgravity.
Beyond the static properties (amplitude and spatial extent), the investigation also seeks to characterize the temporal dynamics of the fluctuations.

The GRADFLEX experiment investigated gradient-driven fluctuations in fluids using a dual approach: a 12-day microgravity flight experiment aboard the Foton-M3 satellite and complementary ground-based tests with the same apparatus.
Two fluid systems (CS₂ and polystyrene/toluene) were subjected to precisely controlled temperature gradients.
Quantitative shadowgraphy, a sensitive optical technique, measured both static (S(q)) and dynamic (S(q,ω)) properties of the fluctuations, with images acquired at specific rates for each.
Data analysis involved Fourier transforms and spectral techniques to extract fluctuation amplitudes and dynamics and to address unexpected noise.
The core of the study was a rigorous, parameter-free comparison of experimental results with theoretical predictions for both terrestrial and microgravity environments.
The approach combined and refined a sophisticated design, enabling robust testing.

In the absence of gravity, thermally-driven fluctuations in a fluid subjected to a temperature gradient will exhibit significantly enhanced amplitude and spatial extent, with their mean-squared amplitude diverging with the size of the fluctuation and exhibiting altered dynamics up to the limits imposed by the sample dimensions.
Throughout the course of this work it has been necessary to constantly improve the experimental method of choice, namely the quantitative shadowgraph.

This development has now reached the stage where it is clear that this method, if handled properly, represents a viable method of carrying out both dynamic and static light scattering at scattering angles so small as to defy the imagination of of anyone who has worked in the field.
Although it is likely to take some time for the knowledge we have gained to be disseminated, there is no reason this method cannot be added to the scattering arsenal.
Furthermore, it can also be applied to X-rays, enabling one to extend the lower limit of X-ray scattering as well.
The consequences of putting a new technique into the hands of researchers is difficult to asses in advance.
Basically, however, this method will enable quantitative measurements of various systems having size ranges that are too large for existing techniques.
Obvious examples are the crystallization process in colloidal systems, gelation processes, and aggregation and flocculation.
Because scattering provides excellent statistical averages, the method should prove quite complementary to visualization techniques such as microscopy.

Isothermal Dendritic Growth Experiment - Second United States Microgravity Payload - 2

The primary objective of the microgravity dendritic growth experiment was to measure definitively the kinetics and morphology of dendritic growth, and to account for the effects of natural convection.

The experimental objective was to use a single,clearly defined experimental parameter, namely, the supercooling, to fully determine the resulting steady-state dendritic growth velocity, V, and tip radius R.
Designated the IDGE, the first flight, manifested on the second United States Microgravity Payload (USMP-2) mission, was launched and operated on the STS-62 on March 4-18, 1994.

This IDGE investigation met the objective of acquiring accurate dendritic growth speed and morphology data under diffusion-controlled conditions, while greatly reducing buoyancy-induced convective heat transport through the reduction of gravity.
The microgravity environment broadened this range of supercooling and permitted for the first time a critical assessment of both the heat transport theory and the interfacial kinetics behavior.

The approach was to observe and image dendritic growth as a function of undercooling such that dendritic tip velocities and radii could both be accurately measured and used as a critical test of theory.

Succinonitrile (SCN), transparent when molten, was used as a model metal analog system for studying dendritic growth since it solidifies like the body centered cubic (BCC) ferrous metal alloys, i.e., with an atomically ''rough'' solid-liquid interface.

In addition, SCN displays convenient properties for solidification experiments, such as a low melting temperature (58.08 °C), optical transparency, and the potential for accurate characterization of its thermophysical properties.
Dendritic growth is initiated inside the experimental chamber by energizing thermoelectric coolers attached to one end a thin capillary injector tube called the stinger.
The other end of the stinger, where the dendrite emerges in the center of the chamber, is notched, much like the tip of a fountain pen.
This helps isolate the leading dendrite and reduces the time needed until the leading dendrite is isothermal and has achieved steady state.
The IDGE flight experiment was divided into 60 operational cycles.
The first cycle, the warm-up cycle, consists of bringing the system up to the operational temperature where all system components are checked and initialized.
The second cycle measured the liquidus temperature of the SCN as a calibration point from which all subsequent supercoolings are measured.
The remaining cycles were dendritic growth cycles where dendrites are grown and photographed at varying supercoolings.

For each dendritic growth cycle, the experiment obtained a time series of stereo-pairs of 35-mm photographic images, low-resolution, binary, digitized electronic images and various data streams characterizing the dendrite's growth conditions during the cycle.
For each image pair, either 35-mm film negative or digitized image, we measured the position of the dendrite tip, and the associated time that the image was recorded.
The dendritic velocity was determined by calculating the slope of the displacement-time curve from the steady-state regime of the growth cycle.
The velocity is then adjusted by appropriate stereographic and magnification factors.
This procedure yields a set of dendrite velocity measurements accurate to about ± 2 percent.

The hypothesis of this investigation is that as a function of the supercooling there exists an explicit dendritic dynamic operating state defined by dendritic tip velocity, V and the dendrite tip paraboloidal radius of curvature, R.
The Peclet number obtained from the Ivantsov solution for each specified supercooling yielded an infinite number of solutions for V and R.

Therefore it is hypothesized that a second independent equation or length scale exists, which, when combined with the Ivantsov diffusion solution, will mathematically select the observed unique dynamic operating state.

Two of the candidates for the additional crystal growth physics that could provide the second crucial equation are the effects from the solid-melt interfacial energy, the influence of temperature fluctuations in the melt, or both.
The size, shape, spacing, and orientation of the dendrites in cast metal alloys have a major effect on the strength, ductility and toughness.
Nearly all cast-metal alloys used in everyday products, such as automobiles and airplanes, are composed of dendritic microstructures.
Metallurgists have long sought to predict and control alloy microstructures.
The development of automated, cost effective manufacturing techniques ultimately depends on the precision with which the problem in non-equilibrium pattern formation can be solved.

In principle, the intent is to incorporate fundamental understanding of microstructures into computer codes that simultaneously help design materials with made to order properties and optimize their manufacturability and performance.
Dendritic growth experiments conducted in the microgravity environment can provide benchmark data to validate such predictive models.

Investigating the Structures of Paramagnetic Aggregates from Colloidal Emulsions-2
InSPACE-2 studied the kinetics of chain formation in DC fields for suspensions of monodisperse, super-paramagnetic colloidal microspheres.
Objectives included:
1) To understand the percolation transition of MR suspensions in microgravity and the behavior of structures around this point (incipient structure).
The fluctuations of these chains can also be used to estimate the microrheological response of the MR fluid.
Additionally, measurements of the chain fluctuations in the final gelled material provide an estimate of the storage modulus of the suspension.
2) To determine the lowest energy configuration of 3D particle structures formed in a magnetorheological (MR) fluid in a pulsed magnetic field.

Visual observations of microscopic structures will yield a better understanding of the interplay of the forces and interactions (magnetizing/demagnetizing, surface energy, and repulsion between structures) in MR suspensions.
The most important dipolar interactions are the demagnetizing field, surface energy, and repulsion between structures.
InSPACE-2 employed a microscopic video technique to study the internal microstructure in MR fluid suspensions.
The investigation studied the assembly of magnetic particles in the presence of a toggled magnetic field.
The microstructure of the suspension as the particles assemble was characterized by light microscopy.
Samples for InSPACE-2 consisted of 1.05 μm diameter colloidal particles suspended in an aqueous phase.
The particles were Dynabeads MyOne Carboxylic Acid from Invitrogen at four different concentrations, 0.40, 0.48, 0.56, 0.65%.
When exposed to a continuous magnetic field each particle in the fluid acquires a magnetic dipole moment.
Such dipoles mutually interact and align to form a particle chain structures.
At sufficient concentrations and field strengths these chains form columns that cross-link to form an interconnected network.
The effects of sedimentation, which prohibits maintaining the particle concentration uniformity throughout the fluid, affect the study of MR fluids.
Mechanical properties of the particle assemblies, especially buckling instabilities, will be characterized.
The primary hypothesis is that energy barriers preventing colloidal phase transition can be overcome by changing the magnetic driving frequency and forces.

In these gel systems, gravity plays a dominant role and would slowly compress and deform the gel structures when similar experiments are performed on Earth, whereas in space these structures can be maintained as long as the magnetic forces are applied.
The MR fluids studied in InSPACE-2 are a unique model system for studying the fundamental mechanisms of phase transitions and self-assembly.

Suspension phase behavior affects the processing, stability and final properties of foods, personal care products, agrochemicals, paints, inks, pharmaceuticals and numerous other products and materials in which fine particles are suspended in fluids.
Additionally, InSPACE-2 research emphasizes how to harness external fields in order to direct the assembly of novel micro- and nano-structured materials and devices.

Such field-directed self-assembly represents a bottom-up approach to material and device fabrication, with the potential to dramatically reduce the cost of advanced technologies in photonics, heat transfer and photovoltaics.
The MR response provides the basis for technologies ranging from actively controlled dampers and actuators to magnetically sealed bearings and sensitive stress transducers.

MR fluids are currently used in wide range of applications, including active automotive shock absorbers, and engineers have explored their use in seismic dampers to protect large-scale structures during violent earthquakes.
Applications for space exploration include their potential use in robots, rovers, and for mobility augmentation crew suits.
Understanding the microstructural evolution of MR suspensions under time-varying conditions provides critical information for engineering and for tailoring their mechanical behavior.

InSPACE-3 investigated the assembly of paramagnetic colloidal ellipsoids in pulsed magnetic fields.
An objective was to study the effect of particle shape on the kinetics of aggregation and structures formed by DC and pulsed magnetic fields in suspensions of superparamagnetic particles.

Specifically, the investigation studied the suspensions of paramagnetic ellipsoid-shaped particles and quantify the effect of particle shape on the interactions of dipolar chains and the resulting suspension microstructure.
InSPACE-3 employed video microscopy to obtain suspension structural information.
Two particle shapes were tested for four frequency conditions and four field strengths, for a total of 24 experimental runs.
Each run took approximately one hour.
Each sample had a particle volume fraction of 0.52%.

This concentration represents an optimum value based on previous microgravity experiments, designed to balance the ability to capture aggregation kinetics at short times in DC fields the structural evolution in pulsed fields such that the final coalescence stage is observed.
For detailed experimental approach please refer Science Requirements Document (SRD).

Based on the science results of InSPACE-2, InSPACE-3 hypothesizes that particle shape will alter the aggregation kinetics, microstructures and microscopic mechanics, such as buckling instabilities that are observed for suspensions of polarizable spheres.

This research will potentially lead to the ability to engineer enhanced properties of these suspensions, including the ability to suppress lateral aggregation in magnetorheological fluid-based electromechanical devices or the ability to create new functional materials that control the flow of electromagnetic and thermal energy.

The quick phase-shifting property of magnetic colloidal fluids studied in InSPACE-3 makes them potentially useful for devices such as optical interfaces, active noise, and vibration dampers inside spacecrafts.

Future uses could include robotics, energy-transfer devices such as clutches, and other control systems and on Earth directed self-assembly of crystalline structures from particles that may eventually allow creation of new nano-materials fabricated from nanoparticle building blocks, with potential applications in medicine, energy storage, chemical separations, and catalysis.
Magnetic colloidal fluid technology is currently used for shock absorbers in race cars and sport cars.
This technology is expanding to include making large-scale building foundation stabilizers for areas prone to earthquakes.

Investigating the Structures of Paramagnetic Aggregates from Colloidal Emulsions-1
InSPACE-1 studied the response of MR fluids under continuous and pulsed magnetic fields in a microgravity environment.
An objective was to determine the true three-dimensional low-energy (equilibrium) structure of an magneto-rheological (MR) emulsion in a pulsed magnetic field.

InSPACE-1 aimed to conduct a microscopic video study of the MR fluid in a pulsed magnetic field to determine the effect of varying magnetic field, pulse frequency, and particle size on the equilibrium microstructures.
A pulsed magnetic field is used to mimic the forces applied to these fluids in real applications, such as vibration damping systems.
A pulsed field also tends to produce intricate, thick structures with different properties than structures produced by a constant magnetic field.
The MR samples for InSPACE-1 were ferrofluid emulsions consisting of iron oxide nanoparticles suspended in a solution of sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS, an anionic surfactant), and ultrapure water.
These samples were comprised of uniform particles sizes of 0.31, 0.40, and 0.66 μm and volume fraction 2 percent.
The parameters varied during the series of tests were the field strength, the particle size, and the pulse frequency.
During experimental runs the Lightbox Assembly provided the backlighting source to illuminate the samples.
The InSPACE Avionics Assembly was used to output an electrical current and frequency that could be adjusted to produce a pulsed-magnetic field inside the Helmholtz coil.
This magnetic field caused the particles in the fluid to group together, or aggregate, and form microstructures inside the fluid.
A camera was used to record the display on the avionic assembly.
The Optics Assembly was composed of two cameras with optic lens for a right angle view and a straight view of the sample.
A Helmholtz coil was mounted on the optic assembly and housed the InSPACE-1 sample.
For InSPACE-1, the Helmholtz Coil Assembly (CA) and the sample Vial Assemblies were integrated as a single unit.
The primary hypothesis is that energy barriers preventing colloidal phase transition can be overcome by changing the magnetic driving frequency and forces.

In these gel systems, gravity plays a dominant role and would slowly compress and deform the gel structures when similar experiments are performed on Earth, whereas in space these structures can be maintained as long as the magnetic forces are applied.
MR fluids can quickly transition into a nearly solid-like state when exposed to a magnetic field and return to their original liquid state when the magnetic field is removed.
Their relative stiffness can be controlled by adjusting the strength of the magnetic field.

Due to the rapid-response interface that they provide between mechanical components and electronic controls, for terrestrial applications MR fluids can be used to improve or develop new brake systems, seat suspensions, robotics, clutches, airplane landing gear, and active damping systems for bridges (to counter act wind gusts) and buildings.
For space exploration the results will lead to MR applications for limb and dextrous motion in robotic components and human-robotic interfaces for EVA suits.

In Space Soldering Investigation
The primary objective is to better understand the quality of solders in a microgravity environment.
In microgravity, gas bubbles, or void spaces are found in the solder joint and at contact surfaces.
These voids reduce the thermal and electrical conductivity and also provide sites for crack initiation.
Bubbles have less chance to escape in the reduced gravity environment of space.

Hence, by designing a systematic series of simple experiments, the objective was to investigate and better understand porosity development, surface wetting, and equilibrium shape formation while soldering in a reduced gravity environment.
The proposed experiments basically consisted of taking pieces of silver-coated copper wire and bending/twisting them into simple configurations for test coupons.

Selected lengths of Kester “44”® 60-40 rosin core solder (5 and 10 cm) were then cut and wrapped around a selected portion of the coupon, to be later melted by heat conduction through the wire using the kit’s soldering iron.
A second set of experiments involved feeding 5 and 10 cm lengths of solder onto similar shaped coupons that were being heated by the iron.
In principle, the soldering iron was never meant to come in contact with the molten solder.

All in all, five soldering sessions were conducted on the ISS that culminated in 86 samples comprising seven different wire configurations, two different solder lengths (5 and 10 cm), and two different melt procedures (conduction melting of wrapped solder and conduction melting of solder being fed onto the wire).
The melting experiments took place in the flame retardant Maintenance Work Area, a portable facility in the ISS used to make repairs and conduct other operations in the ISS.
A digital camera is placed behind the samples to record the melting and subsequent solidification experiments.
Video footage and still pictures were down linked after each experimental session.
Due to minimized buoyancy in the microgravity environment, it is hypothesized that one would expect additional porosity and enhanced surface tension contributions to porosity shape and mobility.
Brazing, soldering, and welding operations in microgravity can be influenced greatly by both wetting and surface tension-driven flows, primary factors in achieving or not achieving a sound joint.

For example, processes that rely on gravity-driven separations in the terrestrial environment, such as the removal of gas bubbles from a liquid, may rely on completely different interfacial phenomenon in microgravity.
An investigation of soldering practices and behavior in a microgravity environment is relevant to our technological needs, particularly with regard to in-space fabrication and repair.

The ISSI payload provides unique insight into microgravity soldering methods, which could play a fundamental role in maintaining the International Space Station as well as provide understanding of repair capabilities on future missions to the Moon and to Mars.
The study of soldering in space could lead to better soldering techniques here on Earth.

IntraVenous Fluid GENeration for Exploration Missions

The main goal of this experiment is to demonstrate in a space environment, a prototype system that produces USP grade SWI, and mixes the SWI with sterile USP sodium chloride to produce a homogeneous Normal Saline IV fluid.
The experiment shall also demonstrate at least one bubble removal apparatus, as this is a critical step to prevent delivering harmful gas emboli to patients when the deployed system is used.
The system will utilize a single flow rate, determined by the maximum volume/hour required for a worst-case-scenario medical event.
The IVGEN investigation employs a comprehensive and well-structured approach to demonstrate and validate the feasibility of producing IV fluids in space.
The approach encompasses a combination of on-orbit experimentation, ground-based testing, and meticulous data analysis, as summarized below:
On-Orbit Experimentation: The core of the investigation involves a flight experiment onboard the International Space Station (ISS), utilizing a prototype IV fluid generation system.
This experiment simulates the conditions and constraints of a space mission, allowing for direct testing of the system's performance in a microgravity environment.

Ground-Based Testing: Prior to the flight experiment, a rigorous ground-based test program is conducted to: -Concept Verification: Validate the design and performance of key system components, such as the bubble separators and mixers, in both normal and reduced gravity environments. -Input Water Analysis: Characterize the quality of potential water sources, including ISS potable water and various CEV water sources, to ensure the system's compatibility and effectiveness. -Temperature Effects: Assess the impact of varying temperatures on the system's performance, particularly on the DI cartridge and the conductivity sensors.

Data Acquisition and Analysis: During the on-orbit experiment, a comprehensive dataset is collected, including: -Environmental Data: Temperature, pressure, and acceleration measurements to understand the system's operating environment and potential impact on performance. -System Performance Data: Conductivity, flow rate, and image data to assess the purification, mixing, and bubble removal processes.
Post-Flight Sample Analysis: The two 1.5-liter bags of NS produced on orbit are returned to Earth for rigorous testing by a certified laboratory, ensuring the produced IV fluid meets USP standards.

Data Interpretation and Scaling: The collected data is meticulously analyzed to: -Validate System Performance: Confirm the successful production of USP-compliant NS solution in microgravity. -Identify Challenges and Limitations: Assess potential issues and areas for improvement based on observed system behavior. -Enable System Scaling: Utilize the data to inform the design and development of a larger, operational system capable of meeting the needs of future exploration missions.

It is hypothesized that a prototype system, utilizing deionization, magnetic stirring, and bubble separation techniques, can effectively produce USP-compliant normal saline solution from readily available spacecraft potable water sources in a microgravity environment.
Due to mass and volume limitations, space vehicles cannot carry sufficient IV fluid for medical contingencies.
A filtering and mixing system that can make IV fluid in situ would provide the treatment capability without the mass and volume constraints.
IVGEN was designed and will be tested to meet that need.
IVGEN technology could be used on Earth to generate IV fluid in Third World countries where medical resources are limited.

Light Microscopy Module Biophysics-1
Specific objectives of this investigation were
On the ISS and concurrently in earth control experiments, compare incorporation of protein aggregates (monomers versus dimers, trimers, etc.) into growing protein crystals.

Detection of aggregates in the crystal will be qualitatively assessed via LMM’s and laboratory fluorescence confocal microscopes and quantitatively measured using mass spectrometry (ion spray and/or MALDI).
Based on the percentage incorporation of larger aggregates within the crystal, the effect of molecular filtering based on differences in diffusion rates will be assessed.
Measure crystal growth rates in 1g versus μg for different size aggregates of proteins with molecular weights ranging from less than 20kDa to more than 1,200kDa.
Compare the defect density and crystal quality via mass spectroscopy and x-ray diffraction quality of crystals grown at different rates in a 1g environment.
A total of four cassettes were sent to the ISS, containing eight samples each.
Each sample could contain either; (1) Lysozyme, (2) pfGST, (3) BSA, or (4) XptA1.
For each protein investigated, preparative size exclusion chromatography (SEC) was used to fractionate protein monomers from the naturally occurring protein aggregates.
The aggregates were then segmented into small, medium, and large categories.

Fluorophores (excitation wavelengths: 594 and 488) were chosen and attached to the macromolecules, producing a bright fluorescent signal (red and green) and each exhibited a slow photo-bleach so that fluorescence was maintained for the duration of the proposed crystallization experiments.
The samples were upmassed frozen at -80C and thawed to ambient temperature (~20C).
After thawing nucleation of the proteins were observable within 24 – 96 hours.

Observations were conducted with a confocal fluorescent microscope where the total fluorescence observed for each crystal (after normalizing for the different crystal volumes) provides an estimation of the relative amount(s) of aggregated (containing the fluorophore) versus monomeric (no fluorophore) protein incorporated within the growing crystal.

This investigation addresses the hypothesis that improved quality of microgravity-grown protein crystals is the result of two macromolecular characteristics that exist in a buoyancy-free, diffusion-dominated solution: • Slower crystal growth rates, due to slower protein transport to the growing crystal surface • Predilection of growing crystals to incorporate protein monomers versus higher protein aggregates due to differences in transport rates

Using three-dimensional protein structure information, researchers can determine how proteins function and in cases where these proteins are involved in disease processes, the structure is often used to design new drugs that specifically interact with the protein.
Many leading drugs today are the product of structure-based drug design.

While enormous strides have been made in the last decade, there remain a large number of important proteins where the difficulty of obtaining crystals of sufficient quality is the chief barrier to their structural analysis.

The impact of this investigation is for one important class of proteins, membrane proteins, comprises a number of targets identified by the pharmaceutical industry as high-value commercial opportunities (membrane proteins were the targets for approximately 67% of all past marketed drugs and it is estimated that they will comprise targets for an equal percentage of all future drugs).

Membrane protein crystallization represents one area where the onset of space commercialization can maximize the impact of the microgravity environment in space-based research applications for the academic, government and pharmaceutical industries.

Other areas include high-value aqueous proteins and protein complexes (based on their functional importance in biological systems) many of which yield crystals of poor quality under 1g laboratory conditions.
Access to unique data optimized in microgravity could have great relevance for understanding protein structures and advancing new drugs into the pharmaceutical market.

Light Microscopy Module Biophysics-3
The primary objectives of this investigation are:
Use molecular biology to produce closely related protein constructs that display differences in growth rate dispersion during crystallization.
Measure the intermolecular ‘attractiveness’ of each construct, then model the inter-particle forces, diffusion and convection.
Measure and compare the growth rate dispersion of ground and microgravity grown crystals.
Growth rate dispersion will be measured for ground control crystals using routine crystallization apparatus.
In addition, growth rate dispersion will be measure for ground and microgravity grown crystals using the flight apparatus.
Characterize the quality of both ground and microgravity grown crystals.
Sophisticated X-ray analysis along with X-ray structural data collection will be used to quantify and characterize crystal quality.

Link the knowledge about inter-particle forces, measured acceleration levels, calculated flow rates and the resultant X-ray analysis to develop a model and predictive ground-based tests to identify those samples producing crystals on the ground that would be improved in microgravity.

Approach: Several cassettes were configured with cassettes identically configured containing three samples, one set in capillaries 1-6, another sample in capillaries 7-12, and the third in capillaries 13-18.
Six constructs and the T4 wild type (WT) were loaded into the capillaries at various concentrations and frozen to -80C.
The samples were thawed and observed in the LMM facility on board the ISS.
Several cassettes were identically configured containing three samples, one set in capillaries 1-6, another sample in capillaries 7-12, and the third in capillaries 13-18.

The cassettes were kept at -80°C until moving to the space station microscope facility.

The capillaries were filled as follows: • Capillaries 1-6 with 50 mg/ml WT* in 0.1 M Zn(C 2 H3 O2 )2 , 0.1 M Tris, pH 8, 35% PEG 8K, and 0.1 M NaCl • Capillaries 7-12 with 64 mg/ml S44E WT* in 0.05 M NaC 2 H3 O2 0.1 M Tris, pH 8 30% PEG 8K and 15% glycerol • Capillaries 13-18 with 53 mg/ml S44F WT* in 0.2 M Zn(C 2 H3 O2 )2 , 0.1 M NaC2H3O2, pH 5 and 20% PEG 20K.
On return to earth X-ray analysis of samples took place using the IMCA (Industrial Macromolecular Crystallography Association) beamline of the Advanced Photon Source.

Removing or greatly reducing the effects of buoyancy-driven convection and sedimentation in microgravity will result in slower, diffusion-controlled molecular transport that can yield larger crystals with fewer defects.
It is postulated that growth rate dispersion is reduced in microgravity due to the diffusive rather than convective flow regime that delivers macromolecules to the crystal.

Based on previous experimental observations it is hypothesized that the presence of growth rate dispersion in macromolecular crystals grown on the ground is an indicator of crystals that can be improved when grown in microgravity.

Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: X-ray crystallography is the main method scientists use to study the molecular structures of biology, but it is difficult to crystallize proteins, with only a poor success rate even in the best laboratories.

This investigation uses ground and microgravity-based observations to predict which proteins would benefit from crystallization in microgravity, improving the information that may be obtained from them.

Long-duration protein crystal growth experiments on the ISS with photo documentation, and subsequent analysis of the comparisons between 1g and μg crystals, will enable a more complete understanding of why proteins and other macromolecules often form more perfect crystals in microgravity than they do on earth.
If it could be predicted which macromolecular samples could be improved by crystal growth in microgravity, then the true potential of this medium could be exploited in an efficient manner.

Structural biology of protein-protein complexes and integral membrane proteins are currently a high NIH priority due to their importance for systems biology, disease mechanisms and structure-guided drug development.

Hauptman Woodward Medical Research Institute has a data archive of millions of time-resolved crystallization images (from over 14,000 different biological macromolecules) that could be used to identify candidates likely to benefit from crystallization in microgravity.

Microheater Array Boiling Experiment

To characterize the boiling curve in a very low g-jitter environment: The experiment aims to determine the boiling curve in a microgravity environment with minimal gravitational disturbances (g-jitter).
This objective is driven by the understanding that g-jitter can significantly influence bubble dynamics and, consequently, the heat transfer process.
By minimizing g-jitter, the researchers hope to obtain a clearer picture of boiling behavior in a true microgravity environment.

To understand the parameters governing the size of the primary bubble and develop a predictive model for it: A key objective is to identify the factors that determine the size of the primary bubble in microgravity.
These parameters could include heater size, nucleation site density, subcooling, gravity level, fluid properties, superheated layer thickness, wall superheat, and surface tension.
By understanding these parameters, the researchers aim to develop a model that can accurately predict the primary bubble size under different conditions.

To investigate the mechanism of critical heat flux (CHF) in microgravity and its relationship to the primary bubble: The research aims to elucidate how CHF occurs in microgravity and to determine its relationship to the size and behavior of the primary bubble.
CHF is a critical parameter in boiling, representing the maximum heat flux that can be transferred from a surface before a transition to film boiling occurs.
Understanding the factors influencing CHF in microgravity is essential for the safe and efficient operation of space-based thermal systems.
To determine the effect of heater size on the formation of the primary bubble and its impact on the boiling curve: MABE investigates the influence of heater size on boiling behavior.

Two different heater array sizes are used, allowing the researchers to compare how heater size affects the formation of the primary bubble, the occurrence of dryout, and the shape of the boiling curve in microgravity.
MABE utilizes a multi-pronged approach to achieve its research objectives.
The experiment combines a carefully designed experimental setup with a comprehensive data analysis strategy.
Here's a breakdown of the key elements of the investigation approach:
Experimental Setup:
Microscale heater array: The experiment utilizes an array of 96 individually controlled platinum resistance heaters deposited on a quartz substrate.
Constant temperature control: Each heater is maintained at a constant temperature, allowing for accurate quantification of substrate heat conduction and reducing the risk of heater burnout.
Variable experimental conditions: The experiment manipulates key parameters such as bulk liquid subcooling, pressure, and heater size to study their influence on boiling.

Multiple gravity levels: The experiment is designed to allow data acquisition in Earth gravity, lunar gravity, Martian gravity, and microgravity, enabling a comprehensive comparison of boiling behavior across different gravitational environments.
High-speed video imaging: A high-speed digital camera captures images of the boiling process beneath the heater array, providing valuable insights into bubble dynamics.
Interferometry: The experiment employs interferometry to measure temperature profiles around the vapor bubble, providing additional data for analysis.
Data Acquisition and Analysis:
Data Acquisition: Data is collected at a high frequency, capturing the instantaneous power dissipated by each heater, bulk fluid temperature, pressure, and acceleration.
Data Processing: Raw data is converted into engineering units, synchronized, and analyzed to generate boiling curves, heat transfer maps, and other relevant data visualizations.

Correlation with video and interferometry data: The heat transfer data is correlated with visual observations from the high-speed video and interferometry data to gain a deeper understanding of bubble behavior and heat transfer mechanisms.
Analytical and Numerical Modeling: The experiment employs analytical and numerical models to simulate the boiling process and validate the experimental findings.
Ground-Based Testing and Validation:

Preliminary Engineering Model: A preliminary engineering model of the experiment is developed and tested on the KC-135 aircraft, providing essential validation of the design and data acquisition procedures.
Calibration and Validation: The heater array is calibrated on the ground and recalibrated in flight to ensure accurate measurements.
This investigation approach combines a sophisticated experimental setup with rigorous data analysis and modeling to provide a comprehensive understanding of boiling in microgravity.

This study will test three central hypotheses: (1) Bubble coalescence dominates heat transfer in microgravity, creating a large primary bubble that induces local dryout; (2) A transition between buoyancy-dominated and surface-tension-dominated boiling regimes occurs depending on the interplay between the heater size and the gravitational acceleration; (3) Heat transfer in the surface-tension-dominated regime shows minimal dependence on gravitational acceleration.
In microgravity, a bubble can cover an entire heater array instead of just a small area, resulting in burnout of components if local hot spots are present.
The increased spatial resolution of these measurements will enable the extent of the dry spot to be measured along with the heat transfer from the liquid surrounding the dry spot.
This technique can be applied to other areas including spray cooling, turbulence measurements and flow boiling.
The proposed research has shown that transient conduction is the dominant heat transfer mechanism in boiling of refrigerants-like fluids.
This research will provide insight into creating more efficient cooling systems on Earth.

Microstructure Formation in Casting of Technical Alloys under Diffusive and Magnetically Controlled Convective Conditions/Comparison of Structure and Segregation in Alloys Directionally Solidified in Terrestrial and Microgravity Environments

The objective of the proposed investigation is to better understand how the intensity of convection and the direction of the flow influences the evolution of the mushy zone, macro- and micro-segregation, morphology of dendrites, the growth mode and spatial arrangement of intermetallic precipitates.
3 different Al-Si alloys were directionally solidified under different thermal gradient and furnace translation velocities.
Along with micro and macro-segregation, dendritic characteristics including primary arm spacing and trunk diameters were quantified.
Microgravity results were compared to those obtained under terrestrial conditions.
A finite volume modeling approach was undertaken in the absence of convection and predictions were compared to data obtained from microgravity and terrestrial samples.
Dendritic metrics of the directionally solidified (DS) samples are expected to have dendritic characteristics that compare very well to model predictions for growth in the absence of convection.
Earth-grown samples are not anticipated to compare well, indicating that the convection in Earth grown alloys does indeed play a role in microstructural development during the solidification process.

Further, Earth-grown samples exhibit a type of macrosegregation called ''steepling” in which the periphery of a DS-ed sample is of eutectic composition and is seen in alloys with solutes that increase the density of the liquid during solidification.
Samples grown aboard the ISS are not expected to have steepling.
The research is relevant to a process known as directional solidification, which is used for producing critical castings that are used in gas turbine engines.
Gas turbine engines power aircraft (i.e., often called ''jet engines'') and are also used to generate electric power.

These castings are made of vacuum melted alloys that are capable of withstanding the demanding conditions at high temperatures and consequently the metallurgical structure of the alloys must be of the highest quality.

The research is leading to an improved understanding of how microstructures and segregation form in directionally solidified castings; hence the science of producing such castings will be enhanced as a result of the research.
In addition, the research findings relate to many other types of castings, including billets and ingots, of alloys (i.e., steel, aluminum alloys, etc.) that are critical for metal fabrication.
In addition, the benchmark microgravity data allows validation of models predicting dendritic metrics such as primary and secondary arm spacing and trunk diameter.
Such validated simulation models can enable optimization of casting parameters.

Microgravity Investigation of Cement Solidification - Multi-use Variable Gravity Platform

The purpose of the MICS-MVP is to investigate and understand the complex process of cement solidification as a function of variable gravity and to advance the use of concrete materials for extraterrestrial infrastructure.
MICS-MVP will identify the differences between the hydration reaction and microstructural formation at the different gravity levels.

Two different mixture combinations of with water and gypsum and tricalcium silicate (C3S) with water were hydrated under 5 different gravity levels, namely, Earth's gravity, microgravity, and simulated gravity levels of the Moon, Mars, and a statistical point at 0.7g.
The different components were each placed in opposing compartments of a plastic pouch and separated by a middle burstable seal.
To burst the seal, the water filled compartment was rolled up from the outside edge towards the middle until enough forward pressure was achieved to burst the seal.

The water is then completely moved into the compartment containing the tricalcium aluminate (C3A) or tricalcium silicate (C3S) and the paste is mixed by a rubber spatula and/or kneaded by hand to reach a homogeneous state.
A plastic clip is then attached to help consolidate the paste at one end of the pouch.
This mixing procedure generally took a few minutes per sample.

The ISS itself provides a microgravity environment, whereas the gravity levels of extraterrestrial bodies that are less than Earths were simulated with centrifugal forces within the Multi-use Variable-gravity Platform (MVP).
Samples at different gravity levels were hydrated for different lengths of time, following which the centrifuge was shut off and the samples continued to hydrate till they were returned to earth.
The samples were characterized for pore size, pore distribution, portlandite size distribution, crystal morphology, and phase content.

It is hypothesized that under variable reduced gravity conditions different transport phenomena such as buoyancy, sedimentation, and convection are minimized and a more diffusion dominant transport will lead to varying degree of uniformity in distribution ofphases, porosity, and crystal morphology.

A different microstructure is expected to form in at different gravity levels which possibly leads to different physical properties of the reduced gravity hardened cement paste with respect to that hardened in terrestrial gravity (1g).
The MICS investigation directly addresses the high priority need for lightweight space structures for habitats that protect crew.

Results from this investigation enable the characterization of microstructural development in the hardening of cement paste and improve understanding of crystal growth and hydration kinetics, phase formations, pore distribution, and material properties.
Also, MICS can increase understanding and control of the crystal growth kinetics, and morphology, to improve concrete properties.
Improved cement properties can lead to improved concrete properties, durability, and lower CO2 emission.

Microgravity Investigation of Cement Solidification

The objective of the proposed investigation is to better understand the complex process of cement solidification by conducting experiments in the microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and further the development of an in-situ lunar concrete material.

Several different mixture combinations of tricalcium aluminate (C3A), tricalcium silicate (C3S), ordinary portland cement (OPC), superplasticizer (SP) and ratios of cement to water were packed in commercially available plastic bags (Burst Pouches®) with separate compartments divided by an internal, burstable seal which allowed mixing of materials under sealed conditions in microgravity and terrestrial conditions.
Space and ground samples were mixed simultaneously and at the same conditions of 20 ºC ± 2 ºC, 1 ATM and 35% RH.
As such, gravity is considered the only variable between the space and ground experiments.

After a specific period of hydration samples were subjected to a wide variety of characterization techniques such as image analysis and mercury intrusion porosimetry (MIP) to assess porosity and pore size distribution, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) to estimate degree of hydration, x-ray diffraction (XRD) for crystalline phase identification, energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) and electron microprobe analysis (EMPA) for compositional analysis.
Phase distribution, pore structures, and crystal morphology as a function of composition and gravity level was documented.

The research hypothesis for the ISS experiments is that minimizing gravity-driven transport phenomena, such as buoyancy, sedimentation, and convection results in a purely diffusion-controlled hydration process.
Without the physical effects induced by gravity, diffusion will lead to a more uniform distribution of phases.

As such, the dissolving cement particles will disperse in the aqueous solution, resulting in greater uniformity of features such as pore structures and crystal morphology in the hardened cement matrix.

A different microstructure is expected to form in microgravity (µg), which possibly leads to different physical properties of µg-hardened cement paste with respect to that hardened in terrestrial gravity (1g).
The MICS investigation directly addresses the high priority need for lightweight space structures for habitats that protect crew.

Results from this investigation enable the characterization of microstructural development in the hardening of cement paste and improve understanding of crystal growth and hydration kinetics, phase formations, pore distribution, and material properties.
Also, MICS can increase understanding and control of the crystal growth kinetics, and morphology, to improve concrete properties.
Improved cement properties can lead to improved concrete properties, durability, and lower CO2 emissions.
