Nucleate Pool Boiling eXperiment
The primary objective of the proposed study is to develop a mechanistic model for nucleate boiling under microgravity conditions.

Specific objectives included: - Single bubble dynamics (nucleation, growth, and departure) under microgravity conditions under constant wall temperature. - Effect of liquid subcooling, wall superheat, and system pressure on single bubble dynamics. - Heat flux variation on the heated surface during single bubble evolution. - Lateral merger of bubbles formed at neighboring sites and mechanism of vapor removal from the surface.
The research utilized a systematic and comprehensive approach to understand the complexities of nucleate pool boiling in a microgravity environment.

The approach was characterized by a strategic ''building block'' strategy, progressing from simpler to more complex scenarios, enabling a gradual and insightful understanding of the underlying physics.
Here's a detailed breakdown of the investigation approach:
Single Bubble Dynamics:
The research commenced by focusing on the behavior of a single bubble nucleating from a pre-fabricated cavity on the aluminum wafer.
This fundamental building block allowed for a detailed examination of bubble growth, departure (if any), and the associated heat transfer processes in microgravity conditions.
Multiple Bubble Mergers:
Building upon the knowledge gained from single bubble studies, the investigation then explored the interactions of multiple bubbles.
Experiments were conducted to study the merger of bubbles nucleating from different cavities.

This stage investigated how bubbles merge in the lateral direction, the mechanisms of vapor removal from the heated surface after merger, and the impact of these interactions on the overall heat transfer rates.
Integral Nucleate Boiling:
The investigation then broadened its scope by conducting experiments with boiling occurring over the entire heater surface.
This aimed to obtain the boiling curve, which depicts the relationship between heat flux and wall superheat, under microgravity conditions.
This provided a macroscopic view of nucleate pool boiling, considering the collective behavior of numerous bubbles.
Numerical Simulations:
The experimental work was tightly coupled with complete numerical simulations of the boiling process.
These simulations employed advanced computational fluid dynamics (CFD) techniques to capture the intricate details of bubble dynamics and heat transfer.

The simulations accounted for a range of factors including time-varying system pressure and temperatures, the presence of dissolved gas in the liquid, surface tension effects, and the influence of microlayer evaporation.
The numerical model was rigorously validated against the experimental data obtained in the NPBX experiments.
Model Development:
The ultimate goal of the research was to develop a mechanistic model for nucleate pool boiling heat transfer under microgravity conditions.

This model, based on the physical understanding derived from experimental observations and validated numerical simulations, aimed to provide a reliable tool for predicting boiling behavior across a wide range of parameters and conditions relevant to space applications.

In microgravity conditions, where buoyancy forces become negligible, it is expected that forces arising from the inertia of the liquid, evaporation, and condensation at the vapor-liquid interface, disjoining pressure, capillary pressure gradient, and the resulting flow field will become more dominant.
The study aimed to understand and quantify the effect of these forces and identify the conditions under which quasi-static or steady-state boiling is possible under prolonged microgravity duration.

While the primary motivation for this investigation was to advance our understanding of boiling heat transfer in the context of space applications, the knowledge gained has significant implications for Earth-based technologies and scientific understanding as well.
Here are some key potential impacts and benefits:
Improved Understanding of Boiling at Earth Gravity:

By studying boiling in a microgravity environment where buoyancy forces are negligible, researchers can gain a clearer understanding of the interplay of other forces and phenomena that influence boiling behavior.
This knowledge can, in turn, enhance our comprehension of boiling processes under Earth's gravity, where buoyancy often masks the effects of these more subtle factors.
Development of More Efficient Heat Transfer Systems:
The insights gained from this research can contribute to the development of more efficient boiling heat transfer systems for a wide range of applications on Earth.
Enhanced efficiency translates to reduced energy consumption, lower operational costs, and a reduced environmental footprint.
Advancements in Miniaturization of Electronics:
As electronic devices continue to shrink in size, effective thermal management becomes increasingly critical.

Understanding boiling in microgravity is crucial for developing innovative cooling solutions for miniaturized electronics, as these devices often operate at high heat fluxes and face challenges in dissipating heat effectively.
New Insights into Fluid Physics:
This research offers valuable insights into fundamental fluid physics phenomena, including the behavior of bubbles, interfacial phenomena, and the dynamics of multiphase flows.
This knowledge can lead to advancements in diverse fields, such as materials science, biomedical engineering, and environmental science.

Observation and Analysis of Smectic Islands in Space
OASIS studies the unique behavior of liquid crystals in microgravity, including their overall motion and the merging of crystal layers known as smectic islands.
Liquid crystals are used for display screens in televisions and clocks, and they also occur in soaps and in cell membranes.
The experiment allows detailed studies of the behavior of these structures, and how microgravity affects their unique ability to act like both a liquid and a solid crystal.

The specific research objectives are: -To exploit the unique characteristics of freely suspended liquid crystals in a microgravity environment to advance the understanding of fluid state physics. -Study basic 2D hydrodynamics/fluid physics, probe droplet/island diffusion, hydrodynamic interactions, and droplet/island coalescence
The OASIS experiment’s goal is to better understand the unique behavior of liquid crystals in microgravity.

OASIS observes the various aspects of liquid crystals behavior in microgravity such as overall fluid motion, diffusion (the movement of particles from an area of high concentration to low concentration) and the merging of liquid crystal film layers called islands, Fundamental studies of complex fluid physics behavior will be accomplished in two dimensional fluids using freely suspended liquid crystals.
The impact of the research is to advance the understanding of two-dimensional system physics of complex fluids.
Space helmets could use ferroelectric liquid crystal micro-displays.
It could advance the understanding of well aligned very high speed electro-optic devices.

In a microgravity environment, freely suspended smectic liquid crystal (FSLC) films will exhibit unique hydrodynamic and interfacial behaviors, such as reduced coarsening rates of island emulsions, enhanced 2D thermocapillarity effects, and distinct equilibrium spatial organization of islands, due to the absence of gravitational forces, convection, and sedimentation, enabling precise tests of theoretical models of 2D hydrodynamics and phase behavior.
Future space helmets may use certain types of liquid crystals in small display screens directly applied to the face shield where astronauts can easily view them.
Understanding how liquid crystals behave in microgravity helps researchers to design liquid crystal displays (LCDs) that can perform better in space.
Liquid crystals can flow like a liquid, but contain molecules that are arranged in a specific pattern, just like a crystal.
Greater understanding of the physics behind these structures could lead to improved liquid crystal display devices, including devices with improved color contrast and response times.
It could also advance research in high-speed electro-optic devices used to control a light beam.

Pool Boiling Experiment
The program described here seeks to improve the understanding of the fundamental mechanisms that constitute nucleate pool boiling.

The vehicle for accomplishing this is an investigation, including experiments to be conducted in microgravity and coupled with appropriate analyses, of the heat transfer and vapor bubble dynamics associated with nucleation, bubble growth or collapse, and subsequent motion.
Certain effects that can be neglected at normal Earth gravity, such as surface tension and vapor momentum, can become quite significant in microgravity.

Momentum imparted to the liquid by the vapor bubble during growth tends to draw the vapor bubble away from the surface, depending on the rate of growth, which in turn is governed by the temperature distribution in the liquid.
Thermophoretic forces, arising from the variation of the liquid-vapor surface tension with temperature, on the other hand, tend to move the vapor bubble toward the region of higher temperature.
The bubble motion will be governed by which of these two effects prevail.
The elements of nucleate boiling, for which research conducted under microgravity would advance the basic understanding, are:
Nucleation or onset of boiling.
Indications are that both heater surface temperature and temperature distribution in the liquid are necessary to describe nucleation.
The dynamic growth of a vapor bubble in the vicinity of the heater surface.
This includes the shape as well as motion of the liquid-vapor interface as growth is taking place.
These are influenced by the liquid temperature distribution at the initiation of growth.
The subsequent behavior of the vapor bubble.
This includes the motion, whether departure takes place or not, and the associated heat transfer.
The approach encompasses a comprehensive experimental methodology designed to dissect the nuances of the boiling process in an environment where gravity's influence is minimal.
This approach aims to isolate and analyze the core mechanisms that drive nucleate pool boiling, offering insights that are obscured under normal Earth gravity conditions.
Here is an outline of the investigation's methodological approach:
Experimental Setup in Microgravity: a.

The investigation utilizes a specially designed experimental apparatus capable of accurately controlling and measuring heat flux, liquid subcooling levels, and temperature distribution within the liquid and at the heater surface.
This apparatus is deployed in a microgravity environment provided by space-based platforms to ensure the minimization of gravity's influence on the boiling process.
Controlled Heat Flux Application: a.
A key component of the approach involves applying a controlled heat flux to a pool of liquid, initiating the boiling process.
The heat flux is carefully modulated to explore a range of boiling conditions, from gentle nucleation to vigorous boiling, under varying levels of liquid subcooling.
High-Resolution Data Acquisition: a.

To capture the dynamics of bubble formation, growth, and departure, the investigation employs high-resolution, high-speed imaging techniques, along with precise temperature and heat flux measurement tools.
This data acquisition setup allows for the detailed observation and analysis of bubble behavior and heat transfer phenomena during the boiling process.
Parameter Variation: a.

The investigation systematically varies key parameters, including the heat flux magnitude, the degree of liquid subcooling, and the pressure within the system, to study their effects on the nucleation process, bubble dynamics, and heat transfer rates.
This parameter variation helps in identifying the critical factors that influence nucleate pool boiling under microgravity.
Data Analysis and Model Development: a.

The collected data undergoes rigorous analysis to elucidate the fundamental mechanisms of nucleate pool boiling, focusing on nucleation criteria, bubble growth rates, and heat transfer characteristics.
Insights gained from the analysis are used to develop and refine predictive models that can accurately describe boiling behavior under a variety of conditions.
Cross-Comparison with Earth Gravity Data: a.
Findings from the microgravity experiments are compared with data obtained from similar experiments conducted under Earth gravity conditions.

This cross-comparison aids in isolating the effects of gravity on the boiling process and contributes to the development of generalized models that can predict boiling behavior across different gravitational environments.

Packed Bed Reactor Experiment - 2
The objective of the flight experiment is to study the hydrodynamics of packed beds in microgravity and under different conditions that lead to different flow regimes.
The hydrodynamics consists of the pressure drop inside the packed bed and the liquid hold-up.
The different regimes are the results of different liquid and gas flow rates, and different initial conditions embodied by gas and liquid pre-flows or flushes prior to beginning of the runs.
Another objective of the experiment was to understand transient flow rates and the hysteresis in the pressure drop as a function of the flow rates.
The PBRE-2 investigations employed a systematic and comprehensive approach to study the hydrodynamics of two-phase flow in packed bed reactors under microgravity conditions.
The approach can be summarized in the following key steps:

Ground-Based Research and Model Development: Prior to the spaceflight experiments, extensive ground-based research was conducted to develop theoretical models and establish a foundation for understanding two-phase flow in packed beds.

This included: Literature review: A thorough review of existing literature on single-phase and two-phase flow through porous media, focusing on pressure drop, flow regimes, and the influence of various parameters.
Development of hydrodynamic models: Formulation of mathematical models, such as the modified Ergun equation, to predict pressure drop and flow regime transitions in microgravity.
Ground-based experiments: Conducting experiments in reduced gravity environments, such as parabolic flights and drop towers, to gather preliminary data and validate initial model predictions.
Design and Development of Spaceflight Experiment: A dedicated experimental facility was designed and developed for operation on the ISS.

This involved: Test facility design: Engineering a flow control system, test section, and data acquisition system capable of operating reliably in microgravity and meeting the specific requirements of the investigation.
Definition of test matrix: Developing a comprehensive test matrix encompassing a wide range of gas and liquid flow rates, pre-flow conditions, and transient flow scenarios.
Execution of Spaceflight Experiments: The PBRE-2 experiments were conducted on the ISS, following the defined test matrix and procedures.
This involved: Preflow procedures: Implementing the chosen pre-flow treatment (liquid flush or gas flush) before each test run.
Flow control: Precisely controlling and varying the gas and liquid flow rates according to the test matrix.
Data acquisition: Collecting data from pressure sensors, temperature sensors, and high-speed cameras throughout each test run.
Downlinking data: Transmitting the acquired data to the ground for analysis.

Data Analysis and Interpretation: The downlinked data was meticulously analyzed to: Characterize flow regimes: Identify and classify the different flow regimes observed in the experiments based on pressure traces and video recordings.
Evaluate pressure drop: Analyze the pressure drop data and compare it with model predictions to assess the validity and accuracy of the models.
Investigate flow regime transitions: Determine the conditions and mechanisms leading to transitions between different flow regimes.
Assess the influence of packing properties and pre-flow conditions: Analyze the impact of packing material wettability, size, and pre-flow treatments on the flow behavior and pressure drop.

Dissemination of Results: The findings of the PBRE-2 investigations were disseminated through: Peer-reviewed publications: Publishing research papers in scientific journals to share the results with the broader scientific community.
Presentations at conferences: Presenting the research findings at relevant scientific conferences and workshops.

It is hypothesized that in microgravity two-phase packed bed flows, pressure drop will be a function of surface tension (captured by a modified Ergun equation), packing wettability and size, and pre-flow conditions.
Furthermore, bubble removal will depend on bubble volume and liquid flow rate, and distinct flow regimes will emerge, with transitions governed by specific gas and liquid flow rate combinations.

Fundamental understanding the impact of reduced or zero gravity on the hydrodynamics (pressure drop, as well as distribution and holdup of each phase) is relevant to systems that involve two-phase flow such as life support systems, fuel cells, in-situ resource utilization, heat pipes, materials processing, production of pharmaceutical-grade water, and transport of nutrients in soils.

Design and operation of many chemical and biological processing systems require this fundamental understanding of two-phase gas-liquid flows through porous media because many of these space-based systems or unit operations involve gas-liquid flows through porous media.

Some examples of current space systems involving two-phase flow through fixed porous media include the Volatile Removal Assembly (VRA), the Integrated Advanced Water Recovery System (AWRS), and IntraVenous Water GENeration system (IVGEN).
The ability to predict flow regimes and corresponding pressure drop in a particular system involving two-phase flow is crucial to the design of the fluid system and the pumping requirements.

Packed Bed Reactor Experiment
The PBRE studies the behavior of gases and liquids when they flow simultaneously through a column filled with fixed porous media.

The porous media or “packing” can be made of different shapes and materials and are used widely in chemical engineering as a means to enhance the contact between two immiscible fluid phases (e.g., liquid-gas, water-oil, etc.).
Packed columns can serve as reactors, scrubbers, strippers, etc. in systems where efficient interphase contact is desired, both on Earth and in space.
The PBRE investigation employs an approach that combines theoretical modeling with rigorous experimental testing to achieve its objectives.
Here's a breakdown of the key aspects:
Theoretical Modeling:
Existing Models: PBRE builds upon existing models for pressure drop and flow regime transitions in packed bed reactors, particularly those developed by Motil et al.
(2003) and Guo et al.
Model Validation: The experiment focuses on validating these models, extending them to lower flow rates relevant to water recovery systems, and bridging them with other models.
New Models: The data collected through PBRE is used to develop new models and scaling laws that accurately predict flow characteristics in 0-g and partial-g environments.
Experimental Setup and Procedures:
Test Sections: PBRE utilizes two identical test sections, each a 60 cm long, 5 cm diameter cylindrical column.
One section is packed with glass beads (wetting), the other with Teflon beads (non-wetting) to isolate surface tension effects.
Fluid Flow: The experiment uses nitrogen and water as the gas and liquid phases, with a wide range of flow rates, from very low to high, to cover operational regimes.
Instrumentation: A comprehensive suite of sensors is used to measure flow rates, temperatures, and pressures.
The experiment also includes two high-speed video cameras to visualize flow patterns.
Test Matrix: The investigation is organized into several test series (''Ops''), each focused on specific flow conditions and packing materials.
Data Acquisition: The experiment meticulously collects data, with careful time-correlation of measurements to ensure accurate analysis.
Addressing Anomalies:
Flow Rate Control: The team encountered anomalies with the GN2 flow rate and pressure fluctuations, leading to troubleshooting and adjustments in the experiment's setup and procedures.
High-Speed Video: The cameras experienced limitations with operating at the desired frame rates, requiring modifications to data acquisition strategies.
Data Analysis:
Model Validation: Data is analyzed to compare experimental results with model predictions, identifying any discrepancies and refining the models.
New Model Development: The collected data is used to develop new models and scaling laws, aiming for greater accuracy and applicability in microgravity environments.
Data Organization:
Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI): The PBRE team meticulously organizes the experimental data in PSI, a database for physical sciences data, to ensure accessibility and analysis.
The PBRE investigation relies on a combination of theoretical modeling, rigorous experimental testing, and comprehensive data analysis to achieve its objectives.

This approach is designed to contribute to a deeper understanding of the behavior of packed bed reactors in microgravity, leading to improved design tools and operational strategies for future space applications.
Dissemination of Results:
The findings of the PBRE-2 investigations were disseminated through:
Peer-reviewed publications: Publishing research papers in scientific journals to share the results with the broader scientific community.
Presentations at conferences: Presenting the research findings at relevant scientific conferences and workshops.
Reports and documentation: Preparing detailed reports and documentation of the experimental procedures, data analysis, and conclusions.

It is hypothesized that the gravity plays a significant role in determining the flow characteristics (pressure drop, flow regime transitions, liquid holdup, and mass transfer) of gas-liquid flows through porous media.
Water-recovery systems, fuel cells and other equipment on the International Space Station use packed bed reactors, but currently none are designed to handle both liquid and gas at the same time.

With improved understanding of how packed bed two-phase flow works in microgravity, scientists are be able to design more efficient, lightweight thermal management and life support systems that use less energy, benefiting the Space Station and future lunar and Mars missions.
Design rules for gas-liquid flows through packed columns are well developed on Earth (i.e., for normal gravity) but lacking for reduced or zero gravity.
The Packed Bed Reactor Experiment seeks to fill this knowledge gap by studying the hydrodynamics of gas-liquid flows in zero gravity through packed columns.

By understanding how gravity affects gas-liquid flows through packed columns (or packed beds, as they are known in the industry) better, more predictive correlations for pressure drops and flow regime maps can be developed with the proper gravity-dependent terms included.

Physics of Colloids in Space

The primary objectives of the PCS investigation were to successfully grow binary colloidal crystal alloy structures to monitor their nucleation and growth kinetics with static and dynamic light scattering, determine their structures using laser light crystallography and the properties of the superlattices using dynamic light scattering.

In addition, the structure and dynamics of gel-like structures formed by colloid-polymer mixtures will be measured using static and dynamic light scattering and the ultimate equilibrium structures behavior of the mixture will be determined.
Finally, large scale fractal colloid aggregates and gels will be grown to measure their mechanical properties using dynamic light scattering, and potentially the cell oscillation techniques.

For binary colloidal crystal alloy the samples will consist of polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) particles, stabilized by a thin coating of poly-12-hydroxystearic acid, and suspended in a mixture of decalin and tetralin adjusted to exactly match the index of refraction of the PMMA.
Once in orbit, the samples will be homogenized by rapidly spinning each sample cell and suddenly stopping it.
Subsequent to homogenization, the nucleation and growth of the binary colloidal alloy crystallites will be monitored by static light scatter in the forward direction.
The small angle light scattering will be complemented by larger angle scattering examining the Bragg reflections of the crystals.
For the colloidal-polymer mixture part of the investigation the colloidal particles will again be PMMA spheres suspended in an index matched fluid.
The volume fractions of these samples will range from about 1% to 30%.
The polymer will be polystyrene, with a molecular weight ranging from about 100,000 to 1,000,000.
The colloid-polymer mixtures will be homogenized using the same procedure used for the binary colloid mixtures.
Immediately after they are homogenized, the small angle scattering will be monitored to measure the formation of the gel-like structure.
Dynamic light scattering will be performed concurrently as the gel forms to obtain a sensitive indication of the final formation of the gel.

Once equilibrium is achieved, if colloidal crystals are formed in one of the phases the growth and structure of the crystals will be studied using both powder average Bragg scattering and dynamic light scattering.
For the fractal colloidal aggregate and gels the aggregation of the colloidal particles will be initiated by mixing the colloidal suspension with another chemical that causes aggregation.
Upon initiation of the aggregation, the growth of the colloidal aggregates will be monitored by both dynamic and static light scattering.

In addition to the light scattering measurements, small amplitude oscillations of the gel structure will be performed to measure the shear modulus of the gel directly and compare with the light scattering measurements.

The availability of microgravity will allow binary colloidal superlattices to be formed from different materials providing new insights into the nucleation and growth kinetics of binary colloidal crystal alloy and thereby establish the new field of “colloid engineering.” This work will unambiguously determine the equilibrium phase diagram for attractive colloidal particles where the attraction is induced by depletion effects through the addition of polymer.
It will also provide important new insight into the transition between equilibrium and kinetically limited behavior, in the absence of sedimentation.

Further, this investigation will also lead to the fabrication of fractal colloidal structures that extend over the largest range of length scales ever produced, providing a critical test of our understanding of the formation of these structures.
With such extended structures, it will be possible to study their physical properties and determine the consequences of the scale invariance on the properties.
It will determine the fundamental limits of the range over which fractal structures can exist.
The long term goal of this research is to establish a new method of fabricating materials, “Colloid Engineering,” where novel materials are fabricated using colloidal particles as precursors.
With appropriate choices of the sizes of the particles, it should be possible to form colloidal alloy crystals of higher volume fraction than can be made with monodisperse particles.
These colloidal alloys may form the precursors for very high quality ceramics.
Alternatively, the particles could be made from different materials, forming colloidal superlattices with novel properties.
Then, for example, one set of particles could be plastic and the other set of particles could be a metal or a semiconductor.

Alternatively, these structures may be useful in forming materials with reduced phase space available for radiation, allowing a much simpler way of fabricating structures which possess photonic band gaps.
Colloid engineering may offer a simple method for making these materials that completely bypasses the difficulties faced by traditional lithography techniques.
The superlattices could also be used as novel optical switches or displays.

Pore Formation and Mobility Investigation
The scientific objective of the investigation was to observe porosity formation and its movement.
Methods to minimize porosity and its influence will also be examined.

Experimental variables that was investigated include, but are not limited to, bubble size, bubble number, imposed temperature gradient, material properties, and the effect of applying vibration to the system.
The role of ''spring and piston'' assemblages and in-situ thermocouples was also investigated and assessed.

The experimental approach consisted of employing a 10mm inside diameter quartz tubes on the order of 30 cm in length that was filled with pure succinonitrile (SCN) and SCN to which a small amount of water has been added to simulate alloy solidification.
To investigate pore formation the sample tubes was filled by, at least, the three following methods.
(1) Pieces of SCN was put in the tube.
(2) SCN was cast into the tube.
(3) SCN was cast into the tube and then be directionally solidified.
Case 1 ensured porosity in the sample, case 2 allowed porosity to develop, and case 3 was prepared with the intent of minimizing porosity.
Each sample tube was outfitted with an effective “spring and piston” assemblage and in-situ thermocouples.
While thermocouples were required to accurately characterize the temperatures and temperature gradients they could also act as sites for pore nucleation and holding.
The sample tubes were then inserted in a directional solidification furnace, which establishes a temperature gradient in the liquid and permits observation of the molten region.
The furnace mounts on g-limit, a MSFC developed vibration isolation platform; this assemblage fits and was designed to operate within the ISS microgravity Glovebox.
Porosity, which forms in the samples, was tracked and recorded with two video cameras set at 90 degrees from each other and orthogonal to the sample tube.

Direct observation of pore/bubble formation and their mobility during processing in a microgravity environment will provide insight regarding the minimization of this detrimental feature during solidification processing of important metal alloys and semiconductors.
PFMI provides insight on how materials solidify in the space environment.
Once this process is understood and improvements are made, future manufacturing processes can take place in the microgravity environment providing robust products.
On Earth, materials that contain pores created and trapped during solidification degrade properties and cause a distinct weakening in the overall structure of the cast product.
Examples of these materials include semiconductors and aircraft turbine blades.

Physics of Hard Spheres Experiment

By significantly reducing gravitational sedimentation the primary objective of this microgravity investigation was to quantify the volume fractions at which dispersions of hard spheres freeze, melt, and become glasses; the equilibrium structure associated with each phase; the dynamics of Brownian fluctuations in each phase; the kinetics of the nucleation and growth of the crystalline phase; the static elastic modulus of the crystalline and glassy phases; the low shear viscosity from the freezing point to close packing, and the yield stress and plasticity of the crystalline phase.
The experiment involved making a series of measurements on approximately 8 different samples of different concentrations (i.e. volume fractions of PMMA in an index matching fluid).
The samples were made from a mixture of decalin, tetralin, and PMMA spheres with a stabilizing polymer grafted onto them.

The decalin (index - 1.48) and the tetralin (index - 1.54) was mixed in a combination which index matches the PMMA (index - 1.51), allowing the use of single photon counting techniques to probe the particle dynamics at different concentrations.
Once in orbit, the experiment was initialized and each of the samples melted to start the nucleation and growth phase.
After melting, each sample was examined to ensure that complete melting has occurred, and immediate static scattering measurements will begin and progress for 24 hours on the nucleating sample.
After each melting phase, a concentration dependent nucleation and growth phase occurred and was monitored by static light scattering measurements.
These measurements proceeded while the experiment entered into an equilibration phase during which longer range order formed.

The static light scattering measurements proceeded until the Bragg peaks were well developed and sufficient data for ensemble averages were taken for a sound statistical basis for the conclusions intended to experimentally ascertain.
Periodic measurements, both static and dynamic, were made to gage the progress and determine if alternate procedures are required.
During this period, dynamic light scattering measurements were performed on the nucleating sample.
Other measurements such as rheology measurements were performed on the other seven samples after this 24 hours period.

Some colloids (a system of fine particles suspended in a fluid) have the ability to act like a gas, liquid, solid, or even glass, depending on the relative concentration between the suspended material and the solution they are suspended in, and/or the presence or absence of gravity.
The behavior of a densely packed colloid here on earth mimics glass in the distribution of its particles, while in space, the same density colloid acts more closely like a solid.
This results in a highly organized, lattice-like arrangement of particles in the colloid.

It is hypothesized that the complete set of data from the microgravity experiments to test scalings proposed in the literature, e.g. the shear rate dependence of the viscosity and the rate of crystal growth with either the short- or the long-term self diffusion coefficient; the relationships among the osmotic pressure, the static shear modulus, and the yield stress for solid phases.

The colloidal engineering process will play a fundamental role in the creation of new materials and products in space, such as optical switches and lasers for communications and displays, and 3D Bragg crystals for controlling light.

Understanding the physics describing the Packing of Hard Spheres has everyday impacts and benefits here on earth including Grain packing; Structure of Liquids, Solids and Glasses; Freezing Transition; Flow and Plasticity of Sand; Optimization of data storage and transmission in the presence of Noise and Opto-electronic Materials, Light Localization and Photonic Bandgaps.

The ultimate payoff will be a definitive set of data for the hard spheres useful for (a) testing fundamental correlations among physical properties, (b) serving as a reference for understanding the behavior of systems with more complex interaction potentials, and (c) guiding attempts to control or modify the structure of densely packed media.

Plasma Kristall-3 Plus
Plasma crystals are a new kind of matter, rediscovered in 1994.
They form under certain conditions in a complex (dusty) plasma.
There, the electrically charged dust particles arrange in a regular macroscopic crystal lattice.
This structure allows for an investigation of the properties of condensed matter on the kinetic level.
This means that basic processes, such as melting, can be followed by observing the motion of individual particles.
PK-3 will give investigators a better understanding of plasma in space and will determine the critical points for the plasma.
Gravity plays an important role for the structure of plasma crystals.
In microgravity large 3-dimensional plasma crystals can be grown and studied in detail on the most fundamental, the kinetic level.
Complex plasmas can be seen as model systems for the investigation of fundamental phenomena in liquids and crystals and provide information on the motion of single particles (“atoms”).
This provides new insights into the field of condensed matter.
PK-3 Plus is a symmetrical driven radio-frequency plasma discharge with special features for the investigation of complex plasmas under microgravity conditions.
As a second generation laboratory, PK-3 Plus provides major new possibilities for these investigations due to its design improvements relative to the first long-term experiment PKE-Nefedov.
The PK-3 Plus apparatus allows investigations at neutral gas pressures between 0.05 - 2.5 millibar and radio frequency (rf) power of 0.01 - 1 W.
The complex plasma can consist of monodisperse particles in a size range from 1 - 20 micrometers.
Up to six particle sizes can be added to the experimental volume.
It is possible to change the number of particles, the composition of particles, the plasma conditions and the neutral gas pressure during one experiment.

The particle cloud can be excited by an electrical low frequency signal on the electrodes (0.1 - 100 Hz at a maximum amplitude of 50 V) or by a low frequency modulation of the rf-amplitude in different wave forms (sinusoidal, square, pulse, etc.).
The PK-3 Plus investigation has two major pieces of equipment: the experimental block, and the telescience system (TS).
The research will be performed on the ISS inside the plasma chamber situated inside of the experimental block.
The experimental block is attached via a tube to the space environment to produce the prevacuum for turbomolecular pump, which can produce pressure in the plasma chamber less than 10-5 millibar.
The TS is the computer in which the chamber conditions can be altered via actuators in the experimental block and the storage unit for the data collected.

Pore-Mushy Zone Interaction during Directional Solidification of Alloys: Three Dimensional Simulation and Comparison with Experiments

The primary objective of this research was to develop a numerical 3D model capable of simulating the pore-mushy zone interaction during directional solidification of Succinonitrile -Water alloys in microgravity and test the simulation results against the Pore Formation and Mobility Investigation (PFMI) microstructural observations, quantitatively and qualitatively.

This investigation exploited forefront methods in microscale solidification and developed models based on phase filed (PF), cellular automaton (CA) and Lattice Boltzmann (LB) to simulate pore formation and its motion during directional solidification.

The results from the Pore Formation and Mobility Investigation (PFMI) experiments were conducted in the microgravity environment aboard the Space Station with the intent of better understanding the role entrained porosity/bubbles play on microstructure during controlled directional solidification (DS).
Several sets of time-temperature-interface-bubble interaction data were extracted and analyzed from the PFMI videos.
The simulation results were tested against the PFMI microstructural observations.

Previous real time observations in transparent analogues of interactions between a bubble and an array of primary dendrites are essentially “two-dimensional” (2D) and are affected by the “wall” effects.
Contrary to earlier belief, it is now recognized that the basic premise of such experiments, i.e.
2D dendrites represent morphology of a three-dimensional (3D) array, is false.

This investigation hypothesizes that understanding pore-mushy zone interaction in real castings requires both the experimental observations and also the theoretical/numerical modeling with 3D array of dendrites.
This investigation helped to explain fundamental aspects of the mechanisms that regulate the formation of microporosities.
The formation of these defects depends on microstructure features that cannot be properly captured by current meso- and macro-scale models based on averaging techniques.

The direct numerical simulation of bubble dynamics in a dendritic network can provide a relation between macroscopically observable variables like cooling rate or temperature gradient and difficult to measure dynamic microscopic features like microporosity distribution, interdendritic permeability, solute redistribution, and dendrite arm spacing.

This research not only provided valuable contribution to the understanding of pore-mushy zone interaction during solidification in the absence of gravity, which would be helpful for future in-space fabrication processes involving solidification, but it was a first step to quantitatively simulate such 3D interactions during terrestrial directional solidification in realistic size sample domains.

Although much observation has been done in pictures of static microstructures at different stages of solidification, it has never been possible to capture the dynamic response of these features in an evolving mushy zone.
This information is critical to assess, validate, and improve macroscale mushy zone models used in current casting and welding codes.

This campaign centered on four main objectives: (i) engineering the RSD to flight proven hardware, (ii) testing measurement and instrumentation methods aboard the ISS, (iii) studying protein kinetics under interfacial shear, and (iv) measuring and modeling protein solution rheology.
The primary obective of this investigation is to quantify the effects of flow on fibrillization in the bulk and at interfaces, specifically at the air/water interface.
This includes studying protein kinetics under interfacial shear, and measuring and modeling protein solution rheology.

The overall objective is project to advance the mechanistic description of fibrillization by determining how shearing flow affects each of the stages of amyloid formation process − protein unfolding and nuclei formation, growth into protofibrils, and elongation and intertwining into mature fibrils and fibril growth − without any influence from solid boundaries.
The Ring Shear Drop (RSD) is used to facilitate amyloidogenesis and study flow dynamics without solid wall interactions.
It uses surface tension to contain fluids in a microgravity environment.
Techniques like Particle Tracking Velocimetry (PTV) are used to measure fluid dynamics and protein interactions.
This information was used to create high-fidelity computational models.
Formation and flow of protein aggregates on the surface of the drop will be imaged by the microscope as a function of time.
The RSD imaged the surface of a 2.50 cm diameter drop of protein solution with shear imposed by the rotation of one of the two sharp-edged rings (essentially knife edges) that constrain the drop.
A separate measure of the turbidity quantified by the extinction of a light beam through the center of the drop provided an independent signal for fibril formation.
A variable degree of shear was imposed on the drop with a negligible contact with solid boundaries.
Velocity of the fluid on the surface of the drop will be determined by standard cross-correlation techniques from images obtained by the microscope.
Details regarding sample composition and experimental parameters can be found in RSD Experimental Table.

The absence of gravity in a microgravity environment will significantly alter the amyloid fibril formation process in proteins.The hypothesis tested was that if protein solutions in microgravity are seeded with fibrils and subject to steady interfacial shear, then amyloidogenesis will occur with the extent of gelation depending on total protein concentration.
Amyloid fibril formation in proteins is of great interest because of its role in diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s.

The microgravity environment aboard the ISS was utilized to study the biophysics of protein amyloidogenesis.

Flow effects on protein fibrillization was studied at fluid interfaces similar to physiological processes, as all brain tissue consists of interfaces with fluidity, being comprised of cell membranes.
The goal is to advance mechanistic descriptions of amyloid fibril formation.

Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I

The objectives of this investigation were to: (1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.
The Saffire-1 experiments was performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS.
The sample material for Saffire-I is a composite fabric called Sibal consisting of cotton on a fiberglass substrate (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight).
It has been used in many space experiments because it burns like cotton but maintains structural integrity after the cotton is consumed.
The sample was approximately 0.94 meters long and 0.4 meters wide, simulating a large piece of flammable fabric.
The Saffire-1 flight unit had a sample card installed in the middle of a large flow duct.
Air is drawn through the flow duct by fans located at the top of the duct with flow straighteners at the bottom of the experiment module.
Saffire-I was conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s.
Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras.

In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole faction, and two anemometer tracked flow velocity.
All data was compressed, and subsequently downlinked.

This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty.
While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return.
There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures.
To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew.
The Saffire-I experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high.
Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame.
Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size.
The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions.
Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.

Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight

Similar to the original SAME investigation, the primary objective of the SAME-R investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment.

One of the problems encountered during the SAME investigation was that after the thermal precipitators were returned to the ground, it was found that all the TEM grids were severely contaminated with some unidentified foreign particles, making these grids unusable although some of them showed shapes of certain types of smoke particles.
Based on that experience the SAME-R investigation employed several modification covering new materials, extended operating conditions, and diagnostic equipments.
SAME-R utilized the SAME hardware used on-orbit.

Based on the experience gained from SAME, SAME-R included the following modifications: 1) a new test material, Pyrell®, an intumescent fire-retardant foam by Foamex, was introduced to replace DBP samples, 2) test conditions were broadened including higher heating temperatures and no-flow during sample heating time, and 3) a new instrument, M-pass, developed in-house GRC, was used to replace one of the two Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures that includes a DustTrak and an ionization detector used in SAME.
SAME-R flight tests were conducted from July 16, to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test points.

After SAME-R flight tests, three major post–flight ground tests were performed to improve data reduction process and to validate the lognormal distribution assumption, the key to the moment method employed by SAME and SAME-R.

The three hypotheses that motivated the original SAME investigation is also applicable for the reflight SAME-R investigation: In a μg environment, with the absence of the strong buoyancy-induced flows, smoke particle growth from a pyrolyzing/smoldering source, as a result of nucleation, condensation, and coagulation, will lead to larger particles compared to those produced in 1g.
The formation of the larger particles is favored by the expected higher vapor concentration and smoke residence times near the source due to the reduced velocities and mixing at μg conditions.

In particular, it is hypothesized that liquid aerosol smokes produced in microgravity will exhibit substantially larger droplet sizes than under the same conditions in normal gravity (with a corresponding decrease in the particle number density for the same mass of smoke).

The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke.

Along with the results from the original SAME investigation, the results from SAME-R can lead to technology for an advanced fire detector for future spacecraft that will be used for long duration missions.
SAME will provide quantitative data on the sensitivity of these detectors to reduced gravity smokes that will allow evaluation of the adequacy of these existing technologies using relevant data.
The current Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression (FPDS) program plan allows for the re-evaluation of future sensor technology, to allow new technology and capability to be utilized.
The results from SAME are needed to provide the reduced gravity baseline data against which future detection technology developments can be evaluated.
The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories.
Accurate detection of smoke in these environments can save lives.

Shear History Extensional Rheology Experiment - II
SHERE-II investigation involves a non-Newtonian fluid that will undergo preshearing (rotation) for a specified period of time, followed by stretching.
This combination of shearing and extensional deformations is common in many earth-based polymer processing and manufacturing operations such as extrusion, blow-molding and fiber spinning.

However, in order to accurately predict the flow behaviour of polymeric fluids under such deformation histories, an accurate knowledge of the extensional viscosity of a polymer system and its variation with strain rate is critical and will be measured during this experiment.

The fundamental understanding and measurement of these complex fluids is important for containerless processing, a key operation for fabrication of parts, such as adhesives or fillers, using elastomeric materials on future exploration missions.

SHERE-II is designed to investigate the effects of a pre-shear history on the transient extensional viscosity in a uniaxial stretching flow for a model filled viscoelastic suspension (consisting of inert rigid non-Brownian spheres dispersed in a dilute polymer solution).This experiment will generate additional scientific data for dilute viscoelastic polymer solutions in a broad subclass of transient uniaxial extensional flows.Understanding extensional rheology is key in understanding how to process thermoplastic elastomers (flexible elastic polymeric materials), which are very resilient and can be made very thin, and hence, lightweight.Understanding the rheological properties of highly viscoelastic suspensions may be of paramount importance for lunar in-situ resource utilization and for the future construction of a permanent lunar base.SHERE can provide data for engineering design tools that are part of computer-assisted manufacturing (CAM) systems to ensure that the rheological properties of polymeric parts have not been impacted in a variable gravity environment

Understanding the extensional rheology of a complex fluid such as a liquid polymer is key for containerless processing because the absence of the bounding walls of a container or vessel removes the shearing component of the deformation which typically dominates earth-based processing operations.
The resulting flow is thus shear-free or extensional in character.
Containerless processing is a central component in the development of in-situ fabrication technology, such as a means of producing new parts on demand or replacing existing parts or tools.
This represents a critical element in the evolution of an autonomous exploration capability.
In-situ fabricated parts, which may include both new and recycled materials, will be composed of plastics, filled polymers, metals, ceramics and composites.

SHERE plays a role in SHERE plays a role in this area by measuring, in microgravity conditions, a material property that has a direct connection to in-situ manufacturing and fabrication of polymeric parts.

In-situ manufacturing operations can occur in microgravity or reduced gravity levels (e.g. on the Moon or Mars) and may include for example, the extrusion and processing of thermoplastic elastomer films, which are very resilient and can be made thin and lightweight.

These elastomeric materials may form the basis of adhesives and fillers utilized in a wide variety of repair applications, especially under a reduced gravity environment, such as the repair of space suits or other similar materials.

Understanding and exploiting the ability to fabricate new parts in-situ from a limited number of precursor components is critical in future space missions where weight plays a critical role in the overall cost of a mission.
Additionally, in-situ repair provides a means of maintaining systems during transport and during future exploration missions.
A fundamental understanding and measurement of the extensional rheology of complex fluids also allows Earth-based manufacturing processes to be controlled and improved.

Ground-based work using variants of the Filament Stretching Rheometer includes studies of spinnability, and the investigations of cohesive and adhesive instabilities which manifests themselves in adhesion and tackiness of materials.
It has lead to the development of a Resin-spinning technology that allows the formation of ultra-fine elastic threads analogous to spider-silks.
Control of the fluid shear history and extensional rheology of test fluid is essential to optimizing the ultimate web properties.

Extensional rheology is of critical importance in optimization of polymer processing operations that involve complex flows, i.e. flows that contain both shearing (rotation) and elongation (stretching) components.
Suspensions of particles in viscoelastic liquids are used in many terrestrial processing operations: polymer melts with fillers, ceramic pastes, biomedical materials, food, cosmetics or detergents.
The final properties of the suspensions are greatly determined by the shape, concentration and size of the filler.
In particular, the fillers can range from nanoscopic to microscopic characteristic dimensions, and this leads to very different types of flow behaviors, filler/matrix interactions and dynamics.

Shear History Extensional Rheology Experiment
The objective of this investigation was to study the effect of pre-shear on the transient evolution of the microstructure and viscoelastic tensile stresses for monodisperse dilute polymer solutions.

The SHERE flight experiment aimed to investigate and quantify, for the first time, the transient extensional stress growth characteristics of a dilute polymer solution after a defined pre-shear history.
Following the initial SHERE campaign a re-flight of the investigation was carried out as SHERE-R with additional experimental runs.

The test fluid used for this investigation was a dilute solution (0.025 wt.%) of a narrow polydispersity high molecular weight polystyrene (Mw equals 2.25×106 g/mol, PDI ≈ 1.02) dissolved in oligomeric styrene oil.
The FM core consists of two endplates and an inner shroud, which is slid back to deploy the fluid column between the two endplates.

A steady shear rate between 0 and 50 s-1 is then imposed on the fluid sample by rotating one endplate from 0 to 500 rpm for a predetermined time (5 to 60 s) while holding the other endplate stationary.

As soon as the rotation ceased, an elongational deformation was imposed by axially translating one of the endplates in an exponential manner in order to generate constant strain rates ranging from 0.1 to 5.0 s-1.
The tensile force and filament shape were monitored during the stretching flow.
The position of the moving plate is recorded to verify the imposed displacement profile.

By backlighting the test fluid with an electroluminescent panel and viewing the fluid column from above with a video camera, one half of the (symmetric) fluid column shape was recorded for subsequent image analysis in order to determine the evolution in the filament profile during stretching and subsequent relaxation.
The fluid and air temperatures were digitally recorded using thermistors for later post-processing and temperature correction.
After cessation of the extensional flow, the experiment monitored the subsequent evolution of the midpoint radius (via a laser micrometer), the filament shape, and the tensile force in the column.

Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment
Objective: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity.
Specific objectives of this investigation were:
To investigate the structure of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity to understand the stabilizing mechanisms at the flames base.
Determine the liftoff velocity limits for different fuels and burner diameters.
Evaluate the impact of fuel dilution with nitrogen on soot formation and flame stability.
Quantify the effects of microgravity on flame length and radiative heat loss compared to normal gravity conditions.
Validate numerical models for flame dynamics, soot production, and thermal radiation in non-premixed flames.
The SLICE apparatus consisted of a fan-driven flow duct, exchangeable burner tubes, and integrated sensors to measure flow rates and temperature.
This setup used several fuels such as methane, ethylene, and nitrogen-diluted mixtures.
Flames were then manually ignited and observed under controlled coflow air conditions.
A high resolution camera captured still images while sensor data was overlaid on these images.

The main objectives of STDCE-1 are to investigate: -The extent and nature of thermocapillary flows in transient periods as well as under steady conditions. -Temperature distributions along the free surface and in the bulk fluid. -The effect of the heating mode and the heating level on the flows. -The effect of the liquid free surface on the flows -The onset conditions and nature of oscillatory flows
The STDCE program employed a comprehensive and multifaceted approach to investigate the complexities of thermocapillary flow.
This strategy encompassed a combination of theoretical analysis, numerical modeling, ground-based experiments, and ultimately, microgravity experiments aboard the Space Shuttle.

Theoretical Analysis Dimensionless Parameters: Researchers derived and identified the key dimensionless parameters governing thermocapillary flow, including the Marangoni number (Ma), Prandtl number (Pr), aspect ratio (Ar), and the novel surface deformation parameter (S).
These parameters facilitated the understanding of the relative importance of different forces and physical mechanisms at play and provided a framework for data analysis and comparison.

Scaling Laws: By analyzing the governing equations and boundary conditions, scientists established scaling laws that characterized the behavior of key flow features, such as boundary layer thicknesses and velocity scales.
This theoretical groundwork offered valuable insights into the expected flow characteristics under different conditions.
Numerical Modeling Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD): Sophisticated CFD models were developed to simulate thermocapillary flow behavior under various conditions.
These models accounted for factors such as heat transfer, fluid properties, surface tension effects, and free surface deformation.

The numerical simulations provided detailed predictions of flow patterns, velocity distributions, and temperature profiles, serving as a basis for comparison with experimental data and for exploring a wider range of parameters than feasible experimentally.

Ground-Based Experiments Reduced-Gravity Simulations: Researchers conducted experiments in drop towers and other reduced-gravity facilities to observe thermocapillary flows under conditions with minimized buoyancy effects.
These experiments served as a stepping stone towards the microgravity experiments and provided preliminary data for model validation and refinement.

Test Fluid and Hardware Development: Extensive ground-based testing was undertaken to optimize the experimental setup, including the selection of the test fluid (silicone oil), the design of the test cell, and the development of flow visualization and temperature measurement techniques.

Microgravity Experiments Space Shuttle Missions: The culmination of the research effort involved conducting the STDCE experiments aboard the Space Shuttle, taking advantage of the extended microgravity environment to study thermocapillary flows over a broader range of parameters and conditions than possible on Earth.
This included meticulous execution of the test matrix, encompassing various heating modes, power levels, and free surface shapes, while collecting detailed flow visualization and temperature data.

Data Analysis and Model Validation Comparison of Results: The experimental data from both ground-based and microgravity experiments were rigorously analyzed and compared with the predictions from numerical models.

This iterative process allowed for the assessment of model accuracy, the identification of areas for improvement, and ultimately, a deeper understanding of the fundamental physics driving thermocapillary flow.

While the STDCE program was primarily driven by the need to understand and predict thermocapillary flow behavior in microgravity environments, its findings and technological advancements have yielded valuable insights and applications for Earth-based processes as well.

Enhanced Understanding of Thermocapillary Flows Fundamental Physics: STDCE significantly advanced the understanding of the fundamental physics governing thermocapillary flows, including the interplay between surface tension gradients, heat transfer, and fluid motion.
This knowledge provides a solid foundation for tackling complex fluid flow problems in various terrestrial applications.
Numerical Model Refinement: The experimental data from STDCE served as a critical benchmark for validating and refining numerical models used to predict thermocapillary flow behavior.
These improved models now offer more accurate and reliable predictions for a wider range of applications, both in space and on Earth.

Technological Advancements Non-Intrusive Measurement Techniques: The development and refinement of non-intrusive measurement techniques, such as infrared imaging and particle image velocimetry, for the STDCE have expanded the toolkit for studying fluid flows in various settings.
These techniques are now widely employed in research and industrial applications on Earth, including the study of combustion processes, crystal growth, and microfluidics.

Flow Visualization and Analysis: The advanced flow visualization and analysis methods developed for STDCE have facilitated the study of complex flow patterns and structures in various terrestrial applications.
These tools enable researchers and engineers to gain deeper insights into flow dynamics and optimize processes for improved efficiency and performance.

Earth-Based Applications Materials Processing: The insights gained from STDCE have direct relevance to materials processing techniques on Earth, particularly those involving free surfaces and high-temperature gradients, such as welding, crystal growth, and the fabrication of thin films and coatings.
Understanding and controlling thermocapillary flows in these processes can lead to improved product quality and reduced defect formation.

Microfluidics: The knowledge gained from STDCE is applicable to the burgeoning field of microfluidics, where surface tension forces play a dominant role in manipulating and controlling fluids at the microscale.
This has implications for the development of microfluidic devices for applications such as drug delivery, medical diagnostics, and chemical analysis.

Overall, the STDCE program, while initially motivated by the challenges of microgravity research, has generated valuable knowledge and technological advancements with far-reaching implications for various Earth-based applications.

The enhanced understanding of thermocapillary flow and the development of advanced measurement and analysis techniques have contributed to the advancement of materials processing, microfluidics, and numerous other fields, demonstrating the profound impact of fundamental scientific research on both space exploration and terrestrial technology.

Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-2
The main objectives of the present work are to investigate:
The onset conditions and nature of oscillatory flows.
The effect of the heating mode and the static free surface shape on the oscillations.
The shape and motion of the free surface during oscillations.
The coupling among the free surface deformation, the surface temperature distribution, and the velocity field.
The STDCE-2 investigation employed a systematic approach to explain the role of free surface deformation in oscillatory thermocapillary flows under microgravity conditions.
This approach comprised:

Controlled Variation of Key Parameters: -Container Size: Utilizing three chamber diameters (1.2 cm, 2.0 cm, 3.0 cm) allowed researchers to examine the influence of scale on the onset of oscillations and assess potential inertial effects. -Heating Mode: Employing both submerged heater (CT mode) and CO2 laser (CF mode) systems enabled the comparison of flow behavior under constant temperature difference and constant heat flux boundary conditions, respectively. -Free Surface Shape: Tests were conducted with flat, concave, and convex free surfaces to explore the interplay between surface curvature and flow dynamics.

Advanced Diagnostic Techniques: -Flow Visualization: The use of tracer particles enabled the visualization and qualitative characterization of flow patterns, including the three-dimensional, time-dependent structures observed during oscillations. -Infrared Imaging: An infrared scanner captured the temperature distribution across the oil's free surface, providing insights into the thermal gradients driving the thermocapillary flow and their evolution during oscillations. -Optical Deformation Measurement: A Ronchi system was employed to measure the free surface deformation and motions, allowing researchers to quantify the dynamic changes in surface shape and correlate them with observed flow behavior and temperature variations.

Interactive Operation: The experiment was conducted interactively, allowing the researchers on the ground to communicate with the astronauts onboard the Spacelab, observe the downlinked video images in real-time, and adjust test parameters based on the observed phenomena.
This flexibility facilitated the exploration of unexpected results and the fine-tuning of the experimental conditions to optimize data collection.
The STDCE-2 investigation gathered comprehensive data aimed at complex dynamics of oscillatory thermocapillary flows and verifying the hypothesized role of free surface deformation in their onset.

The onset of oscillatory thermocapillary flow, particularly in microgravity environments, is significantly influenced by free surface deformation, which acts in conjunction with the Marangoni number (Ma). • Buoyancy masks the true oscillation mechanism in Earth- based experiments: The experimental data on oscillatory thermocapillary flows taken in normal gravity environments are often confusing or contradictory due to the presence of buoyancy.

This suggests that buoyancy may obscure the role of free surface deformation in the oscillation process. • Marangoni number alone is insufficient to predict oscillations in microgravity: The unexpected stability observed in the prior STDCE microgravity experiments, even at Marangoni numbers exceeding the critical threshold observed in ground-based tests, indicates that Ma is not the sole determinant of oscillatory onset in the absence of buoyancy. • Free surface deformation is a key factor: The interaction between thermocapillary forces and free surface deformation plays a key role in the oscillation mechanism.

The objective of the proposed investigation is to better understand the columnar-to-equiaxed grain structure transition (CET) in solidification of metal alloys.

By performing solidification experiments both on earth and in a microgravity environment, the effects of gravity-driven melt convection and sedimentation/floatation of unattached dendrite fragments and equiaxed crystals on the CET will be examined.
The origin of equiaxed grains in non-refined alloys is of particular interest in the proposed experiments.
The benchmark data from these experiments can be used to test theoretical models and computer simulations.
Experiments were conducted in the Solidification Using a Baffle in Sealed Ampoules (SUBSA) furnace to investigate the CET for stationary samples without an imposed temperature gradient.
Most experiments with aluminum-copper (Al-Cu) alloys, namely, Al-4wt%Cu, Al-10wt%Cu and Al-18wt%Cu alloys.
The reason is that Al-Cu alloys are better suited for the duplicate ground-based experiments.
If solidified upward (low temperature at the bottom, high at the top), thermosolutal natural convection of the melt will generally be minimized.
The sedimentation or floatation of dendrite fragments and small equiaxed grains can be controlled by the solute concentration.
For smaller solute concentrations, the solid is heavier than the melt and will sediment, while for higher solute concentrations the solid is lighter and will float.
Hence, dendrite fragments and equiaxed grains in the Al-18wt%Cu alloy will float upwards ahead of the columnar front, and a CET can be expected.
On the other hand, for the Al-4wt%Cu alloy, the fragments will sediment and remain between the primary columnar trunks, and a CET may not occur.
For Al-10wt%Cu alloys, the solid is approximately neutrally buoyant in the melt.
An additional experiment with an unrefined Al-7wt%Si alloy was also conducted.
No grain refiner was used.
In all proposed CET experiments, the samples were first fully melted and then solidified by decreasing the temperature of the SUBSA furnace at a controlled rate.
The samples were not moved, and no temperature gradient were explicitly imposed.
Corresponding flight and terrestrial experiments were conducted.
Samples were analyzed by measuring the grain structure and any macrosegregation.
The primary hypothesis of this investigation is that fragmentation of columnar dendrites can lead to a CET in non-grain-refined alloys.
The secondary dendrite arms that detach from the primary columnar trunks are a potent source of new (equiaxed) grains.
However, for a CET to occur the growth of the primary columnar trunks must be blocked by equiaxed grains.
This can only be accomplished if the secondary dendrite fragments are transported to the columnar front, rather than remain between the primary columnar trunks.
Due to natural convection of the melt and sedimentation or floatation of the fragments, such transport can be expected to readily occur in the gravitational field of earth.
In the absence of gravity, it is not clear if fragmentation alone, without fragment transport, is sufficient to cause a CET.
The CET refers to the transition between the elongated grains in the outer portions of a casting and the more rounded grains in the center.
Understanding this transition is fundamental to determining what type of grain structure forms in castings of most metal alloys (steel, aluminum, copper, etc.).
Often, a fully equiaxed structure is preferred, but the fully columnar structures of many turbine blades are an important exception.
In addition to its high practical significance, the CET represents a “holy grail” in the area of modeling and simulation of casting.
This is because in order to realistically predict the CET, almost every physical phenomenon at every length scale must be taken into account simultaneously.

This investigation will not only provide an improved understanding of the CET, but also models and computer simulations of the grain structure formation in metal castings that can be used by industry to better industry to better understand and optimize their casting processes.

Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis

The objective of this ground investigation was to use flight data obtained from PSI through NASA’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and ultimate fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by isolating the roles of deliberate heating and unintentional drift-induced convection.

Focusing on both small and large droplets, the work mapped stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transitions to hot ignition and warm-flame behavior, and extinction under microgravity.
By leveraging and extending the FLEX data in the PSI, this study produced reusable models and sensitivity analyses that coupled low-temperature chemistry with transport and radiative effects.

OpenFOAM was used to develop a 3-D CFD model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity, coupling variable-density Navier–Stokes flow with low-temperature combustion chemistry, coupled heat and mass transfer, and radiation.

Model fidelity was established against ISS FLEX measurements, after which controlled simulations examined three forcing modes (i) convection alone to mimic droplet drift, (ii) imposed heat flux, and (iii) combined convection plus heating applied to both large (1–4 mm) and sub-millimeter (~0.5 mm) droplets.

To accelerate progress, the study began with simplified chemistry and transitioned to reduced mechanisms for parameter sweeps over forcing amplitude and frequency, ambient composition (including ozone-assisted cases), and pressure.

From each case, predictive observables were extracted (ignition delay, oscillation frequency and amplitude, stand-off and extinction diameters), and were used to construct stability maps that delineated conditions for cool-flame onset, persistence, and quenching.
These maps were reconciled with FLEX observations and were used to guide next-generation test matrices for both large- and small-droplet experiments.

External thermo-convective perturbations (imposed temperature gradients, non-uniform heating, oscillatory/shear inflow) were expected to govern cool-flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition, and extinction by shifting residence time and scalar dissipation.
In microgravity, where buoyancy was suppressed, this forcing was anticipated to dominate transport.
A multidimensional, multi-physics CFD model was used to map perturbation-dependent stability boundaries and predict observables for comparison with FLEX data.
Space Benefits: Potential to improve spacecraft fire-safety modeling by resolving cool-flame/extinction behavior in microgravity; leverages FLEX to define safer operating envelopes/materials.
Earth Benefits: Advances low-temperature combustion understanding relevant to engine knock, efficiency, and emissions; delivers validated CFD tools transferrable to practical combustors.

These objectives ultimately support both NASA’s PSI solicitation by expanding the scientific return from legacy datasets and advancing applied understanding for industrial processes that rely on controlled Marangoni flows, such as wafer drying, thin-film coating, and microfluidic device operation.
The approach combined archival microgravity data analysis, computational modeling, and ground experiments to study surface tension driven convection (STDC).

Video data from the original NASA STDCE-1 experiments were re-analyzed using several modern particle tracking techniques, including four MATLAB-based codes, three ImageJ-based codes, and sub-pixel localization methods, to produce velocity and pressure fields.

These flow fields were compared with theoretical models derived from perturbation methods and with computational simulations performed in COMSOL Multiphysics® v5.6 that incorporated boundary conditions and curved free-surface geometries.
In parallel, ground-based STDC experiments were carried out to examine gravitational effects and to distinguish buoyancy-driven flows from thermocapillary convection.

This combination of data reanalysis, numerical simulation, and experimental testing provided a means to identify the influence of interfacial curvature, surface stresses, and geometry on Marangoni convection.

Re-analyzing NASA’s STDCE-1 microgravity video data with advanced particle tracking and computational modeling to reveal previously inaccessible details of thermo-fluid mechanics in surface tension driven convection.

These insights, validated against ground-based experiments, aimed to clarify the interplay between Marangoni forces, interfacial curvature, and flow instabilities, leading to improved predictive models of thermocapillary flows.
