Provides validated numerical and theoretical models that can guide future ISS and space-based fluid physics experiments, reducing uncertainty from prior low-resolution analyses.
Earth Benefits: Supports industrial applications such as semiconductor wafer cleaning, thin-film coatings, welding, and liquid crystal display fabrication.

Findings also translate to emerging fields like active matter and micro/nano robotics, where Marangoni flows and surface interactions could be harnessed for medical diagnostics, targeted drug delivery, and microplastics removal.

Phase Transitions in Colloid-Polymer Mixtures in Microgravity

The objective of this PSI grant was to advance the understanding of phase transitions in colloid–polymer mixtures under microgravity conditions by integrating experimental observations with predictive modeling.

Specifically, the research sought to determine how depletion interactions, arising from non-adsorbing polymers, influence the kinetics and morphology of phase separation and crystallization in complex fluids.

By analyzing image data from NASA’s Binary Colloidal Alloy Test (BCAT-3 through BCAT-6) experiments conducted on the International Space Station, the project aimed to isolate the effects of gravity on phase behavior, quantify domain growth over multiple orders of magnitude in time and length scale, and develop a theoretical framework that connects these dynamics to hydrodynamic and thermodynamic parameters.

Ultimately, this work sought to establish colloidal systems as model analogues for atomic and molecular phase transitions, providing insight relevant to both fundamental soft-matter physics and applied materials design.

The approach combined data-driven analysis of PSI-archived BCAT imagery with a phase-field modeling framework that coupled the Cahn–Hilliard and Stokes equations to simulate phase separation in colloid–polymer mixtures.

Experimental image sequences were processed for BCAT-3, -4 and -5, using algorithms in ImageJ and MATLAB to remove background noise, enhance contrast, and compute spatial autocorrelation functions for extracting characteristic domain length scales.

Theoretical modeling of BCAT-5 incorporated concentration-dependent mobility and viscosity, along with Korteweg stresses to represent interfacial tension effects, allowing for the inclusion of hydrodynamic interactions that influenced domain coarsening.
The governing equations were solved using a pseudospectral semi-implicit numerical scheme, and simulation results were quantitatively compared to flight data from the BCAT experiments.

Model parameters were tuned using physical data from PSI to validate predictions and refine understanding of hydrodynamic coupling, phase-domain morphology, and kinetic arrest in colloid–polymer systems.
This integrated experimental–theoretical approach yielded a comprehensive, microgravity-validated description of soft-matter phase transformation mechanisms.

Introducing non-adsorbing polymers into colloidal suspensions generates depletion-induced attractions that alter phase-transition kinetics; in microgravity, free from sedimentation and convection, these interactions can be directly modeled to reveal the intrinsic role of hydrodynamics in phase separation.

This research provided benchmark insight into soft-matter phase transitions without gravitational interference, improving predictive capability for self-assembly, crystallization, and gelation relevant to materials manufacturing and fluids research aboard the ISS.

It has also improved understanding of phase-transition kinetics and rheology in colloid–polymer mixtures, informing materials science, pharmaceutical, and chemical engineering applications, and advancing the design of next-generation coatings, gels, and nanostructured materials.

Pool Boiling Heat Transfer Mechanisms in Low Gravity: Numerical Experiments of MABE and NPBX Data

The primary objectives for this PSI grant include establishing a deeper mechanistic understanding of nucleate boiling under low-gravity conditions by conducting high-fidelity numerical simulations that replicate the flight conditions of prior ISS-based boiling experiments, specifically MABE and NPBX.

The investigation seeks to characterize key mechanisms governing bubble growth, waiting time, vapor spreading, coalescence, and detachment under variable gravity levels, degrees of wall superheat, and levels of liquid subcooling.

Central to the objectives is quantifying how heat flux divides between nucleate boiling and natural convection modes, evaluating how the contact angle modulates wall adhesion forces, and determining the precise contribution of microlayer evaporation to heat transfer during low-gravity operation.

By leveraging validated direct-numerical-simulation approaches tied to empirical MABE and NPBX measurements, this objective generates fundamental physics-based insights that enable predictive modeling of boiling processes relevant to spacecraft systems and advanced thermal architectures.

The project approach was to use validated high-fidelity Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) ground-based computational simulations to numerically reproduce MABE- and NPBX-like boiling environments over a controlled range of heater temperatures, wall superheat conditions, and fluid subcooling levels.

The research draws directly from ISS-acquired datasets that include detailed bubble growth dynamics, heat-flux profiles, and heater-surface imaging, which serve as reference benchmarks that guide simulation fidelity.

Multiphase DNS simulations incorporate fluid phase-change physics, contact-line motion, interphase mass transport, and three-dimensional flow-field resolution to connect bubble behavior to instantaneous and time-averaged heat transfer.
Iterative simulation campaigns then probe how variable gravitational acceleration, wettability contrast, bubble confinement, and microlayer evaporation influence overall heat-flux partitioning.

The resulting database enables first-principles analysis of changes in boiling performance between terrestrial and microgravity settings while supporting quantitative model development applicable to spaceflight hardware, thermal architectures, and advanced electronic cooling systems.

The research was based on the hypothesis that, in microgravity, shifts in the relative influence of buoyancy, capillary forces, and microlayer evaporation fundamentally alter bubble-growth behavior and reduce heat-flux performance.

It further hypothesized that these low-gravity effects can be accurately captured using high-fidelity Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS) validated against historic ISS boiling data from the MABE and NPBX experiments.

By exploring variations in gravity, surface wettability, and thermal conditions, the study aimed to test the mechanisms governing bubble dynamics and heat transfer for application to spacecraft thermal management.

Space Benefits: This investigation provides high-resolution insight into how boiling heat-transfer efficiency degrades under reduced gravity, enabling the development of more reliable spacecraft thermal-management systems that do not depend solely on buoyancy-driven vapor removal.

Improved understanding of microlayer-based transport, contact-line wetting, spatial heat-flux distribution, and boiling-mode transition directly supports the design of future ISS and deep-space thermal architectures, power-electronics packaging, life-support thermal management, and compact, energy-efficient cooling platforms for extended-duration missions.

Earth Benefits: The computational foundations and physics-based insights gained through this study directly advance terrestrial thermal-management strategies for high-power electronic systems, including server-class processors, power-dense computing architectures, and high-performance energy-conversion systems.

The work improves predictive control of boiling-induced heat removal, enabling higher operating throughput, greater component longevity, and reduced power consumption in heat-intensive commercial and defense electronics.

Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames

By using the Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) experimental data from the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system of combustion science, the purpose of this grant was to conduct new simulations and ground-based experiments using ozone-sensitized counterflow flames to:
1) Develop a new diagram of the flammability limits of diffusional cool flames affected by radiation, diffusion, and convection.
2) Bridge the knowledge gap between the flammability limits and extinction limits of hot flames and cool flames.
3) Verify the phenomena observed on the ISS flame extinguishment experiments.
4) Obtain new, quantitative data of extinction limit, flame temperature, and species distribution for the validation of kinetic and radiation models involving cool flames.

5) Extend the cool flame experiments from the original ISS droplet experiments to a more general ground-based combustion system involving radiation, diffusion, convection, and low-temperature chemistry while maintaining a one-dimensional geometry.

Using the experimental conditions of FLEX flight, a comparative studies of the oxygen concentration effects on the extinction limits of cool flames was conducted using three different numerical modeling schemes, (a) spark-assisted flame propagation of a n-heptane/air mixture, (b) one dimensional freely-propagating dimethyl ether (DME) flames using an arc-length continuation method and (c) simulated cool flame regimes and burning limits at elevated pressure (up to 20 atm) using DME/air mixtures.

Specific research details are outlined in the publication, ''Dynamics of cool flames'' [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pecs.2019.100787]; '' Understanding Cool Flames and Warm Flames'', [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.proci.2020.09.019] and ''Study of the low-temperature reactivity of large n-alkanes through cool diffusion flame extinction'', [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.combustflame.2017.01.028].

This investigation attempts to answer the critical question as to what conditions causes the hot flames transfer to cool flames and how the cool flame flammable region is related to hot flame flammability limit and extinction limit.
The investigation hypothesizes that factors such as oxygen concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion, and convection transport processes affect the cool flame transition.

Obtaining a fundamental understanding of the warm diffusion flame is particularly relevant to combustion in highly turbulent flow fields and in microgravity environments, owing to the possibility of long residence times.
The results showed that the warm flame has a double reaction zone structure and plays a critical role in the transition between cool flames and hot flames.
At elevated pressures, it was found that the flammable region of warm flames and cool flames expands due to the increase in low-temperature and intermediate-temperature reactivity with pressure.
Since many real engines operate in the 20-40 atm pressure range, therefore, cool flames and warm flames are relevant and important flame regimes for high-pressure near-limit combustion applications.
These calculations from this investigation will serve to advance the understanding of near-limit flame dynamics and provide guidance for experimental observation of different flame regimes.

Fabrication of Amorphous Metals in Space

The primary objective of this investigation was to understand the effect of microgravity processing on composition and microstructure evolution in metallic glass forming alloys or bulk metallic glass (BMG).
Specific questions to be answered were:
(a) How does processing in microgravity change the composition of the matrix of the glass-forming alloys compared to processing in gravity?
(b) How does the volume fraction of the W spheres affect the composition and properties of the matrix?
(c) How does the composition and viscosity of the glass-forming alloy affect the diffusion of W in microgravity?
(d) How do the different diameter of W spheres affect the diffusion of W into the matrix?
(e) Does the dissolved W provide a mechanism to improve the wear resistance and toughness of the matrix by providing reinforcement for brittle phases?

The objective of the flight experiment is to process 12 samples of two glass-forming alloys (Vitreloy 106 and Zr48Cu47.5Al4Co0.5) in microgravity with three different volume fractions of W spheres (5%, 15% and 30%) with two different diameters of W spheres (25-36 μm diameter and 140-150 μm diameter).
The cast composite samples were 15 mm in diameter and 12 mm long cylinders.
The W particles were distributed as homogeneously as possible without sedimentation.
On orbit, the samples were loaded into the Low Gradient Furnace (LGF) on the Materials Science Research Rack.

They were held for 120 minutes at 1,200 °C (1,473 K) in microgravity with the intent to dissolve the W particles into the matrix and to create a fine distribution of W dendrites homogenously distributed throughout.
The samples were then cooled back to room temperature slowly, solidifying the morphology and composition.

The Vitreloy 106 samples were compared with Zr48Cu47.5Al4Co0.5 in terms of composition of the matrix, morphology of the W dendrites, and mechanical properties, with comparisons drawn between samples produced on-orbit and on the ground to distinguish the effects of microgravity.
The hypothesis for the experiment is that microgravity promotes composite formation by stabilizing the interface between the W nano-particle nuclei and the bulk liquid.
In contrast, on Earth, the heavy W particles would fall out of the system as they form.
Therefore, the composition of the solid formed on Earth will differ from that formed in microgravity.

On Earth, the samples should solidify in a manner consistent with the Scheil solidification approximation meaning: (a) liquid diffusion is instant over experimental timescales (b) solid-state diffusion does not occur (solid falls out of the system as it forms) (c) the solid composition profile will follow the solidus as the system cools, until all the liquid is consumed.
In contrast, in microgravity, the solid/liquid interface lifetime is much longer, so there is more opportunity for solid back-diffusion.
For this case, the composition profile will approach (but not reach) that of the equilibrium solidification case.
After processing in both gravity and microgravity, experimental compositional data at the matrix-sphere interface will be obtained.

It is expected that composites formed on Earth will solidify consistent with Scheil solidification and composites formed in microgravity will deviate from Scheil, approaching equilibrium solidification.

Ring-Sheared Drop - Interfacial Bioprocessing of Pharmaceuticals
The Ring-Sheared Drop (RSD) is a Microgravity Science Glovebox experiment that launched in July 2019 to the ISS to study shearing flow in the absence of solid walls.
The major goals of this project were to adapt and use the RSD module to develop and test predictive models of non-Newtonian flow of high-concentration proteins at the interface.

Incorporating non-Newtonian constitutive equations for both interfacial and bulk flows and coupling the interfacial and bulk stresses is essential for mechanistic models that would be capable of predicting behavior under flow conditions of practical interest.
The coupled problem is intrinsically nonlinear and there is a need to develop robust and accurate numerical techniques to interrogate flow dynamics and experimentally validate and verify results.

The ring-sheared drop interfacial bioprocessing of pharmaceuticals-I (RSD-IBP-I) campaign aimed to study non-Newtonian interfacial hydrodynamics of the blood transport proteins bovine serum albumin (BSA) and human serum albumin (HSA) in microgravity.

Specifically, scientific aims focus on the effects of protein primary structure (BSA or HSA), protein concentration (4, 40, or 400 mg/mL), and interfacial shear rate (3, 10, or 30 rpm) on microgravity fluid flow, measured using velocimetry of hollow glass microsphere tracer particles within protein samples.
This campaign intended to confer improved understanding of interfacial protein flows in relation to physiology, the environment, and industry relevant to both spaceflight and Earth.

Preflight preparation included refurbishment of all test cells including modification of test cells S/N 101-106 to include the flight tested (both parabolic and ISS with the assistance of NASA MSFC) integrated deployment tube and upper ring design by TBE, refurbishment of all test cells used in the previous RSD-BPS campaign by TBE, preparation of protein samples and methodological ground controls.
Following sample installation, the RSD drop was deployed by extruding a drop from the deployment tube until pinning is achieved at the far ring.
Shearing was then commenced by rotation of the far ring, measurements recorded for startup, steady, and stop flows each at 3, 10, and 30 rpm.
Each 1.5 min. image sequence was then compressed to a portable video file and downlinked to the ground computer at RPI.
ISS flight campaigns occurred Summer 2022 and Spring 2023, achieving 92% of proposed science objectives with 121.5/132 sample videos successfully collected, meeting the criteria for complete success.
Additionally, 27 videos of interfacial aging and 24 micrographs of extra data were collected.
The RSD hardware concluded the campaign in a nominal configuration with good health and status after four years in space aboard the ISS.
Postflight: Test cells were returned June 30th 2023 on SpX-28 to TBE.
Test cells appear to be in nominal pre-refurbishment configuration.
RSD hardware remains in nominal configuration and good health.

Advanced Colloids Experiment - Imaging, Folding and Assembly of Colloidal Molecules

In ACE-T9, the imaging capability, folding dynamics, and assembly behavior of linear colloidal chains, colloidal dimers, and lock-and-key particles were studied by the combination of a proper design of particle architecture and tunable colloidal interactions (e.g., double layer repulsion and hydrophobic attraction).
In the case of colloidal chains, for example, the single chain dynamics should sensitively depend on the chain flexibility and monomer-solvent interactions.
Under the microgravity environment, we hoped to observe qualitative three-dimensional, real-time dynamics of single colloidal chains (using pre-confocal - bright field and fluorescent microscopy.

We also aimed to observe three-dimensional structures assembled from colloidal dimers and lock-and-key particles and to measure the binding equilibrium constants that are impossible to measure in earth experiments due to the effect of sedimentation.

The imaging goal is to observe (1) real-time and three-dimensional particle centroid positions of colloidal chains over both short (30 minutes) and long period (one week); (2) assembled structures, crystallites, and resolve particle centroid positions for colloidal dimers and Janus spheres.
For short-time imaging, the video should be taken with 5 fps over 30 minutes.
For both cases, the x-y positions of particles should be determined with less than 5% error (with respect to particle diameter).
The z-positions should be determined within 1 micron.
For fluorescence imaging, lamp should be shuttered between image sets to prevent sample bleaching.

In the microgravity environment, we will study the folding dynamics of single colloidal chains where the chain architecture can be varied systematically, and the monomer-solvent interaction can be tuned by varying salt concentrations.

Furthermore, by tuning the balance between electric double layer repulsion and hydrophobic attraction on both colloidal dimers and lock-and-key particles, we aim to study the assembly of those colloidal molecules into complex three-dimensional structures and measure the binding equilibrium constants.
This set of experiments provide insight into the relation between particle shape, colloidal interaction and structure.
With the wide variety of attributes that characterize anisotropic interactions, we will probe previously inaccessible regions of complex phase space.
Our studies will move significantly beyond hard spheres and towards experimental models appropriate for studying fundamental questions associated with complex symmetries.

In-situ manipulation of anisotropic interactions and dynamic pathways, based on rational colloidal particle design and proper use of external fields, could lead to crystalline and a periodic structures beyond those seen in nature.
Results from this study will lead to improved control of non-covalent assembly of molecules, efficient tailoring of lattice symmetries, and the scalable processing of nano-structured materials.
The development of new colloidal molecules and their associated assembled structures have considerable technological impact as well.
Such structures will generally lead to arrays with reduced symmetry and enhanced directionality.

They can interact with a broad range of electromagnetic radiation in unique ways and can exhibit collective photonic, plasmonic, mechanical, electronic, or magnetic properties that are not manifested at the level of single particles.
As a result, they have significant potential as next-generation functional materials.

Advanced Colloids Experiment - Aging Dynamics and Stress-Relaxation in Colloidal Gels Studied in Microgravity
Colloidal stability is critical to soft matter systems, especially to consumer products.
These structures change in time, by processes know as coarsening - meaning the spacing between particles compact.
This compaction continually changes this structure.
When the structures created in the products can longer resist the gravitational stresses (e.g. buoyancy) on the structures, they collapse.
The collapse, such as those that occur in geological formations during earthquakes, is often abrupt and without warning (delayed collapse).
This is the essence of product instability.
For some systems, the gel collapse can be anticipated by precursors, that can potentially be detected and forecasted.
This research will have significant impacts in two areas: • It is not clear how the microscopic structure and its dynamics are related to the gel mechanical properties.
The structure evolution controls the aging of the gel, and, on earth, this eventually leads to collapse.

This work may significantly enhance the knowledge necessary to advance this important area of science. • Second, relaxation of localized stresses in an amorphous solid brought by a rapid solidification process is ubiquitous in nature and can damage and destroy the materials.
Besides affecting the rheological properties of the materials, these dynamics rule the aging of the thermal systems at rest.
The detection of failure precursors, as the ones discovered in our colloidal gel, can potentially allow us to forecast the material failure before catastrophic rupture.
The ACE-T10 experiment exploited the Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) and the Light Microscopy Module (LMM).
The Light Microscopy Module (LMM) is an automated microscope.
It permitted flexible imaging (e.g., bright field, dark field, phase contrast, confocal microscopy) for physics experiments and can be controlled remotely from the ground.
The LMM accommodated sample change-out and fluid containment and included a glove box for on-orbit sample manipulation.
The ACE-T10 experiment used include confocal microscopy, which utilized a 532-nm frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser, a confocal scanner, and an 8- to 12-bit digital CCD camera.
The scanner captured 30 frames per second of confocal images by the CCD camera.
A sample’s three-dimensional crystal structure can thus be reconstructed by assembling individual slices with an image analysis program.
This information, in turn, enabled the observation and measurement of the colloidal growth, structure, and dynamics.
The confocal module was attached and aligned to the side of the LMM.
The microscope used a reflecting mirror to direct the light to and from the sample.
ACE-T10 utilized 6 capillary cells in 2 holding modules.
The capillary cells, each contained about 20 microliters of the sample fluid and a magnetic stainless steel stir bar.
Samples were stirred prior to example.
The sample temperature was adjusted between 20 – 60 °C in order to find the transition temperature where the sample became a gel.
ACE-T10 delivered unique insights into the restructuring behavior of thermo-reversible colloidal gels, a topic of noticeable interest for the community of scientists dealing with soft materials.

In normal gravity experiments, the ACE-T10 science team found evidence that the aging of these soft gels proceed via a sequence of sudden intermittent bursts of dynamical activity that resembles the ‘critical avalanche’ phenomena observed in several driven systems.
The evidence collected suggests that, in a soft solid, these avalanches may be triggered by thermal agitation and occur spontaneously, even in the absence of other external forces.
However, because of the density difference between the fluid and the particles in the gel network, gravity may play a role as well.
Performing the ACE-T10 experiment in microgravity provided a unique opportunity to determine the gravity contribution.
Earth benefits/spin-off applications include understanding the behavior of weak gels and their aging can help materials scientists to make consumer product with longer shelf lives.

In addition, because several features of the failure dynamics of disordered materials are system independent, the results obtained using this model colloidal system can be generalized to other materials.
This potentially can help to develop new way to characterize aging material and suggest their replacement before catastrophic failure.

Advanced Colloids Experiment-Nanoparticle Haloing
Nanoparticle Haloing (NPH) is a colloidal stabilization technique that has been discovered relatively recently.
In NPH, highly charged nanoparticles are used to stabilize much larger (by 2 orders of magnitude or more), non-charged particles.

To accomplish this stabilization, the volume fraction of nanoparticles within the suspension need only be on the order of 1e-5 up to 1e-4 to stabilize at 1 to 2 vol% suspension of the larger particles.

The objective of this work is to gain fundamental insight into the physics of NPH with the aim of addressing the following unresolved questions: • How will NPH suspensions behave in thermal or electrical field gradients as they do under gravity? • How does the halo form or re-form if disturbed? • Can NPH (and manipulation thereof) be used to assemble and reconfigure colloidal crystals? • How does the nanoparticle charge impact halo formation?
The ACE-T12 experiment utilizes the Fluids Integrated Rack (FIR) and the Light Microscopy Module (LMM).
The FIR is built to accommodate a wide range of experiments.

Accordingly, the ACE-T12 experiment included confocal microscopy, which used a 532-nm frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser, a confocal scanner, and an 8- to 12-bit digital CCD camera on a Leica DM-RXA microscope.
The scanner captured 30 frames per second of confocal images by the CCD camera.
ACE-T12 utilizes capillary cells.
Three capillary cells with different concentrations of nanoparticles were provided in a sample module.
Here is a brief high-level descriptive outline of the investigation on-orbit procedures that gives general experiment steps for each capillary.
1- Short mix of sample.
2- Ramp temperature to find critical temperature and reduce temperature and initiate a very long mix of sample.
3- Determine Region of Interest (ROI).
4- Ramp temperature continuously while imaging.
5- Mix sample followed by Single temperature step visits.
6- Mix sample followed by stepwise temperature ramp with image stacks.
When NPH suspensions were allowed to settle under gravity, those that were stabilized (while in suspension) formed highly ordered, 3-dimensional colloidal crystal structures.
Current theory suggests that nanoparticles create a charge layer by forming a cage, or Halo, around the larger particles.
Another hypothesis regarding the NPH stabilization mechanism focuses entirely on nanoparticle adsorption to the surface of the larger particle.

Based on the measurement of the interaction forces between two larger colloidal surfaces in a nanoparticle suspension, it was found that the force curves obtained could be fitted using a model based on nanoparticle adsorption.

Ultimately, the ability to design colloidal particles with a variety of well-controlled three-dimensional bonding symmetries opens a wide spectrum of new structures for colloidal self-assembly, beyond particle assemblies whose structures are defined primarily by repulsive interactions and shape.
Such materials might include photonic crystals with programmed distributions of defects.
Optical technology utilizing such materials may offer intriguing solutions to unavoidable heat generation and bandwidth limitations facing the computer industry.

Micromechanics Based Modeling of Cement Solidified in the Microgravity

Micromechanics‑Based Modeling of Cement Solidified in the Microgravity aimed to advance knowledge of the mechanical properties of cement binders formed in reduced gravity by leveraging microgravity materials data, such as SEM/BSE micrographs, available in the PSI database.

This project sought to connect microstructure (e.g., porosity, phase morphology such as portlandite) observed in ISS‑cured tricalcium silicate (C3S) pastes to bulk mechanical/transport behavior through modeling, thereby informing design and engineering of cementitious materials for extraterrestrial construction and providing validated simulation data that scale sparse flight samples to application‑relevant sizes.
In this work, the micromechanics analysis code with generalized method of cells (MAC/GMC) was used to predict the structure-property relationship of these unique cement samples.
First, the sparse data of cement hydrated in microgravity environment was converted to high-fidelity 3D microstructure with the aid of a deep learning-based microstructure methodology.
The reconstructed sub-volumes were compared against micro-CT data using statistical descriptors.

Second, the sub-volumes (partitioned based on individual constituents) of such reconstructed 3D structures were fed into the NASA Multiscale Analysis Tool (NASMAT) to obtain homogenized properties of the cement.
A semi-automated Python script was developed to complete the workflow.
Owing to the high computational demand, the analyses were carried out in NASA Advanced Supercomputing (NAS) servers.

Phase‑discerned ISS and ground BSE/SEM images were segmented and reconstructed into 3D volumes using a deep learning microstructure framework; these Representative Volume Elements (RVEs) were then analyzed with NASA’s Multiscale Analysis Tool (NASMAT) to homogenize and predict effective properties.
Reconstruction quality was validated against statistical descriptors and micro‑CT data, and the modeling spans length‑scale partitioning to capture porous, multiphase behavior.

The experimental basis originated from the MICS investigation (PSI‑84 in the database), which conducted controlled ISS/ground hydration in sealed Burst Pouches, keeping temperature/pressure/humidity constant so gravity is the sole variable, followed by porosimetry, TGA, XRD, EDS/EMPA, and image analysis to quantify phase fractions and pore structures that feed the modeling pipeline.

Consistent with the microgravity MICS investigation, the central hypothesis was that minimizing gravity‑driven transport (buoyancy, sedimentation, convection) yields a diffusion‑controlled hydration process in microgravity, producing more uniform phase distributions and distinct microstructures (e.g., higher porosity, altered portlandite morphology) relative to 1g; these differences are expected to translate into measurably different mechanical properties for µg‑hardened cement paste versus terrestrial cement.
The grant tested this by quantifying microstructural features from flight/ground samples and propagating them through micromechanics to predict property deltas attributable to gravity effects.

This research provides the first reference simulation data and a practical route to predict how cement (including regolith‑based mixes) behaves when fabricated in space, which can inform Artemis‑aligned or other space-based habitat concepts and construction logistics where transporting bulk materials is prohibitive.

On Earth, the deep-learning-assisted reconstruction and micromechanics workflow developed can be applied to other multiphase materials, enabling materials-by-design even when only a limited samples are available.

By clarifying how processing conditions in microgravity affect cement structure and performance, such as the ~70% porosity and plate-like portlandite observed in ISS samples, this work improves predictive models for optimizing mix designs and curing conditions in constrained environments.
These advances also benefit low-resource or extreme-environment construction on Earth and contribute more broadly to the ICME community.

The origin of fragility in high-temperature oxide liquids - towards fabrication of novel non-equilibrium oxides
This project investigated the high-temperature thermophysical properties of molten metal oxides, with a particular focus on molten titanates.
These property measurements were used to establish correlations with atomic structure and glass formation.

The research exploits the unique capabilities in microgravity to measure the thermophysical properties – density, thermal expansion coefficient, viscosity and surface tension – over a wide temperature range.
Samples, including glasses, were recovered after melt processing in microgravity for ground-based analysis and comparison with materials made on Earth.

The work underpins development of a materials property-structure data set that can help in development of new materials and in meeting requirements of material utilization, processing in space, and exploration.
Density, thermal expansion, viscosity, and surface tension of molten oxides were measured using the Electrostatic Levitation Furnace (ELF) onboard the ISS.
Measurements included silhouette imaging and drop oscillation over a wide range of temperatures, including deep supercooling.

Recovered samples included glasses and polycrystalline materials, which were characterized post-flight using a combination of X-ray scattering, neutron scattering, X-ray tomography, Raman spectroscopy, calorimetry, and electron microscopy.
Space-made glasses were compared with terrestrial analogues to investigate how changes in fluid transport may influence structure and properties.
Glasses are inherently non-equilibrium materials.
Their structure and properties depend directly on the processing route used to form them.
Because gravity affects fluid convection, glass formation and resulting structure may differ between different gravity conditions.

We hypothesize that the superior control of fluid and thermal transport possible in microgravity will enable improved glass forming ability via melt quenching in containerless conditions, particularly for highly fragile liquid oxides.
We hypothesize that the differences in thermal history - between microgravity and Earth-based processing - will manifest as differences in structure and thermodynamic properties.
This project advances the understanding of oxide melt properties, atomic structure, and glass formation.
This builds a foundation for the development of new functional glasses and related technologies, with applications on Earth and in space for exploration and utilization of local resources.

Microgravity experiments enabled melting, drop imaging, drop oscillation and measurements of properties of approximately 30 samples.
First experiments in ELF that used melt processing to make and recover glass in space.
First publications that compare the structure of glasses made in microgravity vs. terrestrially.
First demonstration of laser action in a titanate-network glass and of a glass made by containerless processing.
Results were analyzed in collaboration with a variety of researchers leading to 12 peer-reviewed publications and more than 20 presentations.

The project met all of the stated goals: perform basic research in microgravity, develop applied knowledge to make new materials, build collaborations to advance the field, and establish the basis for new glass materials products made in reduced gravity.

The results are relevant to the applied research mission of NASA's Biological and Physical Sciences (BPS) to enable space exploration and utilize materials based on natural resources that are available in space.
Developed and fostered a productive international collaboration.

Aerosol Sampling Experiment
Aerosols are small particles suspended in the air, and in Earth’s atmosphere, aerosols include soot, dust, pollen and a wide range of other natural and human-made materials.
Smoke does not rise and dust does not settle in microgravity the way they do on Earth, causing aerosols to behave differently and pose hazards for crew members breathing the air.
The Aerosol Sampling Experiment (ASE) collects airborne particles in the International Space Station’s (ISS) cabin air, and returns them to Earth for scientists to study.
The objectives of ASE were: 1- Characterize airborne particulate matter aboard the ISS to assess air quality for crew health and hardware longevity.
2- Identify particle sources (e.g., human skin, equipment wear, biological contaminants) in the spacecraft environment.
3- Improve understanding of particle transport and accumulation in microgravity conditions.
4- Support design of future spacecraft air filtration systems, ensuring they are appropriately targeted for actual airborne particle profiles.

The ASE approach involved passive aerosol sampling in multiple ISS modules using filters placed in air ducts and cabin areas (especially near high-traffic zones and vents) by deploying commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) samplers for long-duration exposure (3 months–1 year).
The sampled filters were returned to Earth for ground-based analysis using: 1- Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), 2- Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) and 3- Gravimetric analysis.
The ISS samples were compared to terrestrial cleanroom and indoor environments to assess relative cleanliness and particle source uniqueness.
Data collected was cross-referenced with previous ISS air monitoring efforts (e.g., TOCA, CCAA) to inform models of contaminant accumulation and mitigation.

Airborne particulate matter aboard the ISS exhibits a different size distribution, composition, and transport behavior in microgravity compared to Earth-based environments, and that particles from crew activity and hardware wear contribute significantly to the aerosol burden as well as the assumption that microgravity reduces sedimentation, allowing finer particles to stay suspended longer and accumulate in regions not typically affected by gravity-based settling on Earth.
Crew members on the ISS are breathing more or less the same fixed volume of air that has been on the ISS for years.
There is no chance to get ‘fresh air’ as we do on Earth, but an advanced air revitalization system processes and cleans the air continuously.
Crew members in space have complained of allergies and nose and eye irritation, which suggests the ISS cabin air has a high concentration of tiny particles that can be inhaled.
The ISS filtration system is designed to remove these particles, but researchers have no way to verify the efficiency or cleanliness of the air.
This investigation generates new data to characterize the quality of the air on the ISS, in terms of particles.
Future space travelers may benefit from this data, as they can be used in the design and selection of particle detectors appropriate for low gravity.
Long-term manned space missions need aerosol measurement capability to ensure crew health and comfort

Microgravity Environments under Extremes of Elevated and Cryo Temperatures

This study addresses the reliability of solder joints in space by pursuing two principal objectives: (1) Characterization of solder-joint formation under microgravity conditions aboard the International Space Station, specifically examining the impact of suppressed convective flow and buoyancy on 40Pb-60Sn alloys utilized in the In-Space Soldering Investigation (ISSI).
(2) Evaluation of the solder’s material and mechanical properties under extreme thermal environments, including elevated and cryogenic temperature exposures characteristic of spaceflight conditions.
The study examined three distinct solder alloys: the ISSI lead-based (40Pb-60Sn) composition, an off-eutectic 50Pb-50Sn formulation, and a lead-free alloy consisting of 95.5Sn-3.8Ag-0.7Cu.

Microstructural characterization was performed on four solder specimens processed in microgravity from the ISSI investigation, one terrestrial ISSI solder, and a freshly fabricated terrestrial 40wt%Pb-60wt%Sn sample.
These analyses elucidated the role of suppressed buoyancy and natural convection in void formation within microgravity environments.
Evidence of void-induced Marangoni convection influencing microstructure development was demonstrated using wire-feed solder processed in space.

The micromechanical response of solders fabricated under both terrestrial and microgravity conditions was further evaluated across a broad thermal range (–157ºC to +121ºC), simulating the conditions encountered externally on the International Space Station.

Investigations under cryogenic conditions focused on the β-to-α phase transformation in Sn below 13ºC, examining associated volumetric expansion, internal stress evolution, and the ductile-to-brittle transition phenomena observed in Sn-based alloys.
At ambient temperature, the influence of accelerated aging on both microstructural stability and mechanical performance was assessed.

In microgravity environments, fluid dynamics are markedly constrained, predominantly governed by solidification-induced volumetric changes, thermally driven density gradients, and Marangoni convection.
This suppression of fluid motion results in diminished mixing, causing voids and gas bubbles to remain entrapped within the solder joint during the solidification process.
Such internal porosity critically impairs the solder’s thermal and electrical conductivity, while also compromising the mechanical robustness of the joint.

To advance the feasibility of extended space missions, this study seeks to elucidate the fundamental mechanisms, observable phenomena, and process parameters that influence the structural and functional integrity of solder joints fabricated under terrestrial and microgravity conditions.
The research presented in this project offers significant contributions across multiple space exploration initiatives:
(i) The project objectives are closely aligned with ongoing NASA initiatives focused on metal joining techniques in reduced gravity environments.

The three solder alloys investigated—selected in collaboration with NASA partners, underscoring the relevance of the study to future space exploration efforts, (ii) The findings are expected to inform the design of future experiments responsive to forthcoming NASA proposal calls, including those associated with the Artemis program, which aims to return humans to the lunar surface, (iii) The insights gained into microgravity fluid behavior and surface tension variation can be extended to a broad range of spaceflight-enabling technologies, such as boiling, heat transfer, combustion, welding, brazing, and soldering.
This research enhances the understanding of gravity-driven separation processes—such as gas bubble removal—that must be accomplished via alternative mechanisms in microgravity conditions.

(iv) The gravity-level-specific protocols (GLSPs) developed for various soldering configurations serve as practical guidance for future investigations into metal joining techniques under reduced gravity.
These protocols may be adopted by scientists and flight personnel for welding, brazing, and soldering applications in spaceflight environments.

Data are from two projects: one related to aging, one related to polydispersity.
The first project has data under folders with a name containing AGING.
The second has data under folders with a name containing POLYDISPERSE.

Project 1: Objectives specific to aging of colloid gels •Quantify coarsening of colloidal gels under microgravity conditions. •Quantify changes in thermal fluctuations of colloidal gels under microgravity conditions. •Understand aging of colloidal gels over time scales range from seconds to tens of hours.

Project 2: Objectives related to structure of polydisperse colloidal gels •Measure fractal dimension of polydisperse colloidal gels (on Earth) •Understand how particle size relates to contact number •Quantify tetrahedral structures, and how particle size influences tetrahedral structure in colloidal gels
Project 1: We studied colloidal gels using the data from the Advanced Colloids Experiment-Microscopy-1 (ACE-M1) experiments.

Colloidal gels are formed from sticky micron-sized solid particles in a liquid, where over time the particles stick together and form random clumps that eventually bridge across the entire sample chamber in tangled networks.
The ACE-M1 data set consists of a large number of optical microscopy movies of colloidal gels.
In microgravity, these gels are long-lived, rather than collapsing under their own weight as happens in ground-based experiments.
We have analyzed these microscopy movies using particle tracking, studying the visible thermal fluctuations and the gel structure as it evolves over time.
Some gels have thick aggregated regions, while others have more tenuous gel strands and free particles.
We show that the structure and dynamics change over the several-day period of each experiment.
Project 2: In a second project, we did ground-based experiments to study the structure of colloidal gels composed of polydisperse particles.
In particular, we used confocal microscopy to image colloidal gels formed from highly polydisperse particles.
We suspended our polydisperse particles in a density matched solvent, and let the particles spontaneously aggregate through the van der Waals force.
The largest particles were more than 15 times the size of the smallest particles.
As expected, larger particles have more nearest neighbors than small ones.

This leads to an over-representation of large particles in tetrahedral structures where four particles are mutually nearest neighbors, showing that large particles help provide rigidity to the gel structure.
The tetrahedral structures also suggest that particles are able to rearrange somewhat during the gelation process, until their motion is stabilized by the multiple contacts with their neighbors.

Project 1: Colloidal gels in microgravity conditions will coarsen over time, and their thermal fluctuations will diminish over time as the gel gets coarser; the coarsening will continue indefinitely because gravitational collapse will not be possible.
Project 2: Large particles play significant roles in highly polydisperse colloidal gels, as they serve as highly connected nodes in the structure.
This research helps us understand the technical challenge of keeping particles dispersed in a colloidal suspension.
A gel is one way to prevent particles from settling, although the long-time behavior of a gel is challenging to study under Earth gravity.

Testing Analytical and Numerical Models in Phase Coarsening using NASA Physical Sciences Informatics System

NASA has supported “coarsening in solid–liquid mixtures” (CSLM) experiments, performed in microgravity on the International Space Station (ISS), with greatly reduced sedimentation rate in partially molten alloys.
CSLM experimental data are stored in NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI).
Microgravity experiments offer a unique opportunity to test existing numerical modeling and theories of phase coarsening.

The objective of this research is to test existing numerical modeling methods for simulation of the microstructure evolution that occurs during phase coarsening, using experimental data for Sn-Pb mixtures currently held in PSI.
Results from this research can be found in the following publications: Wang, K.G., Glicksman, M.E.
Testing Numerical Modeling of Phase Coarsening by Microgravity Experiments.

(1) use data archived in NASA's PSI system from the Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures (CSLM) microgravity experiments to determine mean and maximum particle sizes in each sample processed through the CSLM microgravity experiments; (2) apply a two-dimensional (2-D) phase-field simulation code to allow simulation and evolution of initial microstructures that were observed in the CSLM experiments for Sn-Pb solid-liquid phase mixtures, and which provide input data for our phase-field code to numerically evolve coarsened microstructures over time; (3) calculate particle size distributions (PSDs) from the prior NASA CSLM experiments, our phase-field and multiparticle diffusion simulations, and from diffusion screening theory.

Phase-field and multiparticle diffusion numerical methods can be applied to simulate the evolution of the microstructure during phase coarsening, delivering accurate statistical physical quantities such as the particle size distribution (PSD).
Phase-field modeling can adequately capture the complexity of the microstructures developed during phase coarsening at large volume fraction.
In contrast, multiparticle diffusion modeling can track the evolution of microstructures consisting of nearly spherical particles that develop during phase coarsening at lower volume fraction.
The contributions from our research activities improved the understanding of fundamental materials phenomena, i.e., phase coarsening.
We advanced the state of the art in both theory and simulation.

Better understanding of two-phase microstructures will help engineers improve process designs in economically important areas, including liquid-phase sintering for the production of hard tool materials.

The theory and simulation tools developed herein that are tested by microgravity experiments, will provide technical pointers for the improvement of important processes, microstructures, and materials properties.
The improved knowledge of microstructure evolution in this project will have significant impact on alloy design and service-life strategies for alloy materials.
The theory and simulation tools developed will provide guidance toward exploring the structure and properties of alloys.
Finally, the theoretical and computational tools will save money and time for alloy modification.

Coupled Growth in Hypermonotectics
The overall objective of the Coupled Growth in Hypermonotectics is to understand the fundamental physics controlling solidification in immiscible alloy systems.

Specific experimental goals were (1) to show that production of an aligned fibrous microstructure is possible in hypermonotectic alloys by achieving interfacial stability and steady state coupled growth through microgravity processing, (2) to determine the influence of alloy composition and growth velocity on microstructure, and (3) to determine the growth velocity and composition range over which interface stability is possible in a hypermonotectic alloy system.
The CGH experiment investigation flew aboard the Life and Microgravity Spacelab (LMS) mission during the summer of 1996.
Processing conditions were controlled in an attempt to force the production of an aligned fibrous phase in the microstructure of processed samples.
The Advanced Gradient Heating Facility (AGHF) was used to directionally solidify the immiscible alloys.

Aluminum (Al)-Indium (In) alloys were studied and specialized aluminum nitride (AlN) ampoules were used in order to control several undesirable effects that are sometimes observed during low gravity processing.
Three alloy compositions, namely 17.3 weight % In monotectic, and 18.5 and 19.7 weight percent In hypermonotectic alloys were processed during this mission.
A thermal gradient of 67 C/cm was achieved and all flight samples were processes at a translation velocity of 1 micrometer/s.
Ground based control samples were subsequently processed under conditions identical to those of two of the flight samples in order to allow a direct comparison of the results.

This investigation aimed to answer fundamental unanswered questions concerning solidification of immiscible alloys, namely: (a) is it possible to solidify a hypermonotectic alloy under steady state interfacially stable conditions to produce a fibrous microstructure, (b) can a simple supercooling approach predict stability limits, (c) does extensive diffusion in the liquid phases result in morphological effects not observed in eutectic systems, and (d) what role does surface tension driven flow play at the solidification front.
Many alloys in immiscible systems show great promise for potential applications in areas that include superconductors, magnetic materials, catalysts, and electrical contacts.
For example, some immiscible alloys may be used to produce filters that can remove micron-sized particles for medical applications.
Other alloys are expected to exhibit superconducting characteristics or have unusual magnetic properties.

Plant Water Management
The primary objectives of the Plant Water Management (PWM) experiments were to:
a) Experimentally characterize and validate the use of passive capillary and geometric control for plant watering in microgravity.

The research quantified the stability limits of capillary-driven flow under varying conditions, evaluated aeration and bubble management performance within root-zone analogs, and assessed start-up, shutdown, and drainage behaviors of the fluidic system on orbit and also correlated observed flow regimes and saturation levels with computational capillary flow models to improve predictive design tools for reduced-gravity systems. b) Advance the PWM technology toward higher Technology Readiness Levels (TRL), demonstrating reliable, scalable configurations for integration into future space-based plant growth habitats.
The resulting data and models informed the design of next-generation, low-mass, low-power life-support and food-production systems for long-duration missions on the Moon, Mars, and beyond.
PWM employed passive capillary-based fluidic systems to deliver water and nutrients to plant root zones under microgravity aboard the ISS.
Growth modules were designed with controlled channel geometries and surface-wetting properties to direct liquid flow, manage gas-liquid separation, and maintain root-zone aeration.
Both hydroponic and soil-based configurations were tested to evaluate performance across different growth media.
Measurements included monitoring liquid distribution, root-zone moisture levels, aeration efficiency, and bubble formation, alongside comparing observations to predictive capillary flow models.

By systematically varying system geometry, wetting conditions, and operational parameters, the experiments defined design guidelines for robust, low-maintenance plant growth systems for space and analogous terrestrial applications.

This research was based on the hypothesis that, in microgravity where gravity-driven fluid behavior is absent, capillary forces, surface tension, and geometric design could provide reliable water and nutrient delivery to plant root zones.
Passive physical mechanisms replaced gravity in distributing and reclaiming fluids within the growth systems.
Surface-wetting characteristics and channel geometry were designed to maintain root-zone hydration, facilitate aeration, and manage liquid–gas separation without pumps or active components.
These mechanisms sustained water availability and oxygen exchange, preventing oversaturation or desiccation.
The approach demonstrated that passive capillary systems could support consistent, low-maintenance plant watering and aeration in reduced-gravity environments.
Demonstrating passive fluid management in plant growth systems is enabling reliable water and nutrient delivery in microgravity, supporting long-duration space missions.
Advancing capillary-based irrigation is reducing system mass, complexity, and power requirements.
In relation to agriculture on Earth, results from this research are improving precision irrigation, conserving water, and enhancing root-zone aeration in hydroponic and soil systems.
Generating validated models of capillary-driven flow is guiding efficient, resilient plant growth technologies.
Supporting scalable, low-maintenance systems is fostering innovations in both space life-support and sustainable food production on Earth.

Advanced Colloids Experiment-Temperature 4
Original Objective: The ACE-T4 experiments were designed to explore the disorder-induced transformation between a crystal and a glass.

The experiments introduced disorder by added colloidal dopants into the samples; these dopants introduce structural frustration into the crystals which, in turn, can transform the crystals into disordered solids (polycrystalline) and glasses with novel mechanical properties.

The experiments varied the concentration and character of particle dopants in three-dimensional colloidal crystals and employed direct visualization of an evolving crystal microstructure and dynamics in microgravity to derive fundamental insight into the nature of the transition and the glasses formed.

Revised Objective: Before the ACE-T4 experiment on the International Space Station (ISS) was conducted, the master hard disk controlling the Light Microscopy Module (LMM) failed and delayed starting this experiment by many months.
This extended delay had a detrimental effect on the samples that resulted in the gelation of the samples before the experiment began.

The originally planned experiments were no longer possible due to gelation, but the ACE-T4 experiment based on the changed samples (gels) provided qualitatively different insights into the behavior of 3D colloidal gels over a range of temperatures and temperature gradients.

Some effects were visible with LMM and provide an opportunity to study the microstructure, dynamics, and stresses in gels that can lead to microcracks, an important problem that, for example, could affect 3D printer inks.

The ACE-T4 experiment used confocal microscopy to observe the gels over a range of particle packing-fractions (temperatures), using pure, monodisperse poly(N -isopropylacrylamide) (pNIPA) particles in one sample, and then mixtures of pNIPAM particles with different amounts of particle dopants in five other samples.
All of the samples formed gels.
There was no crystallization in any sample .
The data obtained permits the study of 3D gels with and without dopants as a function of temperature; the temperature changes vary the particle size and thus properties of the gels.
In addition to the revised ACE-T4 experiment, ground-based soft matter research was completed and published.
The ACE-T4 experiments were intended to explore the transformation between a crystal and a glass by varying the density and character of particle dopants in three dimensional colloidal crystals.

The original hypothesis stated that ''dopants introduce structural frustration into the crystals which, in turn, can transform the crystals into disordered (polycrystalline) solids and glasses with novel mechanical properties.

Direct visualization of the evolving crystal microstructure and dynamics in microgravity will provide fundamental insight into the nature of glasses and into processes such as nucleation and melting.''
By frustrating their structural order, the transition from ordered (crystal) to disordered (glassy) materials can alter the macroscopic behavior of ordered materials.
Moreover, these experiments could also provide fundamental insight into the nature of nucleation, aging, and melting in materials with varying degrees of order.
This information could benefit observation and synthesis of new colloidal materials (e.g. g., meta and photonic materials) for many applications ranging from color control to random laser.

Validation of a CFD Model for Gas-Liquid Flows in Packed Bed Reactors to Enable Thermo-Fluid Analysis in Microgravity

Develop and validate computational models for gas-liquid two-phase flow in porous media under microgravity using the PBRE (Packed Bed Reactor Experiment) flight data available in Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI).
Understand capillary-dominated fluid dynamics in low-gravity environments where traditional gravity-driven models fail.
Advance CFD tools to support the design and scale-up of life support and thermal control systems for spacecraft, space stations, and lunar/Martian habitats.
In this grant, our approach combined high-fidelity simulations with reduced-order modeling to better understand and predict two-phase gas-liquid flows through packed bed reactors in microgravity.
We began by developing interface-resolved CFD simulations using the Volume of Fluid (VOF) method to capture detailed bubble dynamics in a representative volume of the reactor.
These simulations were validated using PBRE imagery and pressure data available in PSI.

To address scale-up and improve computational efficiency, we also developed a two-fluid model (TFM), which treats the gas and liquid phases as interpenetrating continua rather than tracking individual interfaces.
We calibrated the drag closure in this model using PBRE data, allowing us to predict pressure drop behavior across different flow regimes.
By combining detailed CFD with a validated TFM, we created a versatile modeling framework that supports the design of life support and thermal systems for future space missions.

Particle Engulfment and Pushing By Solidifying Interfaces

The major scientific objectives of this investigation were as follows: · to enhance the fundamental understanding of dynamics of insoluble particles at the solid-liquid interface; · to obtain experimental data for the critical velocity of particle engulfment in a convection-free environment; · to validate present theoretical models; · to improve the understanding of physics associated with solidification of liquid metals - ceramic particles mixtures; · to investigate aspects of melt processing of particulate metal matrix composites in the unique microgravity environment which will yield some vital information for terrestrial applications; · to further develop the elements of the numerical model into a comprehensive model that takes into account convection effects.
The experimental approach was to perform directional solidification experiments with a pure metal, aluminum, doped with low volume fraction of insoluble particles, ZrO2.
These experiments were carried out during the Life and Microgravity Science (LMS) mission on board the space shuttle Columbia.

In addition, transparent organic matrices such as succinonitrile and biphenyl doped with polystryrene particles or glass beads were used to observe the interaction between the particle and solidification interface in real time.
The experiments with the organic matrices were performed during the United States Microgravity Payload 4 (USMP-4) mission also on board the space shuttle Columbia.
Planar interfaces were produced through appropriate manipulation of the solidification variables, so that a clear pushing/engulfment transition (PET) of the particles could be determined.
Both ground and microgravity experiments were conducted.

Recognizing that the interaction between the particle and the solidification front is not completely a steady state process, a dynamic non-steady-state model was developed based on the fact that a particle, initially at rest, must have an accelerated motion in order to reach the steady-state velocity, which is the solidification velocity.
To account for the solutal fields in alloys a 2D FDM fixed Cartesian grid numerical model was also developed.
The models were validated using benchmark microgravity and terrestrial data.
During solidification of metal-insoluble particles systems the particles interact with the solidification front.
The solutal and thermal field, as well as fluid motion at the solid-liquid interface (SLI) will influence both interface morphology and the particle/interface interaction itself.

This investigation hypothesizes that based on the nature of interaction and balance of forces acting on the particle there is a critical SLI velocity below which particles are pushed ahead of the advancing interface, and above which particle engulfment occurs.
For planar SLI the critical velocity results from the forces acting on the particle.
These forces include particle-SLI interaction force, drag force on the particle, gravitational force, Saffman force, and Magnus force.
The last three are strongly affected by the level of gravitational acceleration.

A fundamental understanding of the phenomena associated with particle/interface interaction during solidification will permit the development of novel techniques for processing of particulate metal matrix composites through melting and solidification.
Similar concepts apply to inclusion management in casting alloys.
As for most other metallurgical applications it is desired to avoid inclusion segregation at grain boundaries.
Results of this research can be extrapolated straightforward to “clean steel” technology.

Another interesting application of particle pushing is in the processing of single crystals ceramic where strong flux pinning particles are desired to be homogeneously incorporated in the superconducting crystal.

Insights from this investigation can also be applied to the field of cryobiology where the study of the interaction of cells (yeast cells, red blood cells) with ice crystals when freezing aqueous solutions makes it possible to investigate the mechanism of the mechanical destruction of biological structures by ice crystals on freezing biological materials.
In addition, this investigation can be extended to the field of frost heaving of soils that can be reduced to the behavior of soil particles (i.e. clay) in a water/ice matrix.

Advanced Colloids Experiment-Temperature 5

The overarching goal of the project was to gain a better fundamental understanding of the relationship between bijel morphology, rheology, mechanical stability, and processability through combined ground-based and microgravity experiments and theoretical calculations.
Mixtures of propylene glycol/nitroethane (PG/NE) at their critical composition were prepared.
Partially hydrophobic silica particles were suspended in the PG/NE mixture and the suspensions were filled in different cuvettes.
On orbit, these cuvettes were heated to 25C, mixed in-situ, and then quenched from 25C to 0C.
Following the quench, an imaging protocol was used to collect a stack of 100 images in the Z direction at a spacing of 5 mm.

This investigation hypothesizes that interparticle interactions have a profound impact on the rheology of bijel particulate suspensions and attempts to answer the fundamental scientific question as to how the various forces at the colloidal scale are affected by Marangoni convection in microgravity.
The nature of interparticle interactions and its impact on rheology has profound implications for the processability of bijels and the ability to transform them into functional materials.

The ability to design and fabricate the unique 3-dimensional bijel structures opens a wide spectrum of new structures for applications that can benefit from synthesis of hierarchically porous monoliths and composites with a spinodal-like microstructure in which every constituent phase is naturally continuous throughout the entire sample volume.
This type of tailored porous microstructures can improve the physical properties and performance of materials used in a number of space and terrestrial applications.
Space exploration applications include improved energy storage batteries and fuel cells, and catalytic microreactors for lower mass and volume designs in spacecraft life support and ISRU systems.

There is a diverse array of potential terrestrial applications in electrochemical energy conversion and storage, tissue engineering, sensing, microstructured composites with optimized mechanical properties for MEMS, microfluidic heat exchangers and catalytic reformers, separations.

text: Experiments and Selected Findings 3.1 Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) Past research, including that conducted in microgravity, had revealed shortfalls in the ability to accurately model flames at the extremes of fuel dilution, namely for sooty pure -fuel flames and dilute flames that are near extinction.

text: Experimental studies of laminar, non-premixed flames of gaseous fuels are underway on the International Space Station (ISS) as part of NASA’s Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments(ACME) project.
doc_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) on the International Space Station (ISS)

text: The research is primarily focused on improving practical terrestrial combustion through fundamental microgravity research, where a secondary objective is spacecraft fire safety.
doc_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) on the International Space Station (ISS)

text: Example goals are to improve understanding of flame stability and extinction limits, soot control and reduction, oxygen-enriched combustion which could enable practical carbon sequestration, combustion at fuel lean conditions where both optimum performance and low emissions can be achieved, the use of electric fields for combustion control, cool flame chemical kinetics, and materials flammability.
doc_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) on the International Space Station (ISS)

text: The microgravity environment avoids buoyancy-induced flicker and enables the creation of spherical flames, allowing numerical models to focus computational power on transport phenomena and chemical kinetics.
doc_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) on the International Space Station (ISS)

text: Compared to normal gravity, microgravity also provides longer residence times and larger length scales, yielding a broad range of flame conditions which are beneficial for simplified analysis, e.g., of limit behavior where chemical kinetics are important.

text: Introduction Microgravity, i.e., apparent near weightl essness, is a unique environment for conducting combustion research.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Many flames are dramatically influenced by the effective elimination of buoyant convection, where the resulting effects are often advantageous.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: For example, it is possible to create spherically symmetric flames en abling one-dimensional analysis.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: More generally, the effective elimination of flicker yields quasi-steady flames.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Furthermore, the length scales are increased in microgravity flames faci litating analysis of the flame structure.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere than normalgravity flames and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: For example, the long residence times in microgravity flames ca n lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Even neglect ing soot, microgravity flames can be appropriate for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: It is also possible to study momentum-dominated flames at low velocities.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: And of course, microgravity is the appropriate environment for studies related to spacecraft fire safety.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Although microgravity combustion research has been conducted in drop facilities and research aircraft flying parabolic maneuvers, spacecraft li ke the International Space Station (ISS) offer significant advantages.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Drop durations, which are ~5 s or less in NASA facilities, are too short for soot to achieve quasi-steady conditions.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The drop durations are also too short to first establish a flame and then vary its flow rate, for example, to investigate stability or extinction
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Meanwhile, low-momentum flames can be dr amatically disturbed by the g-jitter present in the aircraft testing, which is nominally ±0.02 g for a ~20 s duration.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The jitter can be avoided by floating an experiment within the aircraft, but that reduces the test duration to mere seconds.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: As a result, space-based testing is often necessary to get microgravity conditions of sufficient duration and quality for combustion research.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Given the many advantages of space-based com bustion research, five gas-fueled non-premixed flame experiments have thus far been conducted in space, where they are listed chronologically in Table 1.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Three experiments were conducted over a decade ago on the space shuttle, i.e., the Space Transportation System (STS).
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The other t wo were conducted within the last five years on the ISS.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: This past research was focused on gravit y’s effects on the flame structure, soot and stability limits, and vortex interactions.

text: Science The current ACME experiments are primarily focused on energy and environmental concerns, but there is a secondary emphasis (w ith the BRE experiment) on fire prevention, especially for spacecraft.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The primary objective is to ga in fundamental understanding that can enable improved efficiency and reduced emissions in practical combustion processes on Earth, for example through the development a nd verification of models for chemical kinetics and transport processes in computational simulations.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: In addit ion to enhanced performance, improved modeling capability can lead to reductions in the ti me and cost for combustor design.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Some specific goals are to improve our understanding of combustion at fuel lean conditions where both optimum performance and low emissions can be achieved, soot control and reduction, oxygenenriched combustion which could enable practica l carbon sequestratio n, flame stability and extinction limits, the use of electric fields for combustion control, and materials flammability.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Unlike the other current ACME experiments, the Bur ning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is focused on spacecraft fire prevention.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: More specifically, BRE’s objective is to improve our fundamental understanding of materia ls flammability, such as ex tinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the relevance of existing flammability
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The purpose of the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment is to gain an impr oved understanding of flame ion pr oduction and investigate how the ions can be used to control non-premixed flames.

text: Outside review ers concluded that the experiment “ has great prospects of improving our understa nding of nearly every practical combustion device.” The experiment will be conducted with a simple gas -jet flame, where an electric field will be generated by creating a hig h voltage (up to 10 kV) differ ential between the burner and a flat circular mesh above (i.e., downstream of) the burne r.

text: Measurements will be made of the ion current through the flame an d the flame’s response to electric forcing as a function of the field strength, fuel, and fuel dilution.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The primary goal of the Flame Design experiment is to improve our understanding of soot inception and control in order to ena ble the optimization of oxygen enriched combustion and the “design” of non -premixed flames that are both robust and soot free.

text: An outside review panel declared that Flame Design “... could lead to greatly improved burner designs that are efficient and less polluting than current designs." text: ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and two illumination systems, of which three cameras are part of the CIR facility and are already in use on orbit.

text: All but one of the cameras is mo unted outside of the chamber.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Color imaging is provided by two cameras: a hi gh-definition digital camera mounted outside of the chamber and a standard analog camer a mounted on the chamber insert (with a turning mirror).
