text: Introduction 1.1 Combustion in Microgravity Microgravity, i.e., apparent near weightlessness, is a unique environment for conducting combustion research.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Many flames are dramatically influenced by the near elimination of buoyant convection, where the resulting effects are often advantageous 1-2).
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: For example, it is possible to create spherically symmetric flames enabling one-dimensional analysis.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: More generally, the effective elimination of flicker yields quasi -steady flames.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Furthermore, the length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of their structure.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere than normal -gravity flames and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: For example, the long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free due to radiative heat loss.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Even neglecting soot, microgravity flames can be appropriate for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are importan t.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: It is also possible to study momentum -dominated flames at low velocities.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: And of course, microgravity is the appropriate environment for studies related to spacecraft fire safety.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Although microgravity combustion research has long been conducted in dr op facilities and research aircraft flying parabolic maneuvers, spacecraft like the International Space Station (ISS) offer significant advantages.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Drop durations, which are ~5 s or less in NASA facilities, are too short for soot to achieve quasi-steady conditions.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: The y are also too short to first establish a flame and then vary conditions such as the flow rate, for example, to investigate stability or extinction limits.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Meanwhile, low -momentum flames can be dramatically disturbed by the g-jitter present in aircraft testing, which is nominally ±0.02 g for a ~20 s duration.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: The jitter can be avoided by floating an experiment within the aircraft, but that reduces the test duration to mere seconds.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: As a result, space -based testing is often necessary to get microgravity conditions of sufficient duration and quality for combustion research.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Introduction Microgravity, i.e., apparent near weightl essness, is a unique environment for conducting combustion research.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Many flames are dramatically influenced by the effective elimination of buoyant convection, where the resulting effects are often advantageous.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: For example, it is possible to create spherically symmetric flames en abling one-dimensional analysis.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: More generally, the effective elimination of flicker yields quasi-steady flames.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Furthermore, the length scales are increased in microgravity flames faci litating analysis of the flame structure.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere than normalgravity flames and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: For example, the long residence times in microgravity flames ca n lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Even neglect ing soot, microgravity flames can be appropriate for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: It is also possible to study momentum-dominated flames at low velocities.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: And of course, microgravity is the appropriate environment for studies related to spacecraft fire safety.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Although microgravity combustion research has been conducted in drop facilities and research aircraft flying parabolic maneuvers, spacecraft li ke the International Space Station (ISS) offer significant advantages.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Drop durations, which are ~5 s or less in NASA facilities, are too short for soot to achieve quasi-steady conditions.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The drop durations are also too short to first establish a flame and then vary its flow rate, for example, to investigate stability or extinction
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Meanwhile, low-momentum flames can be dr amatically disturbed by the g-jitter present in the aircraft testing, which is nominally ±0.02 g for a ~20 s duration.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The jitter can be avoided by floating an experiment within the aircraft, but that reduces the test duration to mere seconds.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: As a result, space-based testing is often necessary to get microgravity conditions of sufficient duration and quality for combustion research.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Given the many advantages of space-based com bustion research, five gas-fueled non-premixed flame experiments have thus far been conducted in space, where they are listed chronologically in Table 1.

text: Science The current ACME experiments are primarily focused on energy and environmental concerns, but there is a secondary emphasis (w ith the BRE experiment) on fire prevention, especially for spacecraft.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The primary objective is to ga in fundamental understanding that can enable improved efficiency and reduced emissions in practical combustion processes on Earth, for example through the development a nd verification of models for chemical kinetics and transport processes in computational simulations.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: In addit ion to enhanced performance, improved modeling capability can lead to reductions in the ti me and cost for combustor design.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Some specific goals are to improve our understanding of combustion at fuel lean conditions where both optimum performance and low emissions can be achieved, soot control and reduction, oxygenenriched combustion which could enable practica l carbon sequestratio n, flame stability and extinction limits, the use of electric fields for combustion control, and materials flammability.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Unlike the other current ACME experiments, the Bur ning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is focused on spacecraft fire prevention.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: More specifically, BRE’s objective is to improve our fundamental understanding of materia ls flammability, such as ex tinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the relevance of existing flammability
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Introduction 1.1 Combustion in Microgravity Microgravity, i.e., apparent near weightlessness, is a unique environment for conducting combustion research.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Many flames are dramatically influenced by the near elimination of buoyant convection, where the resulting effects are often advantageous 1-2).
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: For example, it is possible to create spherically symmetric flames enabling one-dimensional analysis.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: More generally, the effective elimination of flicker yields quasi -steady flames.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Furthermore, the length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of their structure.

text: Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere than normal -gravity flames and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: For example, the long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free due to radiative heat loss.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Even neglecting soot, microgravity flames can be appropriate for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are importan t.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: It is also possible to study momentum -dominated flames at low velocities.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: And of course, microgravity is the appropriate environment for studies related to spacecraft fire safety.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Although microgravity combustion research has long been conducted in dr op facilities and research aircraft flying parabolic maneuvers, spacecraft like the International Space Station (ISS) offer significant advantages.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Drop durations, which are ~5 s or less in NASA facilities, are too short for soot to achieve quasi-steady conditions.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: The y are also too short to first establish a flame and then vary conditions such as the flow rate, for example, to investigate stability or extinction limits.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Meanwhile, low -momentum flames can be dramatically disturbed by the g-jitter present in aircraft testing, which is nominally ±0.02 g for a ~20 s duration.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: The jitter can be avoided by floating an experiment within the aircraft, but that reduces the test duration to mere seconds.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: As a result, space -based testing is often necessary to get microgravity conditions of sufficient duration and quality for combustion research.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: 1.2 Previous Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuels Conducted in Space Five different experiments burning gaseous fuels were conducted during space shuttle missions in 1997 and 2003 .
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: The ACME experiments are primarily focused on energy and environmental concerns, but there is a secondary emphasis with the BRE experiment on spacecraft fire prevention.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: The primary objective is to gain fundamental understanding that can enable improved efficiency and reduced emissions in practical combustion processes on Earth, for example through the development and verification of models for chemical kinetics and transport processes in computational simulations.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: In addition to enhanced performance, improved modeling capability can lead to reductions in the time and cost for combustor design.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Some specific goals are to improve our understanding of combustion at fuel lean conditions where both optimum performance and low emissions can be achieved, cool flame chemistry, flame stability and extinction limits, materials flammability, oxygen-enriched combustion which could enable practical carbon sequestration, soot control and reduction, and the use of electric fields for combustion control.

text: Experiments and Selected Findings 3.1 Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) Past research, including that conducted in microgravity, had revealed shortfalls in the ability to accurately model flames at the extremes of fuel dilution, namely for sooty pure -fuel flames and dilute flames that are near extinction.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: This investigation’s objective is to extend the range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and experimentally verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels .
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: The dependence of normal coflow flames on injection velocity and fuel dilution is carefully examined for flames at both very dilute and highly sooting conditions.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Measurements including flame temperature, CH* concentration, soot temperature, and soot volume fraction are made of the structure of diluted methane and ethylene flames in an air coflow , where the fuel and air velocities are typically matched.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Lifted flames are a focus of the research to avoid flame dependence on heat loss to the burner, where examples from ISS testing can be seen in Fig.

text: The results are directly applicable to practical combustion issues such as turbulent combustion, ignition, and flame stability.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Experimental studies of laminar, non-premixed flames of gaseous fuels are underway on the International Space Station (ISS) as part of NASA’s Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments(ACME) project.
doc_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) on the International Space Station (ISS)

text: The research is primarily focused on improving practical terrestrial combustion through fundamental microgravity research, where a secondary objective is spacecraft fire safety.
doc_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) on the International Space Station (ISS)

text: Example goals are to improve understanding of flame stability and extinction limits, soot control and reduction, oxygen-enriched combustion which could enable practical carbon sequestration, combustion at fuel lean conditions where both optimum performance and low emissions can be achieved, the use of electric fields for combustion control, cool flame chemical kinetics, and materials flammability.
doc_title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) on the International Space Station (ISS)

text: The microgravity environment avoids buoyancy-induced flicker and enables the creation of spherical flames, allowing numerical models to focus computational power on transport phenomena and chemical kinetics.

text: Compared to normal gravity, microgravity also provides longer residence times and larger length scales, yielding a broad range of flame conditions which are beneficial for simplified analysis, e.g., of limit behavior where chemical kinetics are important.

text: Introduction Microgravity, i.e., apparent near weightl essness, is a unique environment for conducting combustion research.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Many flames are dramatically influenced by the effective elimination of buoyant convection, where the resulting effects are often advantageous.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: For example, it is possible to create spherically symmetric flames en abling one-dimensional analysis.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: More generally, the effective elimination of flicker yields quasi-steady flames.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Furthermore, the length scales are increased in microgravity flames faci litating analysis of the flame structure.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere than normalgravity flames and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: For example, the long residence times in microgravity flames ca n lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Even neglect ing soot, microgravity flames can be appropriate for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: It is also possible to study momentum-dominated flames at low velocities.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: And of course, microgravity is the appropriate environment for studies related to spacecraft fire safety.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Although microgravity combustion research has been conducted in drop facilities and research aircraft flying parabolic maneuvers, spacecraft li ke the International Space Station (ISS) offer significant advantages.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Drop durations, which are ~5 s or less in NASA facilities, are too short for soot to achieve quasi-steady conditions.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The drop durations are also too short to first establish a flame and then vary its flow rate, for example, to investigate stability or extinction
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Meanwhile, low-momentum flames can be dr amatically disturbed by the g-jitter present in the aircraft testing, which is nominally ±0.02 g for a ~20 s duration.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The jitter can be avoided by floating an experiment within the aircraft, but that reduces the test duration to mere seconds.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: As a result, space-based testing is often necessary to get microgravity conditions of sufficient duration and quality for combustion research.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Given the many advantages of space-based com bustion research, five gas-fueled non-premixed flame experiments have thus far been conducted in space, where they are listed chronologically in Table 1.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Three experiments were conducted over a decade ago on the space shuttle, i.e., the Space Transportation System (STS).
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The other t wo were conducted within the last five years on the ISS.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: This past research was focused on gravit y’s effects on the flame structure, soot and stability limits, and vortex interactions.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: In e ach experiment, the flame configuration was the laminar gas-jet diffusion flame, where vortices were created in the TGDF experiment by varying the air entrainment (through mechanical control of an iris centered near the burner tube outlet).
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The research has included flames in both quiescent a nd coflowing atmospheres.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The LSP and TGDF experiments were conducted in sealed combustion chambers.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: In contrast, the flame was enclosed within a small flow duct (with a 76-mm squar e cross-section) in the ELF, SPICE, and SLICE experiments.

text: In all cases, the atmosphere consisted of ~21% oxygen (by volume) with a balance of nitrogen.

text: Science The current ACME experiments are primarily focused on energy and environmental concerns, but there is a secondary emphasis (w ith the BRE experiment) on fire prevention, especially for spacecraft.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The primary objective is to ga in fundamental understanding that can enable improved efficiency and reduced emissions in practical combustion processes on Earth, for example through the development a nd verification of models for chemical kinetics and transport processes in computational simulations.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: In addit ion to enhanced performance, improved modeling capability can lead to reductions in the ti me and cost for combustor design.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Some specific goals are to improve our understanding of combustion at fuel lean conditions where both optimum performance and low emissions can be achieved, soot control and reduction, oxygenenriched combustion which could enable practica l carbon sequestratio n, flame stability and extinction limits, the use of electric fields for combustion control, and materials flammability.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Unlike the other current ACME experiments, the Bur ning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is focused on spacecraft fire prevention.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: More specifically, BRE’s objective is to improve our fundamental understanding of materia ls flammability, such as ex tinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the relevance of existing flammability
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: 5 test methods for low and partial-gravity environments.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: A flat porous burner fed with gaseous fuel will simulate the burning of solid and li quid fuels, where measurements are made of the thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon which the vaporization of c ondensed-phase fuels is dependent.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: A small number of gaseous fuels (including mixtures with inert gases) will be used to simulate the burning of fuels such as paper, plastic, and alcohol by matching properties such as the heats of combustion and gasification, the surface temperature, and smoke point.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Research, including that already conducted in microgravity, has revealed that our current predictive ability is signific antly lacking for flames at the extremes of fuel dilution, namely for sooty pure-fuel flames and dilute flames that are ne ar extinction.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The goal of the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) expe riment is to extend the range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and experimentally verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The dependence of normal coflow flames on injection velocity and fuel dilution will be carefully examined for flames at both very dilute and highly sooting conditions.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Measurements will be made of the structure of diluted methane and ethylene flames in an air coflow.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Lifted flames will be used as the basis for the research to avoid flame dependence on heat loss to the burner.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The results of this experiment will be directly applicable to practical combustion issues such as turbulent c ombustion, ignition, flame stability, and more.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The SLICE experiment was conducted as a precursor to ACME’s CLD Flame experiment, in order to maximize its science, e.g., through refinement of the test matrix.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: An electric field can strongly influe nce flames because of its effe ct on the ions produced by the combustion reactions.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The direct ion transport and the induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the soot or flammability limits, direct heat transfer, an d reduce pollutant emission.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The purpose of the Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment is to gain an impr oved understanding of flame ion pr oduction and investigate how the ions can be used to control non-premixed flames.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Outside review ers concluded that the experiment “ has great prospects of improving our understa nding of nearly every practical combustion device.” The experiment will be conducted with a simple gas -jet flame, where an electric field will be generated by creating a hig h voltage (up to 10 kV) differ ential between the burner and a flat circular mesh above (i.e., downstream of) the burne r.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Measurements will be made of the ion current through the flame an d the flame’s response to electric forcing as a function of the field strength, fuel, and fuel dilution.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The primary goal of the Flame Design experiment is to improve our understanding of soot inception and control in order to ena ble the optimization of oxygen enriched combustion and the “design” of non -premixed flames that are both robust and soot free.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: An outside review panel declared that Flame Design “... could lead to greatly improved burner designs that are efficient and less polluting than current designs." Flame Design will investigate the soot inception and extinction limits of spherical microgravity flame s created with porous spherical burners.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Tests will be conducted with various conce ntrations of both the fuel (i.e., ethylene or methane) and oxygen in order to determine the role of the flame structure on the soot inception.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The effect of the flow direction on soot formation will be assessed by studying both normal flames and inverse flames, where in the latter case an oxygen/i nert mixture flows from the spherical burner into a fuel/inert atmosphere.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The Flame Design ex periment will explore whether the stoichiometric mixture fraction can characterize soot and flamm ability limits for non-p remixed flames like the equivalence ratio serves as an indicator of those limits for premixed flames.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: 6 The purpose of the Structure a nd Response of Spherical Flame s (s-Flame) experiment is to advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of both soot-free and sooty flames.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The spherical flames will be ignited at non-steady conditions and allowed to transition naturally toward extincti on.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Tests will be conducted with various inert diluents, in both the fuel and chamber atmosphere.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The fuel gases include hydrogen and methane mixtures for soot-free flames, and ethylene for sooty flames.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: One experiment objective is to identify the extinction limits for both radiative and conv ective extinction (i.e., at high and low system Damköhler numbers, respectively).
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Another objective is to determine the existence, onset, and nature of pulsating instabilities that ha ve been theoretically predicted to occur in such flames with fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number.

text: NASA/TM-20210011385 3 1.0 Summary of Burning and Suppression of Solids—II Experiments The first section of the report provides an overview of the experiment operations and results.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Each of the five principal investigators (PIs) for Burning and Suppression of Solids—II (BASS–II), in alphabetical order, have summarized their research in separate sections of this report.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Appendix A includes test matrices from each PI, Appendix B describes the dilution model and verification testing, Appendix C describes the anomalies encountered, Appendix D describes a thermal analysis, while Appendix E contains the BASS and BASS–II current papers and presentations created through the summer of 2020.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: 1.1 Background BASS–II tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, O2 concentration, temperature, etc.).
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: NASA tests and controls materials from a flammability perspective using an upward burning test in normal gravity, which is considered to be the worst-case geometry for flammability of the material on Earth.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: However, it may not be conservative for flammability in space.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: One objective of the BASS–II tests is to identify what is the worst case for material flammability in spacecraft environments, and how does that compare to the terrestrial upward burning used to screen the materials for safe use aboard spacecraft.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Detailed combustion models can be validated by data obtained in the simpler flow environment in microgravity.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Once validated, they can be used to build more complex combustion models needed to capture the important details of flames burning in normal gravity.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: These models have wide applicability to the general understanding of many terrestrial combustion problems.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The main variables tested were the effects of ambient O2 concentration, ventilation flow velocity, and fuel type, thickness, and geometry.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Many of the tests focused on finding a minimum O2 concentration or flow velocity where a material will burn in space, to compare with the Earth-based limits.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Flame growth rates are also of interest, to determine how quickly a fire in space can grow and if the flames reach a finite size or continue to grow.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: This has implications for firefighting strategies in spacecraft.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: BASS–II utilized the gaseous nitrogen (GN2) available on International Space Station (ISS) to vitiate the atmosphere in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) from standard ISS “air” down to the low O2 flammability limits.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: BASS–II also utilized onboard O2, CO, and CO2 sensors to evaluate the completeness of the combustion.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: A total of 126 tests were conducted as part of BASS–II.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: This is more than the planned 103 tests, since some samples were burned more than once.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: There are some samples that could be burned further, should future operational time become available.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: For the first time on ISS, BASS–II utilized MSG working volume vitiation with GN2.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: We developed a perfectly stirred reactor model to determine the GN2 flow time and flow rate to obtain the desired reduced O2 concentration in the working volume for the tests.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: This worked out extremely well for operations, and added a new vital variable, ambient O2 level, to our test matrices.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: 1.2 Experiment Description The MSG in the Destiny Lab of the ISS provides a contained atmosphere in which fire safety experiments can be conducted (Ref.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The MSG, shown in Figure 1.1, has a set of filter banks that capture particulates and convert the CO to CO2 using an ambient temperature catalyst.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The BASS–II hardware is shown inside the MSG working volume in Figure 1.1.

text: NASA/TM-20210011385 4 Figure 1.1.—Microgravity Science Glovebox Facility (MSG) working volume aboard the International Space Station (ISS) with the Burning and Suppression of Solids—II (BASS– II) experiment hardware installed.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Working volume of MSG was diluted using ISS N2 gas.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Compound Specific Analyzer-Combustion Products (O2 and CO) and Carbon Dioxide Monitor (CO2) sensors were used to obtain before and after burn gas concentrations.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The BASS–II hardware consists of a flow duct, still camera, video camera, video and power boxes, external control box and associated plumbing, and mounting systems.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The black anodized 7.6- by 7.6- by 17-cm rectangular flow duct with rounded corners was originally built to perform gas jet diffusion flame studies (Ref.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: It was adapted to accommodate solid samples for the BASS experiments.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The flow was blown through the duct using a variable speed fan.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Two additional flow restrictors could be used at the fan inlet to increase the pressure drop and thus reduce the flow through the duct to the desired value for the test point.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: With no restrictors, the maximum flow velocity was ~55 cm/s, and with two restrictors this was reduced to ~35 cm/s.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The flow then passed through a honeycomb flow straightener and an inlet screen to reduce swirl.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: An omnidirectional spherical airspeed transducer (TSI Incorporated 8475) was positioned between the honeycomb and the screen and was used to measure the steady-state flow through the duct.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The air velocity transducer probe had a response time of approximately 1 minute.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Inside the test section was a nozzle for N2 flow, a movable scale, and an Oriel® 71768 thermopile detector (Newport Corporation) with a CaFl window (spectral range of 0.13 to 11 μm) in the downstream top back corner of the duct viewing the upstream direction.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The test section of the duct had two orthogonal windows; the top one was replaced for BASS to provide a mounting rail system for the solid samples.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The top window was used by a Nikon D300s 12.3-megapixel digital color still camera with a 60-mm lens that provided 4,320- by 2,968-pixel images.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The duct exit contained a perforated copper plate followed by a brass screen to provide heat rejection and a cold surface for soot deposition.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The flow turned 90° to exit the duct, which facilitated mixing of the hot combustion gases with the cool ambient air.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The front window also had interlocks for the igniter and N2 flow.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: A Panasonic Corporation color video camera
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The video camera had an overlay that displayed the N2 flow rate (cm3/min), fan voltage (10× V), air velocity transducer reading (cm/s), and the radiometer signal.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The fan voltage was calibrated with the airspeed transducer at the end of every operations day.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The radiometer signal was not calibrated but provided a measure of the flame dynamics and steadiness.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The external control box had controls for the fan voltage, N2 flow rate, enable switches for the igniter and N2 flow, and a radiometer gain level setting.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: A number of sample geometries were used in BASS–II: cast polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) samples were shaped as rods of various diameters (6.35 to 12.7 mm), thin to thick slabs (0.125 to 5 mm), or a section of a 4-cm-diameter sphere.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: In addition, flat cotton-fiberglass blended fabric samples were also burned.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: These samples could generally be mounted so that they could be burned in either the opposed or concurrent flow direction.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The samples were manually ignited with a Kanthal® A–1 29-gauge hot-wire igniter coil with a nominal hot wire resistance of 0.8 to 1 Ω, powered by 3.5 to 3.8 amps when the astronaut manually pulled the deployment lever to move the igniter into position.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Samples were burned within the duct and the combustion products exited the duct and mixed with the gas in the work volume.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Example flame images are shown in Figure 1.2.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Samples were returned to Earth and evaluated for mass loss.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: To evaluate the levels of combustion products produced during microgravity fires, BASS–II requested the use of available onboard sensors to measure the O2 depletion and the completeness of combustion (CO and CO2) for microgravity combustion tests under spacecraft ventilation flow rates to provide scientific data on the stoichiometry of the diffusion flame reactions and heat release rates (HHRs).
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The data reported here is the first extensive data on the stoichiometry and toxicity of combustion products in microgravity.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: O2 concentrations in the MSG working volume were varied during the testing from ambient ISS O2 levels (~21 percent O2) down to ~14 percent O2 for very near limit flames.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The CO sensor in the CSA-CP is zero calibrated every 60 days, with a range of 0 to 1,000 ppm and a resolution of 1 ppm.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The CO2 sensor was within its calibration window and had a range of 0 to 5 percent and a resolution of 0.1 percent by volume of CO2.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The sensor data provided initial and final conditions for repeated tests in a sealed working volume and allowed us to determine when the working volume needed to be purged.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Many of the BASS–II tests required a diluted atmosphere, which typically took 1 to 3 h to achieve by dilution of the MSG working volume using ISS N2 (from the hose connecting the BASS–II duct to the back wall of MSG in Figure 1.1).
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The N2 was regulated with a small (<0.5 liters per minute (LPM)) MKS Instruments 179A mass flowmeter and entered the flow duct through a small nozzle just downstream of the fan.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The fan in the flow duct was turned to maximum (>100 LPM) during the N2 flow to mix and blow the gas into the working volume and circulate it continuously throughout the hours-long dilution.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: 1.3 Validation of Microgravity Science Glovebox Dilution—Continuously Stirred Tank Reactor Model To utilize the capabilities of MSG to reduce the O2 in the working volume in a controlled manner, a dilution model based on a continuously stirred tank reactor (CSTR) model was developed.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: In this model, the mixing in the working volume (via the BASS–II duct fan) is assumed to be “instantaneous,” so that the outflow “leak” concentration from the MSG work volume to the ISS cabin is the perfectly mixed instantaneous concentration.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: This perfect mixing approximation is valid as long as the residence time (volume per flow rate or V/R) is at least 5 to 10 times as long as the mixing time, which is met by the 100 LPM N2 flow rate during dilution (250 liters/100 LPM ~ 2.5 min mixing time).
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: For the MSG volume and N2 flow rates, the working volume residence time is V/R = 500+ min, and the mixing time is shorter than 50 min, so the assumption is valid.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The model assumes the work volume is at constant pressure and temperature and constant volume.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Thus, the leak rate out of the work volume is equal to the rate of N2 supplied (r).
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The sensor data is used to measure the O2 depletion and the completeness of combustion (CO and CO2) for each microgravity combustion test under spacecraft ventilation flow rates.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The O2 depletion data is compared to the CO2 production for each BASS–II test that used PMMA as the fuel.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: NASA/TM-20210011385 7 The data, taken over a wide range of initial O2 concentrations, forced opposed or concurrent flow velocities, and using various sample geometries, is compared with this 6:5 stoichiometric ratio of O2 to CO2 in Figure 1.3.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: As shown, the data agrees very well with stoichiometric ratios for the wide range of test conditions.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Other than unburned fuel (primarily methylmethacrylate vapor), which does contain some O2 as shown in Equation (1.4), the only other (nontrace quantity) potential species with O2 is CO, which was also measured, as shown in Figure 1.4 to Figure 1.6.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Figure 1.4 shows that the concurrent rods produced on average 550 ppm of CO for every 1 percent of CO2.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The opposed rods had a very nonlinear response, which may be indicative of a flow effect.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The longer the burn, the more CO2 was formed, and the nominal test procedure for most samples was to turn the flow down in increments.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: At very low velocities, the tail region of the opposed-flow flames opened up, which presumably allowed incomplete combustion products to escape the flame zone.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Interestingly, the concurrent procedure was very similar, but the concurrent flame always had an open tail, allowing incomplete combustion products to exit throughout the burn.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The opposed thick slabs fall somewhere in between, producing on average 370 ppm of CO for every 1 percent of CO2.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The one outlier point from Figure 1.3 at 2.8 percent CO2 is not included in Figure 1.4 since the CO sensor was over-ranged for this test (>1,000 ppm full scale), so we have no quantitative value for CO for this test.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: During this test, the long burn of the relatively strong flame caused overheat damage to the downstream lower corner of the front window in the area where a flow duct leak was occurring.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The leak was repaired on orbit, and operations proceeded without further incident.

text: 1.6 Overall Conclusions As part of the Burning and Suppression of Solids—II (BASS–II) experiment, we conducted a number of tests with different geometries, flow velocities, and initial O2 concentrations.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The last variable was enabled using gaseous N2 to dilute the working volume.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: To adequately characterize this dilution, we developed a continuously stirred tank reactor model and verified it against sensor readings.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Sensor data from the tests showed that the O2 was burning nearly stoichiometrically to CO2, and that CO levels appear to be a function of geometry and, in some cases, the flow velocity and geometry combination.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The CO to CO2 ratios for these fires are an order of magnitude higher than for efficient flue gases, indicating that these flames are not efficient.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The heat release was estimated for the tests using O2 consumption calorimetry.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: This showed that most of the tests released well below 100 W.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: In the one long test that released close to 100 W, we sustained some damage to the downstream corner of the front window, due to a leak that directed the heat from this energetic flame to that location during the prolonged burn.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Using the mass loss and O2 consumption data, the global equivalence ratio for the tests is estimated to be 1.3 on average, which indicates the flames were burning fuel rich under the low-velocity forced-flow conditions.

text: 2.1.2.1 Extinction Velocity Each test is started by establishing a steady flame spread in the presence of a forced flow and then reducing the flow velocity in a gradual manner, as shown in Figure 2.1.

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: After the flame propagated across half the sample length at a steady spread rate of 2.2 mm/s, the flow was abruptly cut off and the flame was observed to extinguish within 2 s, as shown by the radiometer signal drop in Figure 2.2.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: To pin down the extinction flow velocity, a second test was done under the same conditions except the flow velocity was set at 3 cm/s and after the flame propagated about half the sample length, the flow was gradually reduced.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The flame spread rate of the leading edge, as plotted in Figure 2.3, shows that the flame extinguishes at about 30 s after ignition.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The fan voltage at that time indicates a flow velocity of about 1.1 cm/s.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The sequence of images in Figure 2.1 shows the pathway to radiative extinction.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: As the flow speed is gradually reduced from about t = 27 s, the flame size starts shrinking and the orange color disappears and the flame becomes completely blue, most possibly because of the temperature drop brought about by radiative losses, which is enhanced by the increased residence time at low flow velocity.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The signal from the radiometer, shown in Figure 2.2, is also consistent with a cooling and shrinking flame as the signal starts decreasing from right about t = 27 s.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: After t = 30 s, there is no visible flame and the radiometer data (Figure 2.2) indicate a sudden change in slope at that time, possibly because the radiation is emitted mostly by the sample holder with the combustion products swept away by the flow.

text: NASA/TM-20210011385 19 2.2 Critical Flow Velocity for Radiative Extinction in Opposed-Flow Flame Spread in Microgravity Environment: Comparison of Experimental, Computational, and Theoretical Results1 2.2.1 Abstract The effect of opposing flow on flame spread rate over thin solid fuel is investigated with the help of scaling theory, a comprehensive computational model, and experiments conducted aboard the International Space Station.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: While spread rate over thin fuels is independent of the opposing flow velocity in the thermal regime, in the microgravity regime, where the opposing flow can be very mild or even completely absent in the absence of buoyancy-induced flow, the spread rate is known to decrease as the opposed flow is reduced.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Under certain conditions, this can lead to flame extinguishment at a low enough flow velocity.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: This report combines scaling arguments with computational results to predict a critical flow velocity for such flame extinction.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Results from the recently conducted limited number of space-based tests, presented in this report, seem to confirm the prediction validating the closed-form formula for the critical extinction velocity.

text: 2.2.3 Experimental Setup The Burning and Suppression of Solids—II (BASS–II) apparatus (Ref.

text: 12) in the ISS is depicted in Figure 2.6.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: It is a combustion tunnel, a 76-mm square duct, where the PMMA fuel samples, 20 mm wide and about 95 mm long with the thickness ranging from 100 to 400 μm, are burned in an opposed-flow configuration.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: A fan forces a flow of an O2-N2 mixture through flow straighteners from the right to the left and the sample is ignited at the left end.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Depending on the flow velocity and O2 concentration, a steady flame is established that spreads from the left end of the sample towards the right end.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The O2 level can be adjusted to 21 percent or below and the flow velocity can range from 0 to 50 cm/s.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: A hot wire anemometer is used to calibrate the flow velocity with fan voltage, which is used to determine the flow velocity.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Experiments were conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox of the ISS by two crew members.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Operation instructions were communicated from NASA Glenn Operations Center in realtime as the experiment progressed.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The igniter is then turned off and the flame is photographed with a high-resolution digital still camera with a frame rate of 1 per second.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: A radiometer is used to confirm flame extinction when the visible flame goes out.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: 2.2.5 Extinction Velocity Each test is started by establishing a steady flame spread in the presence of a forced flow and then reducing the flow velocity in a gradual manner.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: In the first test, a steady flame was established over a 100-μm sample.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: After the flame propagated across half the sample length at a steady spread rate of 2.2 mm/s, the flow was abruptly cut off and the flame was observed to extinguish within 2 s.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: To pin down the extinction flow velocity, a second test was done under the same conditions except the flow velocity was set at 3 cm/s and after the flame propagated about half the sample length, the flow was gradually reduced.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The flame spread rate of the leading edge, as plotted in Figure 2.8, shows that the flame extinguishes at about 30 s after ignition.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The fan voltage at that time indicates a flow velocity of about 1.1 cm/s.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The sequence of images in Figure 2.9 shows the pathway to radiative extinction.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: As the flow speed is gradually reduced from about t = 27 s, the flame size starts shrinking and the orange color disappears and the flame becomes completely blue, most possibly because of the temperature drop brought about by radiative losses, which is enhanced by the increased residence time at low flow velocity.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The signal from the radiometer, shown in Figure 2.10, is also consistent with a cooling and shrinking flame as the signal starts decreasing from right about t = 27 s.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: After t = 30 s, there is no visible flame and the radiometer data (Figure 2.10) indicate a sudden change in slope at that time, possibly because the radiation is emitted mostly by the sample holder with the combustion products swept away by the flow.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The independence of spread rate with opposing flow velocity was interpreted as a constant kinetic effect by the buoyancy-generated flow.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: However, given the simplicity of the chemical kinetic model (one-step overall reaction) used in the computational model, a definitive conclusion cannot be made from computational results alone.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: One way to experimentally establish if there is kinetic effect in downward spread rate is to reduce the strength of the buoyancy-generated flow or eliminate it altogether as in a microgravity environment.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: If the flow velocity is reduced below 40 cm/s, the increased residence time would reduce and weaken the kinetic effect and the spread rate can be expected to increase (in a kinetically controlled flame) until the thermal limit is reached.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: On the other hand, if the thermal limit is already established in the downward experiment (see Figure 2.14), then the spread rate is expected to remain unaltered as the opposing flow velocity is reduced in the absence of buoyancy.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: A comparison of experiments in the downward configuration with that in a microgravity environment, therefore, can be used to establish the thermal regime for a given O2 level.

text: 2.3.5 Microgravity and Normal-Gravity Experiments There are only a handful of experiments conducted on flame spread in a microgravity environment, an excellent review of which can be found as a book chapter by T’ien (Ref.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The only long-duration opposed-flow experimental facility is offered by the BASS–II apparatus (Ref.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: It is a combustion tunnel, a 76-mm square duct, where the PMMA (C2H8O2) fuel samples, 20 mm wide and about 95 mm long with the thickness ranging from 100 to 400 μm, are burned in an opposed-flow configuration.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: A fan forces a flow of an O2-N2 mixture through flow straighteners from the right to the left and the sample, 2 cm wide, is ignited at the left end.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Depending on the flow velocity and O2 concentration, a steady flame is established that spreads from the left end of the sample towards the right end.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The oxidizer mixture consists of O2 and N2 where the O2 level can be adjusted at 21 percent or below.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: During the experiment, an O2 sensor monitors the O2 level, which has been found to drift by less
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: A hot wire anemometer is used to calibrate the flow velocity with the voltage of the fan (see Figure 2.16) used for creating a flow of 50 cm/s or below.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The total pressure is also monitored, which varied from 99.2 to 99.5 kPa in the tests reported.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Experiments were conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox of ISS by two crew members.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Operation instructions were communicated from NASA Glenn Operations Center in realtime as the experiment progressed.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Each test starts by creating a desired opposing flow by adjusting the fan voltage.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: After the flow stabilizes, the igniter is turned on until a visible flame is observed.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The igniter is then turned off and the top view of the flame propagation is photographed with a high-resolution digital still camera with a frame rate of 1 per second.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: A video camera captures the side view of the flame propagation.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: In some of the tests, the flow velocity is changed during the spread to maximize the test matrix without having to burn additional samples.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: For downward spreading experiments, the Flame Stabilizer apparatus (Ref.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: 4) is used, where a 2-cmwide sample of PMMA is held vertically by a stainless steel sample holder and ignited at the top with a top-view camera recording the flame spread.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The sample holders used in the microgravity and downward experiments are shown in Figure 2.17.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: While the BASS sample holder has a built-in igniter, piloted ignition is used in the downward experiments.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The downward experiments were performed in the atmospheric condition (pressure 101 kPa, O2 level 21 percent).
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Ideally, the controllable parameters in a flame spread experiments include oxidizer mixture (percent of O2 by volume), oxidizer pressure, oxidizer velocity, fuel type, fuel thickness, fuel width, fuel length, and external radiation.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: In the data presented, the fuel thickness is the most important parameter of interest.

text: 2.3.6 Data Analysis The still images from the BASS experiments are converted to videos and posted along with those from the downward experiments at http://flame.sdsu.edu.

text: A MATLAB®- (The MathWorks, Inc.) based image processing application called Flame Analyzer has been developed at San Diego State University (SDSU) to obtain flame spread rate and other information from a top-view video.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Video analysis has been used in fire research for a long time not just for tracking flame spread (Ref.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: 21) but also for estimating flame temperature (Ref.

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: A typical color image of the top view 18 s after ignition is shown in Figure 2.18(a) for downward flame spread over a 75-μm-thick sample.

text: The dots along the axis, 6 mm apart, are superimposed on the image to help display the spatial resolution of the image.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The red green blue (RGB) values of each pixel of the central slice are then converted to an intensity value using built-in MATLAB® tools.

text: Across the width of the section, these intensity values are averaged, producing a 2D representation of the flame as shown in Figure 2.18(b).
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The variation of the width-averaged intensity along the x direction (axis) is shown in Figure 2.18(c).

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: 2.3.7 Results and Discussion The average spread rate over the 100-μm-thick sample in the normal-gravity experiments is found to be 2.0 mm/s (see Figure 2.19(b)).
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Although the instantaneous spread rate fluctuates slightly, the average spread rate and the flame shape remain relatively steady throughout the experiment.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The opposed flow being generated by buoyancy, a steady spread is expected.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Any variation is probably due to surface irregularities and other random factors.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: In a microgravity environment, the opposed flow is much lower with experiments conducted mostly at very mild opposed-flow velocities.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: For the same fuel thickness, the highest spread rate obtained is about 2.2 mm/s even though the opposing flow velocity was varied from
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: At very high flow velocity, kinetically driven blowoff extinction was observed and at very low velocity (at about 1 cm/s) radiative extinction was observed.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The highest spread rate in the microgravity environment, 2.2 mm/s, is about the same as the downward spread rate.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The overall flame shapes are also quite similar as shown in Figure 2.20(a) and (b) where flame images for spread over samples of different thicknesses are compared.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The leading edges in the downward spread show slight dripping effect and the flame is sootier, but the overall shape and size are quite similar as are the spread rates.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: This indicates that at 21 percent O2 level, downward spread over PMMA can be considered thermally controlled with minimal kinetic effect.

text: 2.3.8 Conclusion In this work, results of experiments on flame spread over thin sheets of polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) in the quiescent downward configuration and opposed-flow configuration in the microgravity environment are compared.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Based on adiabatic flame temperature, F is only about 3 percent greater.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Data from downward spread in ambient air is shown to correlate well (within the experimental uncertainty) with the microgravity data, establishing that the thermal limit is extended to downward spreading configuration in atmospheric condition on Earth.

text: With F evaluated, experimental data for flame spread over thick PMMA is used to determine the effective velocity induced by buoyancy as 1.9 cm/s.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Equating the thermal regime spread rate expressions for thin and thick limits, a formula for the transition between thin and thick fuels for downward spread in ambient atmosphere is obtained.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: For PMMA in ambient air, this transition thickness is evaluated to be 5.2 mm.

text: NASA/TM-20210011385 46 3.0 Project Scientist Report: Ferkul 3.1 Nomex® Flammability The objective of the Nomex® (DuPontTM) sample tests was to evaluate the flammability of Nomex®, since it is heavily used aboard the International Space Station (ISS) as a fire barrier.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: A secondary objective was to burn any unused Burning and Suppression Solids—I (BASS–I) samples, of which there was a single wax candle.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: 3.1.1 Results The three Nomex® samples did not ignite, which is an excellent result for fire safety aboard the ISS.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The wax candle test successfully ignited in an opposed flow (akin to holding a candle upside down) and burned at five different flow velocities corresponding to the test matrix potentiometer settings as shown in Figure 3.1.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: At the initial 3 cm/s, the sooty flame has an aspect ratio that is longer rather than wide.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: As the flow reduced, the flame became hemispherical.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: At the lowest pot setting, the flame becomes short rather than wide and turns mostly blue.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The ejected wax droplet shown in Figure 3.1(b) typifies the flame spread hazard associated with melting plastics in microgravity.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: If the melt viscosity is low enough, burning droplets can be ejected and possibly ignite other materials.
