text: 5.2 Introduction The NASA Burning and Suppression of Solids—II (BASS–II) tests examine the combustion of different solid materials and geometries in microgravity.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: While flames in microgravity are driven by diffusion and weak advection due to ventilation systems and crew movement, the current NASA spacecraft material selection test method (NASA–STD–6001 Test 1) (Ref.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: 1) is driven by buoyant forces since gravity is present.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: So, the BASS–II results will be used in comparison with ground-based experimental setups aimed at replacing NASA’s current test method for screening materials used onboard spacecraft.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The data gathered will also help us understand and know more about behavior of fires in space so that space travel can be made safer in the future.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The BASS–II experiments have provided us with an extensive thick fuel microgravity database that did not exist previously.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Previously, thick-fuel true microgravity data was obtained by Olson and others in a study involving Sounding Rocket experiments (Ref.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The study comprised a series of combustion experiments on polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) at very low velocity opposed flow and external radiant flux.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The institutions taking part in BASS–II operations are Case Western Reserve University; University of California, Berkeley; NASA Glenn Research Center; San Diego State University; and Michigan State University (Ref.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: There are three categories of samples: flat samples, rod samples, and a section of a large solid sphere.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The flat sample materials will include acrylic films and sheets of different thicknesses, and a cotton-fiberglass fabric blend Solid Inflammability Boundary at Low-Speeds (SIBAL) fuel.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The rod samples are made of black or clear acrylic and will provide solid fuel regression rates and extinction limits for both opposed and concurrent flow.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The large solid spherical section, also made of acrylic, will be used to study ignition of thick materials and flame growth over the thick material.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: 6.1.3 Experimental Setup The BASS–II hardware used for these tests has been described in detail in Reference 14.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: It consists of a black-anodized flow duct that provides a low-reflection backdrop for imaging flames with a color video camera at 30 frames per second and an orthogonal digital still camera (4,320 by 2,968 pixel images) at ~1 frame per second.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The tests were performed in the 250-L free volume Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) in the Destiny Lab of the International Space Station (ISS).
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The hardware setup is shown in Figure 6.1.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The flow duct measured 7.6 by 7.6 by 17 cm with rounded internal corners for smooth laminar flow through the duct.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The front window opened to install samples and igniters.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: A top window allowed still camera imaging.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: A noncalibrated radiometer in the downstream top back corner of the flow duct provided a relative flame strength reading at 5 Hz.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The three primary variables were flow velocity through the duct, PMMA rod radius, and O2 concentration of the working volume.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The flow was generated using a small variable-speed fan at the upstream end of the duct.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The voltage to the fan was displayed and could be set.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Up to two flow restrictors could be used at the fan inlet to increase the pressure drop and thus change the output flow range.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: With no restrictors, the maximum flow velocity was ~55 cm/s, and with two restrictors this was reduced to a maximum of ~35 cm/s.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The flow then passed through a honeycomb flow straightener and an inlet screen to reduce swirl.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: An omnidirectional spherical air velocity transducer (TSI Incorporated 8475) was positioned between the honeycomb and the screen and was used to measure the steady-state flow through the duct.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The air velocity transducer probe had a response time of approximately 1 min and its digital display only read out to the units place (no decimals) yielding an effective resolution of ±0.5 cm/s.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: A fan calibration was performed at the end of each operational day to associate the fan voltage with the flow velocity for each flow restrictor, after the fan had adequate time for warmup.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: NASA/TM-20210011385 67 To obtain the desired O2 concentration for the test, the initial ISS air filling the MSG working volume was diluted using N2 as described in Reference 14.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: O2 sensor readings, calibrated with the onboard mass spectrometer, provided initial and final O2 concentrations for each test.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The readings were used to verify the CSTR model and measure the O2 consumption within the test.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: 6.1.4 Experimental Results 6.1.4.1 Ignition Delay Time The astronaut would manually position the igniter within a millimeter of the tip of the rod and activate the igniter until a stable flame was achieved.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: It could be difficult to see the flame in the glare of the igniter, so the astronaut would turn off the igniter to assess flame viability.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: If the flame appeared to be going out, the astronaut would quickly turn the igniter back on to strengthen the flame and again check flame viability after a few seconds of applying power.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: This igniter on and off cycle might occur several times in a given test.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The ignition delay (tign) in each test was defined as the time from when the igniter was first turned on to the last time the igniter was turned off and a stable flame persisted.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Ignition generally occurred at a forced flow of 5 cm/s, so the ignition delay is plotted in Figure 6.2 against the initial O2 concentration alone.

text: The symbol sizes reflect the initial rod radius.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Because the igniter is positioned and activated manually, there is some inherent scatter in the ignition time, but some trends are clear.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: At higher O2 concentrations, ignition occurred within approximately 40 s.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Below an initial O2 concentration of 16 percent, the ignition delay time increased significantly.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Larger rods take longer to ignite, especially at lower O2 concentrations (up to 230 s).
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: If the sample is not ignited within this nondimensional time τ (the empirical factor 0.7 is selected so that τ = 1 at the ignition limit), it is likely not flammable, as shown for all values τ ≥ ~1 that fall below the ignition limit of ~14.5 percent O2.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: 6.1.6 Conclusions For the first time, a series of concurrent rod flammability tests were conducted in microgravity aboard the International Space Station (ISS).
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: A small flow duct was used to create 0- to 55-cm/s flows past the three sizes of clear and black PMMA rods.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Ignition delay time increased significantly as the minimum limiting O2 concentration is approached.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Ignition limits are found to be at higher O2 concentrations than the flammability limits due to the added heat loss to the initially cold fuel rod present at ignition.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The ignition delay time can be up to almost 10 times longer than the NASA STD–6001 standard igniter on time.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Detailed observations of near-quenching flames are described, including flame standoff distance trend with O2 and stretch rate a.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The flame shrinks to a hemispherical blue shape just before quenching.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Prequenching extinction oscillations at 1.1 Hz are observed with a radiometer and are similar to previously reported quiescent candle flame oscillations in microgravity.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: As flow speed is increased, blowoff extinction is initiated by the formation of a hole in the flame sheet in the stagnation region of the flame.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Once the stagnation region is blown far enough downstream of the stagnation region (greater than one gas-phase thermal length l), the flame is unable to propagate back upstream even when the flow is reduced.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: This is consistent with observations that at the low O2 concentrations of interest, an opposed-flow flame cannot be established.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Blowoff extinction limits from the ISS experiments agree well with Zero Gravity Research Facility 5.18-s drop test limits.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The lower portion of the flammability boundary, with O2 concentration and a as coordinates, was outlined as stochastic region between stable flames and extinguished flames.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: A curve fit including an exponential and linear term was used to empirically define the boundary.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The minimum in the flammability boundary is at a of 8 to 12 s–1, where the a is modified to account for the various rod sizes tested through the gas-phase l scale.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The linear blowoff branch may lend itself to extrapolation of normal-gravity flammability testing to zero stretch to estimate the lower microgravity flammability limit.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Gas sensor data and rod mass loss estimates indicate that the flames are globally stoichiometric at higher O2 concentrations but become more globally fuel rich as the minimum O2 concentration is approached.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: This is due to excess pyrolyzate leakage out of the open tail of the hemispherical flames.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: CO production also increases significantly at low O2 levels.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The CO to CO2 ratio increases as well at low O2 concentrations.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: This data suggests that the limiting reactant at the lowest O2 concentrations is the O2 rather than the fuel.

text: NASA/TM-20210011385 93 7.0 Individual Principal Investigator Report: T’ien 7.1 Concurrent Flame Growth, Spread, and Extinction Over Composite Fabric Samples in Low-Speed Purely Forced Flow in Microgravity3 7.1.1 Abstract As a part of the NASA Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) and BASS–II experimental projects aboard the International Space Station, flame growth, spread, and extinction over a composite cotton-fiberglass fabric blend (referred to as the SIBAL (Solid Inflammability Boundary at Low Speed) fabric) were studied in low-speed concurrent forced flows.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The tests were conducted in a small flow duct within the Microgravity Science Glovebox.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The fuel samples measured 1.2 and 2.2 cm wide and 10 cm long.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Ambient O2 was varied from 21 percent down to 16 percent and flow speed from 40 cm/s down to 1 cm/s.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: A small flame resulted at low flow, enabling us to observe the entire history of flame development including ignition, flame growth, steady spread (in some cases), and decay at the end of the sample.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: In addition, by decreasing flow velocity during some of the tests, low-speed flame quenching extinction limits were found as a function of O2 percentage.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The quenching speeds were found to be between 1 and 5 cm/s with higher speed in lower O2 atmosphere.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The shape of the quenching boundary supports the prediction by earlier theoretical models.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: These long-duration microgravity experiments provide a rare opportunity for solid fuel combustion since microgravity time in ground-based facilities is generally not sufficient.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: This is the first time that a low-speed quenching boundary in concurrent spread is determined in a clean and unambiguous manner.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: 7.1.2 Introduction Flame spread and extinction over condensed fuels in a microgravity environment has been the subject of extensive theoretical and experimental studies due to the importance of fire safety in human space missions (Refs.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Compared with burning in normal gravity, diffusion flames in microgravity are not affected by buoyancy-induced flow, thus providing a chance to study the fundamental mechanism(s) of low-speed flame quenching (Ref.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Transition from solid diffusion flame spreading to quenching extinction is a slow heat loss process characterized by a relative increase in the rates of radiative and conductive heat losses compared to the rate of heat generation (Ref.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Long-duration microgravity time is desired for such studies, which in general cannot be achieved by ground-based facilities.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Recently, NASA’s Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS–II) project examined the burning and extinction characteristics of a variety of solid fuel samples aboard the International Space Station (ISS).
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Different thermally thin and thermally thick solid fuels were burned in concurrent, opposed, or stagnation flow configurations in a small flow duct.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Each experimental run took tens of seconds to minutes, depending on the sample type and flow conditions.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The challenge with thin solid samples in concurrent flow, compared with other configurations, is that flame spreads much faster, and flames can become quite long.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Because of size limitations, the fuel sample is relatively short and so a concurrent spreading flame may not reach fully steady spread within the sample length.

text: 7.1.3 Experimental All tests were conducted in a small flow duct (shown in Figure 7.1) within the MSG aboard the ISS.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The sample used is a composite cotton-fiberglass fabric blend (75 percent cotton and 25 percent fiberglass).
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The thickness of the sample is about 0.32 mm with an area density of 18.2 mg/cm2.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The fabric is custom made for a previous project Solid Inflammability Boundary at Low Speeds (SIBAL) (Ref.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: 8), hence it is referred to here as the SIBAL fabric.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: One major advantage of this fuel sample is the retention of sample structure integrity after the combustible (i.e., cotton cellulose) is consumed because of the fiberglass mesh.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: It does not crack or produce curly ash typically seen in pure cellulose samples such as paper or cloth.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: In addition to Reference 8, experimental studies using SIBAL fabric can be found in References 9 and 10.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: In the experiment, SIBAL fuel samples of two different widths, 1.2 and 2.2 cm, were used.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The samples were mounted in stainless steel sample holders.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The fuel sample mounted to the holder was placed in the small flow duct of cross-sectional size 7.6 by 7.6 cm.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The flow speed could be varied from 1 to 55 cm/s.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The tests were conducted in ambient O2 molar fraction of 16 to 21 percent.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: It should be noted that for a given test the O2 concentration was fixed while the flow speed could be varied.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: A Kanthal® hot wire was used to ignite the fuel sample leading edge so that the flame can spread in a concurrent configuration.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The flame growth process was recorded by two cameras.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The side-view video camera provided edge-on images of the flat samples at standard video framing rates (29.97 frames per second).
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The top-view digital camera looked down on the top fuel surface and provided high-resolution still images of the flame at a rate of about one image every 1.2 s.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: When flow speed and O2 concentration were low, the flame became very dim blue and was difficult to see in the side video camera.

text: 7.1.4 Results and Discussion A total of 27 tests were carried out for the fabric samples in BASS–II, including six quenching tests, three nonignited tests, and one blowoff test.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: NASA/TM-20210011385 101 7.1.5 Conclusions Concurrent flame growth and extinction over a thin flat cotton-fiberglass composite fabric sample was studied as part of the Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) and BASS–II space experiments aboard the International Space Station.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: These long-duration microgravity experiments provided rare opportunities for solid fuel combustion studies.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: By reducing the flow velocity during the tests, quenching extinction limits were obtained accurately.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The quenching velocities are small (between 1 and 5 cm/s), and an accurate determination is necessary to resolve the slope of the quenching boundary.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The experimental data obtained supports earlier theoretical predictions (at least qualitatively) of solid flammability limits at low flow velocities due to radiative and conductive losses.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The flame image sequence at quenching shows the flame shrinks both in length and width and the flame goes out in a three-dimensional manner.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: In addition to obtaining quenching limits, the sequence of sample ignition, flame growth, and steady spread to final decay across the entire sample in low-speed purely forced flows were experimentally recorded.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: These are precious data to help us to understand the entire process of flame development in microgravity.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: They also provide the basis to check the theoretical model development.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Currently, we are measuring and deducing the pyrolysis rate constants for Solid Inflammability Boundary at Low Speeds (SIBAL) fabric in order to perform quantitative comparisons between the model and experiment.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: D.3 Purpose of the Analysis Burning and Suppression of Solids—II (BASS–II) samples are larger than previously flown samples, and there is a concern that the hardware will become overheated and be damaged by the burning of these large samples.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: This analysis is to estimate the temperature rise of the BASS experiment assembly for a worst-case flame for this large thick sample.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: It should be noted that we have no plans to run a test like this.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Assumptions: • Th e worst-case sample is the 0.5-cm-thick, 8.5-cm-long, and 2-cm-wide polymethylmethacrylate (P MMA) slab sample. • Th e worst-case flame is a concurrent flame, which is expected to be larger than an opposed flame.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: D.4 Background The basis for the burning rate estimates presented here are based on both a computational study looking at the burning rate distribution for boundary layer flow combustion of a PMMA plate in forced flow, shown in Figure D.1, (Ref.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: 1), and BASS test results from a 1-cm PMMA sphere burning in a stagnation flow (which captures the burning of the exposed base of the sample).
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: A thick PMMA slab will take time to ignite and grow to a steady-state size, and the sample burning rate distribution is an important quantity to determine how much heat is being generated by the flame.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: D.5 Analysis As can be seen in Figure D.2, the base of the flame (at x = 0) has the highest burning rate and there is an exponential decay in the regression rate away from that peak burning rate.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Using peak regression rate (rmax) for the four flow profiles given, we can extrapolate down to the 30-cm/s flow of interest.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The exposed base of the flame (the upstream most point) will be the strongest part of the flame, and the burning rate is expected to be a maximum there.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Based on data in the Section D.7 from a 1-cm-sphere BASS test, we estimate the regression rate to be 3.05 mm/min, which is in keeping with the estimates from Figure D.2, as shown in Figure D.3.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The downstream regression rates will decay exponentially from there, as shown in Figure D.2.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Note that this is way beyond the still camera card limit of 7 min.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: The flame will take some time to grow the steady-state size.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: To estimate the growth rate, we use an expected power law growth rate (Ref.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: This growth rate is quite reasonable, since a previous BASS test showed that a PMMA slab sample took over 3 min to grow to steady size, as shown in the Section D.7.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Using the experimental growth history and peak regression rates, we can estimate the regression rate profiles as a function of time.
doc_title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II  (BASS-II) Summary Report

text: Results: Thin Fuel Flame Spread and Extinction ♦ Opposed flow: • flame quickly reached steady spread • spread rate was fastest at an intermediate value of flow speed ♦ Concurrent flow: • Flame spread rate increased linearly with increasing flow. • Quenching extinction was observed (around 1 cm/s) ♦ This is the first time that detailed transient flame growth data was obtained in purely forced flows in microgravity. ♦ Long-duration experiments validate a number of theoretical predictions and also provide the data for a transient flame growth model under development.

text: The P-Trak, a hand-held instrument, can count individual particles as small as 20 nm in diameter in an aerosol stream.

text: Particles are drawn into the device by a built-in suction pump.
doc_title: Fundamental Research Applied To Enable Hardware Performance in Microgravity

text: Upon entering the instrument, these particles pass through a saturator tube where they mix with an alcohol vapor (see the following figure).
doc_title: Fundamental Research Applied To Enable Hardware Performance in Microgravity

text: This mixture then flows through a cooled condenser tube where some of the alcohol condenses onto the sample particles, and the droplets grow in a controlled fashion until they are large enough to be counted.
doc_title: Fundamental Research Applied To Enable Hardware Performance in Microgravity

text: These larger droplets pass through an internal nozzle and past a focused laser beam, producing flashes of light that are sensed by a photodetector and then counted to determine particle number concentration.
doc_title: Fundamental Research Applied To Enable Hardware Performance in Microgravity

text: The operation of the instrument depends on the proper internal flow and recycling of isopropyl alcohol in both the vapor and liquid phases.

text: 1.0 Introduction The spherically symmetrical combustion of a liquid fuel droplet in a quiescent ambient gaseous oxidizing atmos phere is a classical problem in combustion research, having been addressed first more than 50 years ago by Godsave (1952), Hall and Diederichsen (1953) , and Spalding (1952, 1953).
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Numerous reviews of the subject are now available in the literature, among them those of Wise and Agoston (1958), Williams (1973), Faeth (1977), Law (1982), Sirignano (1983), and Choi and Dryer (2001).
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: An advantage of spherical sym metry is that only one spatial dimension enters the description of the combustion process, so that one-dimensional (spherically symmetrical) time -dependent conservation equations apply.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: This greatly facilitates both computational and theoretical descriptions of the problem, thereby enhancing understanding of experimental results, which becomes much m ore difficult, uncertain, and inaccurate in multidimensional situations.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Natural convection, however, destroys the spherical symmetry of combustion in normal gravity, as was quite evident in the earliest experiments of Hall and Diederichsen (1953) and Goldsmith (1956).

text: 3.1.2 Error Analysis The error or uncertainty in the measurement of droplet diameter comes from a few sources.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The first is the spatial resolution of the camera.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: For all but the first few tests, the HiBM s operated at full frame (not binned), or 1024 by 1024 pixels.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Therefore, the minimum spatial resolution was ±29.5 μm.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: There was additional uncertainty in estimating the appro priate segmentation value, especially since the background gray level in the HiBMs view was not spatially uniform.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The FLEX science team performed extensive ground testing in the func tionally identical (to the CIR HiBM s on the ISS) Ground Interface Unit (GIU) HiBM s system with precision spheres of known size.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: This testing provided the guidelines for setting the appropriate threshold (segmentation) value to determine the edge of the droplet.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Also, it was obvious that there was noise in the image that could contribute to the uncertainty in droplet size.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The uncer tainty as a result of the se last two sources was greatly reduced by measuring the projected area (as opposed to a single spatial dimension) of the droplet.

text: 5.2 Fuel Needle Contamination During the assembly of the MDCA hardware , a conformal coating was applied to the fuel-dispensing needles.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The product was applied in two layers, a primer ( Dow Corning 1204) and a conformal coat (Dow Corning 3140 RTV ( MIL–A–46146) coating).
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Subsequent testing showed that the coating can both dissolve and “ flake” off in both methanol and heptane.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: When this occurred, the deployed fuel droplet was clearly not pure but contained an unknown amount of the conformal coating.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Once this problem was discovered, the mitigation was to prepare and fly new uncoated needles.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: All tests subsequent to these (to be reported in the future) will not have contamination.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: From extensive testing, careful analysis of the experimental data, comparison with space -based data from uncontaminated
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: NASA/TP—2015-216046 17 needles, numerical modeling efforts, and ground-based testing, we can make the following assertions about the experimental data reported herein: (1) Burning-rate constants were average, and the droplet history was minimally influenced by the con taminant.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The contaminant was likely present in trace amounts and was a very low volatility compound.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Because methanol and heptane are relatively high volatility fuels, the droplet regression history was dominated by the fuel not by the contaminant.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: (2) The flame size and flame history were similarly minimally influenced by the contaminant.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: (3) In the few tests where unusual features were observed in the flame view , such as minor disruptions and visual “sparklers,” these features were probably influenced, and possibly caused, by the presence of the contaminant.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: (4) Disruptive extinction of methanol is probably due to the presence of the contaminant.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: (5) Disruptive extinction of heptane may be due to the presence of the contaminant.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Subsequent tests with clean needles and fuel, however, also exhibited disruptive extinction at small droplet sizes, so no conclusion can be drawn regarding disruptive burning for heptane in the tests reported herein.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: (6) The diffusive extinction droplet diameters (smaller diameters) for methanol (where there is no disruption) were minimally influenced by the presence of the contaminant.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: (7) Radiative extinction droplet diameters (larger diameters) were not influenced by the presence of the contaminant.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: (8) Distorted droplets (e.g., the HiBMs video from the FLEX–088 test) for methanol droplet burning (approxi mately four tests) are probably the result of the contaminant.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus Flame Extinguishment Experiment (MDCA-FLEX) will assess the effectiveness of fire suppressants in microgravity and quantify the effect of different possible crew exploration atmospheres on fire suppression.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The goal of this research is to provide definition and direction for large scale fire suppression tests and selection of the fire suppressant for next generation crew exploration vehicles.

text: Research Summary: • The combustion and extinction characteristics of liquid fuel droplets in microgravity are determined by the complex interaction of fuel vapor and oxidizer transport, fuel vaporization, conductive, convective and radiative heat loss and chemical kinetics.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: All of these phenomena are critical in real fire scenarios and thus in understanding the complex issues involved in the design of an effective fire suppression system. • The simplicity of the droplet geometry lends itself to detailed theoretical and numerical studies.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: By comparing the results of the experiments to these detailed treatments it is possible to develop validated chemical kinetic and heat and mass transport mechanisms for liquid fuels.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: From these fundamental mechanisms it becomes possible to develop validated, predictive, reduced-scale mechanisms that are appropriate for modeling real fire suppression scenarios aboard future spacecraft. • The Multi-User Droplet Combustion Appara tus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment (MDCA- FLEX) investigation will yield both a quantitative measure of the effectiveness of various suppression agents and more importantly a set of predictive tools that will allow the effective, efficient design of future spacecraft fire suppression systems.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Detailed Research Description: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment (MDCA-FLEX) will map the flammability boundaries for liquid fuel combustion in reduced gravity to quantify the suppressant efficacy of various gaseous suppressants over the range of candidate
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: atmospheric pressures and oxygen concentrations.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: This investigation will develop predictive theoretical and numerical codes and chemical kinetic schemes to model flammability boundaries as a function effective gravitational acceleration on the unique ambient conditions encountered in space exploration applications.The development and validation of these models will require detailed spatially and temporally resolved measurements of droplet burning rate, flame extinction, flame radiation, soot concentration, soot temperature, etc.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: This investigation will also develop improved and validated reduced (simplified) theoretical and numerical sub-models of important physical processes (chemical kinetics, radiation, soot formation/destruction) that can be used in simulations of large scale, realistic fires.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The independent experiment variables analyzed by MDCA-FLEX are: Oxygen Mole Fraction: The ambient oxygen mole fraction in a typical space environment can vary from high concentrations in EVA pre-breathing environments down to that typically found in air.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: At high oxygen concentrations, however, the chemical times are small enough (relative to the characteristic flow times) such that the droplets will burn to completion rather than exhibiting flame extinction.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Therefore, it is also necessary to study low oxygen concentrations, down to the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI).
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: It is also important to determine the LOI in order to verify the chemical mechanisms.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The oxygen mole fractions in the present study will vary from 0.10 to 0.50.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The chamber must also be large enough such that there is no significant decrease in ambient oxygen mole fraction during an experiment (i.e. the droplet burns in an essentially constant ambient).
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Diluent (non-suppressant): The ambient mixture will consist of oxygen mixed with a suppressant and the balance of an inert diluent gas.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The diluent gas for these studies will be primarily nitrogen since that is the typical diluent on Earth and expected in space.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: There will be a small number of tests with a helium diluent gas.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The reason is primarily for baseline comparisons with the Droplet Combustion Experiment, which used helium as the diluent gas and also to vary the physical properties of the diluent gas.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Suppressant Type: The tests will examine candidate gaseous suppressants that have widely varying physical, chemical and radiative properties.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: This will enable model and sub-model development and validation over a wide range of ambient conditions to improve the predictive capabilities of the models.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The suppressants are carbon dioxide and helium.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The expected concentrations range from 0.00 mole fraction to the limit where no flame can exist (0.70 expected for the least active suppressant).
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Pressure: Ambient pressure does not significantly influence the droplet burning rate, but does influence chemistry at sufficiently low values.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: In addition, one strategy for extinguishing a fire is to isolate the habitat where it exists and vent the cabin to space.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: It is therefore beneficial to have verified suppressant data at low pressures.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The pressure for the tests will range from 0.5 to 1.0 atm (standard atmosphere).
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: As with the oxygen mole fraction, it is important that the test chamber be sufficiently large so that the pressure is essentially constant during an experiment (i.e. the droplet burns in a constant pressure ambient).
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Fuel Type: The advantage of the droplet geometry is that the fuel is relatively simple and better characterized than typical fuels in fire safety studies (e.g.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: This is also a disadvantage since it does not represent a practical fuel.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The study will use two typical hydrocarbon fuels, an alcohol, methanol (CH3OH ) and an alkane, heptane (C7H16 ).
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: There is a relatively large experience base with these fuels.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Methanol has a fuel-bound oxygen atom, and burns with a very dim blue flame (not much soot production) with a small standoff distance, so it has widely different radiative characteristics than heptane.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Therefore, studying these two fuels gives a wide range of fire scenarios to verify model and submodel performance over.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Droplet Diameter: The droplet is ignited in the flammable region and then burns in a constant oxygen mole fraction ambient until flame extinction.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Under the assumption of quasisteady burning, the initial droplet size should not significantly influence the determination of the extinction droplet size.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Transient influences, however, will be present, so some variation in initial droplet diameter is necessary to determine the deviation from quasi-steady behavior.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The initial droplet size in the proposed study will vary between 2 and 5 mm.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Operations Location: ISS Inflight Brief Research Operations: • MDCA-FLEX will be setup and operated in the Combustion Integrated rack (CIR) on ISS. • The investigation will generate droplets from met hanol or heptane as required by the test point. • The data will be recorded via video using the CIR optics bench.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Operational Requirements: The MDCA-FLEX investigation will be setup in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The CIR chamber will be filled with the appropriate atmosphere depending on the test point.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: A total of 196 test points are required for completion of MDCA-FLEX.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Fuel will be dispensed followed by ignition.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: All activities will be captured in near real-time download with the CIR color camera video.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Operational Protocols: Following setup and initialization of the MDCA-FLEX investigation the chamber shall be filled with the appropriate atmosphere, which depending on the test point, will vary in pressure from 0.5 atm to 3.0 atm, will vary in oxygen concentration from 0.1 to 0.4 mole fraction, and will vary in suppressant concentration from 0 to 0.7 mole fraction.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: A settling time of approximately 2 minutes will elapse prior to initiating the test in order to ensure that the temperature and pressure of the chamber gases have stabilized.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: This settling time will be followed by the dispensing of a predetermined amount of fuel (based on the target droplet size) onto the support fiber.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: When sufficient fuel has been dispensed the
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: dispensing needles will be retracted and a dwell period of at least 10 seconds will be allowed for the droplet internal fluid motion induced by deployment to subside.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: This will then be followed by initiating power to the igniter for a selectable amount of time ranging from 1 second to 5 seconds after which the igniter will be retracted from the field of view.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: If the flow field is to be generated by translating the droplet then droplet motion would commence at the same time that the igniter is retracted.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: A near real-time download of the color camera video will be required in order to verify successful droplet deployment, ignition, and overall progress of the experiment.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Pressure and temperature data of the chamber environment will also be required in near real time.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: At least 2 minutes must be allowed after filling chamber to ensure that the chamber gas temperature and pressure has stabilized.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: For droplet dwell time allow at least 10 seconds to ensure all droplet motion imparted by droplet deployment and needle retraction has subsided.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Chamber purity for fuel vapor mole fraction of less than 0.005 in the atmosphere for tests without carbon dioxide and less than 0.02 mole fraction (each species) of carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and other products.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Stemming from the need to prevent, detect and suppress on-board spacecraft fires, the NASA microgravity combustion research program has grown to include fundamental research.
doc_title: FLEX: A Decisive Step Forward in NASA's Combustion Research Program

text: From early experiment, we have known that flames behave differently in microgravity, and this environment would provide an ideal laboratory for refining many of the long held principals of combustion science.
doc_title: FLEX: A Decisive Step Forward in NASA's Combustion Research Program

text: A microgravity environment can provide direct observation of phenomena that cannot be observed on Earth.
doc_title: FLEX: A Decisive Step Forward in NASA's Combustion Research Program

text: Through the years, from precursor work performed in drop towers leading to experiments on the International Space Station (ISS), discoveries have been made about the nature of combustion in low gravity environments.
doc_title: FLEX: A Decisive Step Forward in NASA's Combustion Research Program

text: These discoveries have uncovered new phenomena and shed a light on many of the fundamental phenomena that drive combustion processes.
doc_title: FLEX: A Decisive Step Forward in NASA's Combustion Research Program

text: This paper discusses the NASA microgravity combustion research program taking place in the ISS Combustion Integrated Rack, its various current and planned experiments, and the early results from the Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) Experiment.
doc_title: FLEX: A Decisive Step Forward in NASA's Combustion Research Program

text: The Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) experiment that is currently underway in the Combustion Integrated Rack facility onboard the International Space Station is aimed at understanding the effects of inert diluents on the flammability of condensed phase fuels.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: To this end, droplets of various fuels, including alkanes and alcohols, are burned in a quiescent microgravity environment with varying amounts of oxygen and inert diluents to determine the limiting oxygen index (LOI) for these fuels.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: In this study we report experimental observations of methanol droplets burning in oxygen-nitrogen-carbon dioxide and oxygen-nitrogen-helium gas mixtures at 0.7 and 1 atmospheric pressures.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: The initial droplet size varied between approximately 1.5 mm and 4 mm to capture both diffusive extinction brought about by insufficient residence time at the flame and radiative extinction caused by excessive heat loss from the flame zone.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: The ambient oxygen concentration varied from a high value of 30% by volume to as low as 12%, approaching the limiting oxygen index for the fuel.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: The inert dilution by carbon dioxide and helium varied over a range of 0% to 70% by volume.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: In these experiments, both freely floated and tethered droplets were ignited using symmetrically opposed hot-wire igniters and the burning histories were recorded onboard using digital cameras, downlinked later to the ground for analysis.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: The digital images yielded droplet and flame diameters as functions of time and subsequently droplet burning rate, flame standoff ratio, and initial and extinction droplet diameters.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: Simplified theoretical models correlate the measured burning rate constant and the flame standoff ratio reasonably well.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: An activation energy asymptotic theory accounting for time-dependent water dissolution or evaporation from the droplet is shown to predict the measured diffusive extinction conditions well.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: The experiments also show that the limiting oxygen index for methanol in these diluent gases is around 12% to 13% oxygen by volume.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: 1 Introduction Studies of droplet combustion are of interest from both fundamental and applied viewpoints, the latter in connection with both combustor performance and safety issues.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: Influences of carbon dioxide and helium, as well as increased nitrogen, in the atmosphere on the combustion characteristics and on extinction bear on questions of fire extinguishment.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: Liquid fuel droplets also are convenient vehicles for investigating relevant combustion processes from fundamental viewpoints, and 1
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: 5th US Combustion Meeting – Paper # 070HE-0303 Topic: Spray and Droplet methanol, as a non-sooting fuel, offers an opportunity to examine an important simplified case.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: Although there have been a number of studies of methanol droplet combustion and extinction in the past, influences of different atmospheres are poorly understood.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: For these reasons, the present research is designed to advance our knowledge of methanol droplet combustion in such atmospheres.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: Extensive data of this kind on the combustion of methanol droplets have now been obtained in the FLEX program onboard the International Space Station (ISS).
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: More than 100 droplets have been burned.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: Here we repost much of these new data and offer simplified analyses of the results.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: Methanol droplet vaporization in a humid environment apparently was first studied by Law and co-workers in 1987 [1].
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: They showed that, when a methanol droplet vaporizes in a humid environment, water condenses on the cold droplet surface and is transported into the interior.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: The latent heat of water released during condensation was stated to increase the methanol vaporization rate.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: Subsequently, the combustion of methanol droplets in a quiescent microgravity environment [2, 3] and in free falling conditions [4] was investigated.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: Cho et al. [2] conducted methanol dropletcombustion experiments in helium-oxygen mixtures, chosen because extinction diameters could be accurately measured in a short-duration microgravity facility as a result of the increased burning rates produced by highly conductive helium mixtures.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: Yang et al. [3] also showed experimentally that pure methanol droplets burning in air exhibit extinction at a non-zero droplet diameter.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: Lee and Law [4] studied the combustion of freely-falling methanol and ethanol droplets and demonstrated that they absorb water produced during the combustion process.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: They also measured the water content of the droplet as a function of burning time and the extinction diameters for both methanol and ethanol droplets.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: Droplets of initially pure methanol and methanol-water mixtures, diameters 2-5 mm, were burned in a space-shuttle experiment aboard Columbia during the USML-2 mission [5].
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: The results showed that for pure methanol, unlike the alkane droplets that were also studied on that mission, the extinction diameter varies linearly with the initial droplet diameter.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: Okai and co-workers [6], as a part of their methanol-dodecanol droplet-array experiments, measured the extinction diameter for a single methanol droplet at atmospheric pressure, and additional data from the USML-2 experiments has been reported and analyzed [7].
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: Marchese et al. [7] show that for small methanol droplet burning in air, radiation is unimportant, and the flames extinguish by diffusion-controlled mechanisms, similar to the diffusive-extinction results of the present study.
doc_title: Methanol Droplet Combustion in Oxygen-Inert Environments in Microgravity

text: They also show that when the initial droplet diameter is greater than roughly 4 mm, the droplet flame extinguishes through excessive radiative heat loss, as predicted in the analysis of Chao et al. [8].

text: Thomas Avedisian Cornell University Ithaca, New York 14853 Executive Summary The Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) program is a continuing set of experiments on droplet combus tion, performed employing the Multi -User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA), inside the chamber of the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), which is located in the Destiny module of the International Space Station (ISS).
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: This report describes the experimental hardware, the diagnostic equipment, the experimental procedures, and the methods of data analysis for FLEX.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: It also presents the results of the first 284 tests performed.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The intent is not to interpret the experimental results but rather to make them available to the entire scientific community for possible future interpretations.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The apparatus for the FLEX experiments was transported to the ISS and installed late in 2009.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: It includes canisters for fuel storage, two opposed-needle syringes for injecting fuel to form a droplet, two opposed hot -wire igniters for initiating combustion, and a long, fine fiber that can be used to tether the droplet and move it at a programmable low velocity through the gas in the chamber.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The combustion history is recorded photograph ically, with a visible -light color camera that views the entire field, a backlit camera that highlights the droplet to determine its diameter accurately as a function of time during burning, and a camera with a filter centered at 310 nm, intended to record emissions from excited hydroxyl radicals produced in the flame (Low Light Level Ultra -Violet, LLUV) , thereby providing a measure of the flame diameter .
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Although the ISS crew must change the fuel canisters and the gas bottles needed to establish the atmosphere in the combustion chamber, each droplet burning experiment is run remotely from the Telescience Support Center at the NASA Glenn Research Center i n
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: During periodically scheduled experiment intervals, about 4 to 10 droplets are burned in this remote operation, with use made mainly of the color camera to guide the procedure, which involves a number of manual steps.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: In addressing the experimental procedures and data analysis, this report details the methods, data downlink, and format, and it provides error estimates.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The results include histories of droplet diameters obtained from the backlit camera and histories of flame diameters obta ined from both the hydroxyl filter camera and the color camera.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Both flame diameter measurements are of the outer edge of the flame, and the diameters in the color-camera images are the smaller of the two, approximately three- fourths of the LLUV results.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Average burning-rate constants for each burn also are reported, as are extinction diameters, for the cases where the flame extinguished at a finite droplet size .
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Both radiative and diffusive extinctions occurred during the testing.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The fuels studied in thes e experiments were methanol and n-heptane.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The droplets had initial diameters between 2 and 5 mm, and they were burned in oxidizing atmospheres at ambient temperature and various pressures between 0.70 and 3.05 atm, over ranges of dilution of oxygen with nitrogen, with carbon dioxide, and with mixtures thereof.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Most of the tests were conducted at pressures between 0.7 and 1 atm, and many of the tests were in air.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: A principle objective was to determine the limiting oxygen index (LOI), the oxygen percentage below which combustion would not occur.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: This objective reflected the FLEX focus on investigating fire safety in spacecraft.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Observed LOI values for these fuels appear to be slightly lower than initially expected.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Besides documenting both radiative extinc tion at higher dilutions and diffusive extinctions at lower dilutions for both fuels, the results exhibited disruptive extinctions and provided information pertinent to soot production for heptane.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The continuing experiments are providing additional data for these two fuels, as well as droplet -combustion data for other fuels, and NASA intends to catalog these data in similar reports.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: 1.0 Introduction The spherically symmetrical combustion of a liquid fuel droplet in a quiescent ambient gaseous oxidizing atmos phere is a classical problem in combustion research, having been addressed first more than 50 years ago by Godsave (1952), Hall and Diederichsen (1953) , and Spalding (1952, 1953).
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Numerous reviews of the subject are now available in the literature, among them those of Wise and Agoston (1958), Williams (1973), Faeth (1977), Law (1982), Sirignano (1983), and Choi and Dryer (2001).
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: An advantage of spherical sym metry is that only one spatial dimension enters the description of the combustion process, so that one-dimensional (spherically symmetrical) time -dependent conservation equations apply.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: This greatly facilitates both computational and theoretical descriptions of the problem, thereby enhancing understanding of experimental results, which becomes much m ore difficult, uncertain, and inaccurate in multidimensional situations.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Natural convection, however, destroys the spherical symmetry of combustion in normal gravity, as was quite evident in the earliest experiments of Hall and Diederichsen (1953) and Goldsmith (1956).
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) is a droplet combustion experiment performed on the International Space Station (ISS).
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: FLEX is the first experiment in the multipurpose facility develop ed at the NASA Glenn Research Center —the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The CIR provides the combustion chamber, most of the diagnostics, the gas- mixing system, and the primary interface between the ISS and the ground controllers at Glenn.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The Multi -User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) is the hardware that deploys and ignites the liquid fuel droplets and provides some of the diagnostics.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The MDCA is located in the CIR combustion chamber, but it communicates through the CIR to ground controllers at Glenn.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The purpose of this report is to detail and permanently archive the results of a subset of the FLEX experiments, namely those occurring between March 2009 and the end of December 2011.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: It is not intended to interpret the data from those experiments or to draw any scientific conclusions ; that will occur through future NASA reports and peer-reviewed journal articles that reference this report .

text: 5.0 Observations and Discussion 5.1 General Observations The primary objective for this report was to detail and archive the results from the FLEX exper iments from March 2009 to December 2010.

text: Appendix B presents the detailed results for the droplet size (droplet diameter squared) and flame sizes (from both the LLUV and color camera views) as functions of time.
