text: These results , along with the raw experiment data, are available from the NASA Physical Science Informatics data repository (psi.nasa.gov, registration required).
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: In each test, there is a clear ambiguity in the droplet size during ignition (after deployment and before the igniters withdraw).
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: This was the result of the broadband glow from the igniters changing the discrimination between the droplet and the background.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: This was especially present from the FLEX– 001 test to the FLEX–009 test.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: For these tests, the shutter speed (integration time of the array) was 1/30 s (inverse of the framing rate).
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: After the FLEX–009 test, the shutter speed decreased to a much smaller value (1/1000 s) with a corresponding increase in the illumination level.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: This minimiz ed the image distortion caused by the igniters and the broadband flame radiation (from soot for heptane), resulting in more accurate droplet size data.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The great majority of the tests were of free -floating droplets (no support tether).
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: For these tests , the droplets were rarely completely motionless ; they ha d some residual velocity from deployment and ignition and then drifted more as a result of the residual acceleration of the spacecraft (g -jitter).
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: As a result of this, the droplets did drift out of the FOV of one (typically the HiBMs) or more of the CIR cameras.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: For tests where the droplet drifted out of the FOV of the camera, the data end abruptly (e.g., the droplet regression during the FLEX–011 test).
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: This does not correspond to the end of the test, just to the end of the data from that particular view (note that the flame histories continue during the FLEX–011 test).
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: For a minority of tests, the droplet drifted out of the HiBM s FOV as a result of the deployment , ignition, and/or g -jitter.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: However, it then actually drifted back into the FOV.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: In this case, there is a gap in the history of that view ( e.g., the droplet history for the FLEX–013 test).
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The sharp decline in the droplet size on either side of that gap corresponds to the time when the droplet (usually) or flame (rarely) was partially in and partially out of the FOV.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: For some tests, some of the CIR cameras failed to record data for a portion of the test, and for other tests, none of the test was recorded.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: These show up in the plots in Appendix A as either missing traces or gaps in the data (e.g., the FLEX–024 test, for which the HiBMs failed to record any data).
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The detailed data plots in Appendix B show two different measurements of flame diameter, one from the LLUV camera and the other from the color camera.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: For almost all of the tests, the diameter measured by the LLUV is larger than that measured by the color camera.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The flame diameters from the color camera are typically about three-fourths of those from the LLUV camera.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: This discrepancy is not unusual and is a re sult of the LLUV being sensitive to the OH • chemiluminescence, which typically peaks outside of the visible flame.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: For heptane tests, where there is significant soot luminosity (which is not visible in the LLUV, but dominates the color camera), the discrepancy is even larger because the peak of the soot luminosity is typically inside the blue flame envelope.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: 5.2 Fuel Needle Contamination During the assembly of the MDCA hardware , a conformal coating was applied to the fuel-dispensing needles.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The product was applied in two layers, a primer ( Dow Corning 1204) and a conformal coat (Dow Corning 3140 RTV ( MIL–A–46146) coating).
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Subsequent testing showed that the coating can both dissolve and “ flake” off in both methanol and heptane.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: When this occurred, the deployed fuel droplet was clearly not pure but contained an unknown amount of the conformal coating.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Once this problem was discovered, the mitigation was to prepare and fly new uncoated needles.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: All tests subsequent to these (to be reported in the future) will not have contamination.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: From extensive testing, careful analysis of the experimental data, comparison with space -based data from uncontaminated
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: NASA/TP—2015-216046 17 needles, numerical modeling efforts, and ground-based testing, we can make the following assertions about the experimental data reported herein: (1) Burning-rate constants were average, and the droplet history was minimally influenced by the con taminant.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: The contaminant was likely present in trace amounts and was a very low volatility compound.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Because methanol and heptane are relatively high volatility fuels, the droplet regression history was dominated by the fuel not by the contaminant.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: (2) The flame size and flame history were similarly minimally influenced by the contaminant.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: (3) In the few tests where unusual features were observed in the flame view , such as minor disruptions and visual “sparklers,” these features were probably influenced, and possibly caused, by the presence of the contaminant.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: (4) Disruptive extinction of methanol is probably due to the presence of the contaminant.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: (5) Disruptive extinction of heptane may be due to the presence of the contaminant.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Subsequent tests with clean needles and fuel, however, also exhibited disruptive extinction at small droplet sizes, so no conclusion can be drawn regarding disruptive burning for heptane in the tests reported herein.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: (6) The diffusive extinction droplet diameters (smaller diameters) for methanol (where there is no disruption) were minimally influenced by the presence of the contaminant.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: (7) Radiative extinction droplet diameters (larger diameters) were not influenced by the presence of the contaminant.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: (8) Distorted droplets (e.g., the HiBMs video from the FLEX–088 test) for methanol droplet burning (approxi mately four tests) are probably the result of the contaminant.
doc_title: Detailed Results from the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011

text: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus Flame Extinguishment Experiment (MDCA-FLEX) will assess the effectiveness of fire suppressants in microgravity and quantify the effect of different possible crew exploration atmospheres on fire suppression.

text: The goal of this research is to provide definition and direction for large scale fire suppression tests and selection of the fire suppressant for next generation crew exploration vehicles.

text: The goal of this research is to provide definition and direction for large scale fire suppression tests and selection of the fire suppressant for next generation crew exploration vehicles.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Research Summary: • The combustion and extinction characteristics of liquid fuel droplets in microgravity are determined by the complex interaction of fuel vapor and oxidizer transport, fuel vaporization, conductive, convective and radiative heat loss and chemical kinetics.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: All of these phenomena are critical in real fire scenarios and thus in understanding the complex issues involved in the design of an effective fire suppression system. • The simplicity of the droplet geometry lends itself to detailed theoretical and numerical studies.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: By comparing the results of the experiments to these detailed treatments it is possible to develop validated chemical kinetic and heat and mass transport mechanisms for liquid fuels.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: From these fundamental mechanisms it becomes possible to develop validated, predictive, reduced-scale mechanisms that are appropriate for modeling real fire suppression scenarios aboard future spacecraft. • The Multi-User Droplet Combustion Appara tus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment (MDCA- FLEX) investigation will yield both a quantitative measure of the effectiveness of various suppression agents and more importantly a set of predictive tools that will allow the effective, efficient design of future spacecraft fire suppression systems.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Detailed Research Description: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment (MDCA-FLEX) will map the flammability boundaries for liquid fuel combustion in reduced gravity to quantify the suppressant efficacy of various gaseous suppressants over the range of candidate
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: atmospheric pressures and oxygen concentrations.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: This investigation will develop predictive theoretical and numerical codes and chemical kinetic schemes to model flammability boundaries as a function effective gravitational acceleration on the unique ambient conditions encountered in space exploration applications.The development and validation of these models will require detailed spatially and temporally resolved measurements of droplet burning rate, flame extinction, flame radiation, soot concentration, soot temperature, etc.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: This investigation will also develop improved and validated reduced (simplified) theoretical and numerical sub-models of important physical processes (chemical kinetics, radiation, soot formation/destruction) that can be used in simulations of large scale, realistic fires.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The independent experiment variables analyzed by MDCA-FLEX are: Oxygen Mole Fraction: The ambient oxygen mole fraction in a typical space environment can vary from high concentrations in EVA pre-breathing environments down to that typically found in air.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: At high oxygen concentrations, however, the chemical times are small enough (relative to the characteristic flow times) such that the droplets will burn to completion rather than exhibiting flame extinction.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Therefore, it is also necessary to study low oxygen concentrations, down to the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI).
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: It is also important to determine the LOI in order to verify the chemical mechanisms.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The oxygen mole fractions in the present study will vary from 0.10 to 0.50.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The chamber must also be large enough such that there is no significant decrease in ambient oxygen mole fraction during an experiment (i.e. the droplet burns in an essentially constant ambient).
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Diluent (non-suppressant): The ambient mixture will consist of oxygen mixed with a suppressant and the balance of an inert diluent gas.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The diluent gas for these studies will be primarily nitrogen since that is the typical diluent on Earth and expected in space.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: There will be a small number of tests with a helium diluent gas.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The reason is primarily for baseline comparisons with the Droplet Combustion Experiment, which used helium as the diluent gas and also to vary the physical properties of the diluent gas.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Suppressant Type: The tests will examine candidate gaseous suppressants that have widely varying physical, chemical and radiative properties.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: This will enable model and sub-model development and validation over a wide range of ambient conditions to improve the predictive capabilities of the models.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The suppressants are carbon dioxide and helium.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The expected concentrations range from 0.00 mole fraction to the limit where no flame can exist (0.70 expected for the least active suppressant).
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Pressure: Ambient pressure does not significantly influence the droplet burning rate, but does influence chemistry at sufficiently low values.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: In addition, one strategy for extinguishing a fire is to isolate the habitat where it exists and vent the cabin to space.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: It is therefore beneficial to have verified suppressant data at low pressures.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The pressure for the tests will range from 0.5 to 1.0 atm (standard atmosphere).
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: As with the oxygen mole fraction, it is important that the test chamber be sufficiently large so that the pressure is essentially constant during an experiment (i.e. the droplet burns in a constant pressure ambient).
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Fuel Type: The advantage of the droplet geometry is that the fuel is relatively simple and better characterized than typical fuels in fire safety studies (e.g.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: This is also a disadvantage since it does not represent a practical fuel.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The study will use two typical hydrocarbon fuels, an alcohol, methanol (CH3OH ) and an alkane, heptane (C7H16 ).
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: There is a relatively large experience base with these fuels.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Methanol has a fuel-bound oxygen atom, and burns with a very dim blue flame (not much soot production) with a small standoff distance, so it has widely different radiative characteristics than heptane.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Therefore, studying these two fuels gives a wide range of fire scenarios to verify model and submodel performance over.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Droplet Diameter: The droplet is ignited in the flammable region and then burns in a constant oxygen mole fraction ambient until flame extinction.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Under the assumption of quasisteady burning, the initial droplet size should not significantly influence the determination of the extinction droplet size.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Transient influences, however, will be present, so some variation in initial droplet diameter is necessary to determine the deviation from quasi-steady behavior.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: The initial droplet size in the proposed study will vary between 2 and 5 mm.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Operational Protocols: Following setup and initialization of the MDCA-FLEX investigation the chamber shall be filled with the appropriate atmosphere, which depending on the test point, will vary in pressure from 0.5 atm to 3.0 atm, will vary in oxygen concentration from 0.1 to 0.4 mole fraction, and will vary in suppressant concentration from 0 to 0.7 mole fraction.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: A settling time of approximately 2 minutes will elapse prior to initiating the test in order to ensure that the temperature and pressure of the chamber gases have stabilized.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: This settling time will be followed by the dispensing of a predetermined amount of fuel (based on the target droplet size) onto the support fiber.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: When sufficient fuel has been dispensed the
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: dispensing needles will be retracted and a dwell period of at least 10 seconds will be allowed for the droplet internal fluid motion induced by deployment to subside.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: This will then be followed by initiating power to the igniter for a selectable amount of time ranging from 1 second to 5 seconds after which the igniter will be retracted from the field of view.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: If the flow field is to be generated by translating the droplet then droplet motion would commence at the same time that the igniter is retracted.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: A near real-time download of the color camera video will be required in order to verify successful droplet deployment, ignition, and overall progress of the experiment.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Pressure and temperature data of the chamber environment will also be required in near real time.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: At least 2 minutes must be allowed after filling chamber to ensure that the chamber gas temperature and pressure has stabilized.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: For droplet dwell time allow at least 10 seconds to ensure all droplet motion imparted by droplet deployment and needle retraction has subsided.
doc_title: Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus - Flame Extinguishment Experiment

text: Since 2012, a series of Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire) have been under development by the Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (SFS Demo) project, funded by NASA's Advanced Exploration Systems Division.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: The overall objective of this project is to reduce the uncertainty and risk associated with the design of spacecraft fire safety systems for NASA's exploration missions.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: The approach to achieving this goal has been to define, develop, and conduct experiments that address gaps in spacecraft fire safety knowledge and capabilities identified by NASA's Fire Safety System Maturation Team.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: The Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire-I, -II, and -III) are material flammability tests at length scales that are realistic for a spacecraft fire in low-gravity.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: The specific objectives of these three experiments are to (1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA's normal gravity material flammability screening test.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: The experiments will be conducted in Orbital ATK's Cygnus vehicle after it has unberthed from the International Space Station.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: The tests will be fully automated with the data downlinked at the conclusion of the test before the Cygnus vehicle reenters the atmosphere.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: This paper discusses the status of the Saffire-I, II, and III experiments followed by a review of the fire safety technology gaps that are driving the development of objectives for the next series of experiments, Saffire-IV, V, and VI.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: Experiment Development As a spaceflight experiment, Saffire has undergone the typical suite of programmatic and design reviews during its life cycle.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: However, to meet th e schedule imposed by AES, the reviews were heavily tailored with several reviews being combined.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: NASA’s milestone reviews are planned to assess hardware and software readiness before moving into the next phase of development, i.e., a System Requirements Review is the gate between requirements development and the design phase; a Critical Design Review is the gate between the design phase and manufacturing.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: The philosophy behind th e timing and content all the reviews in the Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration Project was to demonstrate the required r eadiness but push the hardware into the next phase of development as rapidly as possible, thereby shortening the overall development cycle.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: With three flight systems and their numerous sub-systems being simultaneously fabricated, assembled, and tested, this philosophy was essential for maintaining project cost and schedule.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: Spacecraft Fire Safety Technology Needs for Exploration From the outset, the objective of the Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration project was to address technology and knowledge gaps related to fire safety.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: These gaps were identified by the Spacecraft Fi re Safety Systems Maturation Team (SMT) in 2013 and are shown in Table 1.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: They have remained relatively unchanged since then as the SFS Demo project and other activities continue to address them.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: What is lacking in the verification of these technologies is a large scale demonstration of fire response in a spacecr aft that makes use of these .
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: This was recognized by AES and in 2014 they requested that the SFS Demo project de velop three more Saffire experiments that will not only continue to investigate large-scale fires in long-duratio n low-gravity but also draw on the on-going ground-based work to demonstrate technologies for fire detection, monitoring, and cleanup.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: Of course, making the jump from technologies and performance gaps to a well-defined experiment that effectively demonstrates these technolo gies requires considerable effort.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: Re searchers and technologists in the SFS Demo project as well as the Fire Safety in Space internati onal topical team have developed objectives that would be conducted in a Saffire-IV, V, and VI series of flights and that address these gaps.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: This series of flights will make use of not only the Saffire flow chamber to burn samples but also the Cygnus vehicle itself to obtain data on how the heat, smoke, and gaseous combustion products interact with the spacecraft volume.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: The list of experiment objectives for Saffire-IV-VI are shown in Table 2 in the order of priority based on de liberations of the Spacecraft Fire Safety SMT.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: Also shown in this table are the investigations that will address these objectives.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: There are several significant factors illustrated in this table.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: First, all of these objec tives require a demonstration to anchor the technology in the environment of use, i.e., long-duration low-gravity on a vehicle scale.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: Several of these gaps are addressed on Saffire-I-III but others will require implementation on Saffire-IV-VI.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: Also, many require a more intensive parametric study that can only be achieved through a supporting ground-based investigation.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: One interesting aspect of the objectives shown in Table 2 is that the fire behavior and modeling objective is a primary objective – emphasizing the need to obtain data that can be used to extrapolate results to the different vehicles and habitats required to perform NASA’s explor ation missions.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: Another observ ation is the priority placed on material flammability in exploration atmospheres – e.g. in ambient conditions having oxygen mole fractions up to 0.34 and pressures of 8.2 psia.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: These conditions bound those considered for exploration missions.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: While elevated oxygen and reduced pressure conditions are generally considered for planetary or asteroid operations where frequent extravehicular activities (EVA) are requir ed, the Cygnus environment provides the unique opportunity to explore these conditions at relevant scales and obtain data that can anchor computational models that will be applied during analysis of fire scenarios.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: Spacecraft Fire Safety Technology Gaps for Exploration Missions Technical Area Tech Goal addressed Gap Low- and partial-gravity Material Flammability Accurate definition of the risk from material flammability in low-g (identify material flammability limits in low-g environment) • Quantification of risk from NASA-STD- 6001 Test 1 normal-g data • Growth rate of fire hazard Fire Detection Common fire detectors for exploration.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: International Conference on Environmental Systems 8 For fire detection, the size of smoke particulate produced in low-gravity has been investigated by the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) 7,8.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: Transport models of smoke and combustion products have been developed based on these results but the models themselves have not been validated.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: The Saffire-IV-VI experiments in a Cygnus vehicle provide the unique opportunity to obtain this data.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: Similarly, the transport and detection of gaseous combustion products, especially acid gases like hydrogen fluoride (HF) and hydrogen chloride (HCl) that have a propensity to attach to smoke particulate and ot her surfaces must be quantified to define fire response protocol.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: Additionally, the demonstration of a post-fire monitoring technology for these chemical species will significantly advance the technology readiness level (TRL) of this instrument and bring it closer to implementation both on ISS, Orion, and future exploration vehicles.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: Obtaining data on the ability of advanced sorbents to remove carbon monoxide (CO) from the atmosphere in a spacecraft environment will ai d spacecraft environmental control and life support (ECLS) designers to develop systems that can rapidly clean-up the cabin atmosphere fo llowing a fire event.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: The Cygnus vehicle provides a unique environment to demonstrate this technology and provide data essential for the design of clean-up systems for exploration vehicles and habitats.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: The ground tests in post fire monitoring and cleanup indicated in Table 2 are pla nned for a Spacecraft Flow Simulator Facility being constructed at NASA-GRC.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: This f acility will be similar to the geometric and volumetric configuration of the Cygnus vehicle with the ability to in clude advanced diagnostics to characterize particulate and gaseous combustion product transport in a relevant environment.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: It will also be used to test various ground development units developed for Saffire-IV-VI.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: One technology for which additional low- g validation is currently not planne d is fire suppression using fine water mist extinguisher.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: Forced convection is the primary driver when a water mist extinguisher is activated making ground demonstrations highly effective in validating its performance.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: Also, determining the minimum amount of suppression agent required to extinguish a fire requires multip le tests to obtain statistically significant results and, therefore, is not conducive to the limited demonstration opportunities in the Saffire-IV-VI experiments.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: Concepts for the Saffire-IV-VI hardware are being developed along with the set of engineering requirements that encompass science, safety, and vehicle requirements.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: A Mission Concept Review/System Requirements Review is planned for June 2016 with the designs being completed later in 2016.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: Flight hardware availability for Saffire-IV is currently planned for Fall 2018.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: International Conference on Environmental Systems 9 V.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: Conclusion The Saffire series of experiment provides the unique o pportunity to address gaps in knowledge and capabilities regarding fire safety aboard spacecraft.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: The Saffire-I, II, an d III flight systems will address large-scale flame spread and material flammability limits, both essential components of understanding fire behavior and quantifying fire risks aboard spacecraft.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: Continuing these investigations and addressing other knowledge gaps will require a more ambitious experiment in Saffire-IV-VI but, by simulating a more complete fire response scenario and demonstrating post-fire monitoring and cleanup capabilities, these experiment s will significantly improve crew safety on all future exploration missions.
doc_title: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire)

text: Since 2012, the Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) has been under development by the Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (SFS Demo) project that is funded by NASA's Advanced Exploration Systems Division in the Human Exploration and Operations Mission Directorate.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The overall objective of this project is to reduce the uncertainty and risk associated with the design of spacecraft fire safety systems for NASA's exploration missions.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: This is accomplished by defining, developing, and conducting experiments that address gaps in spacecraft fire safety knowledge and capabilities identified by NASA's Fire Safety System Maturation Team.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: This paper describes the three Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire-I, -II, and -III) that were developed at NASA-GRC and that will conduct a series of material flammability tests in low-gravity and at length scales that are realistic for a spacecraft fire.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The experiments will be conducted in Orbital ATK's Cygnus vehicle after it has unberthed from the International Space Station.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The tests will be fully automated with the data downlinked at the conclusion of the test and before the Cygnus vehicle reenters the atmosphere.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The objectives of these experiments are to (1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA's normal gravity material flammability screening test.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The hardware for these experiments has been completed and is awaiting their respective launches, all planned for 2016.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: This paper will review the objectives of these experiments and how they address several of the knowledge gaps for NASA's exploration missions.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: THE SPACECRAFT FIRE EXPERIMENT (SAFFIRE) - OBJECTIVES, DEVELOPMENT AND STATUS William Schoren(1), Gary A.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Glenn Research Center, 21000 Brookpark Road, Cleveland, OH 44135, Email: william.r.schoren@nasa.gov ABSTRACT Since 2012, the Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) has been under development by the Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (SFS Demo) project that is funded by NASA’s Advanced Exploration Systems Division in the Human Exploration and Operations Mission Directorate.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The overall objective of this project is to reduce the uncertainty and risk associated with the design of spacecraft fire safety systems for NASA’s exploration missions.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: This is accomplished by defining, developing, and conducting experiments that address gaps in spacecraft fire safety knowledge and capabilities identified by NASA’s Fire Safety System Maturation Team.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: This paper describes the three Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire-I, -II, and -III) that were developed at NASA-GRC and that will conduct a series of material flammability tests in low-gravity and at length scales that are realistic for a spacecraft fire.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The experiments will be conducted in Orbital ATK’s Cygnus vehicle after it has unberthed from the International Space Station.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The tests will be fully automated with the data downlinked at the conclusion of the test and before the Cygnus vehicle reenters the atmosphere.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The objectives of these experiments are to (1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The hardware for these experiments has been completed and is awaiting their respective launches, all planned for 2016.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: This paper will review the objectives of these experiments and how they address several of the knowledge gaps for NASA’s exploration missions.

text: INTRODUCTION Tests on full-scale transportation vehicles, buildings, homes, and habitats have been common on earth to more fully understand the fire hazards associated with each application and how best to protect the passengers and inhabitants from a potential fire.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Fire safety on spacecraft has been a significant concern for NASA during the decades of crewed spaceflight and will remain so as NASA plans future exploration missions.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Many microgravity combustion experiments have been performed on the Space Shuttle and continue to be performed on the International Space States (ISS) and the data from these experiments have contributed to our understanding of how to prevent and protect crewed spacecraft from fire.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: However, none of these experiments have studied sample and environment sizes typical of those expected in a spacecraft fire [1].
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Prior experiments have been limited to samples no larger than 10 cm in length and width whereas a serious spacecraft fire would likely be much larger and consume much more material.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Because of the large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, there is a significant lack of data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Despite their obvious importance, full scale spacecraft fire experiments have not been possible because of the inherent hazards involved with conducting a large fire test in a crewed vehicle.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: To address this knowledge gap, a project was proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: In October 2011, the NASA Advanced Exploration Systems (AES) Division of NASA’s Human Exploration and Operations Mission Directorate funded this project to develop and demonstrate spacecraft fire safety technologies in relevant environments.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The keystone demonstration to be performed was a largescale fire safety experiment to be conducted on an ISS re-supply vehicle after it has left the ISS and before it enters the earth’s atmosphere.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The project team led from NASA’s John H.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Glenn Research Center (GRC) was identified and began formulating such an experiment.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The NASA team was augmented by an international topical team assembled by the European Space Agency (ESA) [2].
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The participation of members from other countries and space agencies not only brings additional skills to the science team but also facilitates international cooperation in the development of an approach to spacecraft fire prevention and response for
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The current spaceflight experiment funded and being developed by NASA addresses two objectives.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The first objective is to understand the flame spread and growth of a fire over a large piece of flammable material, consistent with clothing or other fabric likely to be in a spacecraft cabin.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: This sample material is approximately 0.94 meters long and 0.4 meters wide.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: This will be at least an order of magnitude larger in both dimensions than any prior low-g flame spread experiment.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The second objective is to examine the flammability limits of materials in low gravity for comparison with results of NASA’s terrestrial normal gravity evaluation tests.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The status of the development of the flight experiment and the individual contributions of the topical team will be discussed in subsequent sections.

text: SAFFIRE EXPERIMENT SAFETY Even though this experiment will be conducted during the un-crewed portion of the flight, the Cygnus vehicle berths with the ISS and, therefore, the experiment is subject to many of the same safety considerations as other ISS payloads.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The major safety hazard is inadvertent igniter activation prior to the Cygnus deberthing from the ISS.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: This would result in the exposure of the flight crew to toxic gases that are produced from the combustion event.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: It should be noted that this hazard is a concern prior to Cygnus berthing to the ISS since the toxic gases would be present when the Cygnus hatch is opened to the ISS.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The power and communication interfaces between Cygnus and Saffire are utilized to control this hazard.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Cygnus provides two power feed circuits to Saffire due to power requirements.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: One power feed circuit provides power to the Saffire avionics, the other provides power to the igniter circuitry.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: There are two latching relays in each of these two power feed circuits, one in the power feed side, one in the return.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: These four latching relays are contained within the Saffire flight unit but are controlled and monitored by Cygnus avionics.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: A separate ground command to the Cygnus avionics is required to close each of these four latching relays.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Igniter activation requires that all four relays be closed.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: This is because Saffire avionics provides an enable command to a DC/DC converter in the igniter circuitry and also provides commanding to solid state relay switches on the igniter control card within the igniter power feed circuitry.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: In addition, a ground command to the Saffire avionics via Cygnus avionics is required to initiate an igniter activation for an experiment run.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Cygnus avionics and the associated ground commanding provide the required failure tolerance for control of the Saffire hazard of inadvertent igniter activation.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Significant focus was placed on these four latching relays due to their safety criticality.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: This attention is reflected in the environmental testing performed as shown in Table 3.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The relays for all three flight units were vibration tested at the component level.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Tailoring of the environmental testing resulted in only Saffire I being vibration tested at a system level.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Therefore, vibration testing was performed on the Saffire II and III Power Management Systems that includes the relays to address the criticality of these relays and the associated risk of this tailored system-level vibration testing.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Safety engineering input was critical to developing a design solution that was acceptable from an ISS payload safety perspective due to the interface limitations between Saffire and Cygnus.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: This hazard along with the other typical ISS payloads hazards are documented in the Saffire Unit I Flight Safety Data Package.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The ISS Payload Safety Review Panel (PSRP) reviewed and approved this Package at the Phase I/II level in August of 2013 and again at the Phase III level in March 2015.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: These Payload Safety Reviews were augmented by a handful of Technical Interchange Meetings (TIMs) with the PSRP including TIMs to address the inadvertent igniter activation hazard.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: These TIMs were of tremendous value in the overall safety approval process by providing a focused review of specific safety issues.

text: SPACECRAFT FIRE SAFETY KNOWLEDGE GAPS AND FUTURE EXPERIMENTS The experiments being developed for Saffire-I, -II, and –III will be the first of their kind to evaluate low-g material flammability with direct implications for fire safety on future exploration vehicles.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: One of the drawbacks of these experiments is that a relatively small number of tests will be conducted (two large samples and nine smaller samples).
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: A thorough evaluation of these phenomena would require many more samples and range of materials.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Also, if they are typical of most low-g combustion experiments, the findings will raise additional significant questions for material flammability in spacecraft.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The Saffire hardware and the Cygnus vehicle provides a unique opportunity to demonstrate other fire safety technologies including fire detection, fire suppression, post-fire cleanup and monitoring.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Needs in these areas have been identified by NASA’s Spacecraft Fire Safety Systems Maturation Team and are summarized in Table 5.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Because of the importance of addressing these remaining needs to crew safety in exploration missions, AES management authorized the SFS Demo project to plan for three more Saffire experiments, Saffire -IV, V, and VI, that will address objectives not achieved in Saffire-I-III.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Of particular note is that many of these objectives require supporting ground-based experimentation to perform the parametric investigations that are required to fully understand the phenomena in question.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The objective of the flight experiment is to anchor the ground-based experiments with flight data.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: While the planning for the follow-on experiments is underway, the development process is intended to mirror the processes executed with Saffire-I-III.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The Mission Concept Review/System Requirements Review is planned for June 2016 with a design review planned for December 2016.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: CONCLUSIONS The Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration Project has designed, manufactured, assembled and tested three Saffire flight units.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The decision to develop flight units of nearly identical design allowed for the tailoring of environmentally testing that resulted in cost and schedule savings without introducing significant risk.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: This design similarity also allowed for the comparison of test results to verify consistency when testing was performed across all three flight units.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Safety engineering input was critical to developing an acceptable design solution to control the inadvertent igniter activation hazard due to the interface limitations between Saffire and Cygnus.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Technical Interchange Meetings (TIMs) with the ISS Payload Safety Review Panel proved to be invaluable to the overall safety approval process by providing a focused review of specific safety issues.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Conducting these three experiments will be a milestone for spacecraft fire safety .
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: The data and follow on analysis will provide verification of spacecraft fire safety design and operations for future exploration vehicles and their crews.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: Development of the Saffire-IV – VI flight units will extend spacecraft fire safety knowledge related to the combustion by-products and fire detection.
doc_title: The Spacecraft Fire Experiment (Saffire) - Objectives, Development and Status

text: National Aeronautics and Space Administration www.nasa.gov 32 Conclusions • For the conditions tested, the materials emit most of their particulate in the submicron range. • The ISS detector showed a relatively weak signal for some Teflon runs doubtless a result of the particle size. • Particle morphology varies widely across the range of expected sample materials.

text: National Aeronautics and Space Administration www.nasa.gov 33 Implications and Future Work • Dust rejection may be achievable by detecting at the sub-micron level. • Given the effects of aging and the slow mixing seen in spacecraft, it is probably unwise to focus entirely on small particle sizes for fire detection • Size selective smoke detection will improve reliability and false alarm rejection.

text: Appropriate design of fire detection systems requires knowledge of both the expected fire signature and the background aerosol levels.
doc_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Research at NASA Glenn Research Center

text: Terrestrial fire detection systems have been developed based on extensive study of terrestrial fires.
doc_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Research at NASA Glenn Research Center

text: Unfortunately there is no corresponding data set for spacecraft fires and consequently the fire detectors in current spacecraft were developed based upon terrestrial designs.
doc_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Research at NASA Glenn Research Center

text: In low gravity, buoyant flow is negligible which causes particles to concentrate at the smoke source, increasing their residence time, and increasing the transport time to smoke detectors.
doc_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Research at NASA Glenn Research Center

text: Microgravity fires have significantly different structure than those in 1-g which can change the formation history of the smoke particles.
doc_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Research at NASA Glenn Research Center

text: Finally the materials used in spacecraft are different from typical terrestrial environments where smoke properties have been evaluated.
doc_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Research at NASA Glenn Research Center

text: It is critically important to detect a fire in its early phase before a flame is established, given the fixed volume of air on any spacecraft.
doc_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Research at NASA Glenn Research Center

text: Consequently, the primary target for spacecraft fire detection is pyrolysis products rather than soot.
doc_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Research at NASA Glenn Research Center

text: Experimental investigations have been performed at three different NASA facilities which characterize smoke aerosols from overheating common spacecraft materials.
doc_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Research at NASA Glenn Research Center

text: The earliest effort consists of aerosol measurements in low gravity, called the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), and subsequent ground-based testing of SAME smoke in 55-gallon drums with an aerosol reference instrument.
doc_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Research at NASA Glenn Research Center

text: Another set of experiments were performed at NASAs Johnson Space Center White Sands Test Facility (WSTF), with additional fuels and an alternate smoke production method.
doc_title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Research at NASA Glenn Research Center

text: Measurements of these smoke products include mass and number concentration, and a thermal precipitator was designed for this investigation to capture particles for microscopic analysis.

doc_title: An Experimental and Computational Study on Soot Formation in a Coflow Jet Flame Under Microgravity and Normal Gravity

text: The Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) determines the point at which gas-jet flames (similar to a butane-lighter flame) begin to emit soot (dark carbonaceous particulate formed inside the flame) in microgravity.
doc_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment

text: Studying a soot emitting flame is important in understanding the ability of fires to spread and in control of soot in practical combustion systems space.
doc_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment

text: Previous experiments show that soot dominates the heat emitted from flames in normal gravity and microgravity fires.
doc_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment

text: Control of this heat emission is critical for prevention of the spread of fires on Earth and in space for the design of efficient combustion systems (jet engines and power generation boilers).
doc_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment

text: The onset of soot emission from small gas jet flames (similar to a butane-lighter flame) will be studied to provide a database that can be used to assess the interaction between fuel chemistry and flow conditions on soot formation.
doc_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment

text: These results will be used to support combustion theories and to assess fire behavior in microgravity.
doc_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment

text: The Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) will lead to a o improved design of practical combustors through improved control of soot formation; o improved understanding of and ability to predict heat release, soot production and emission in microgravity fires; o improved flammability criteria for selection of materials for use in the next generation of spacecraft.
doc_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment

text: The Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) will continue the study of fundamental phenomena related to understanding the mechanisms controlling the stability and extinction of jet diffusion flames begun with the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP) on STS-94.
doc_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment

text: SPICE will determine the laminar smoke point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the properties of the largest laminar jet diffusion flames that do not emit soot) for several fuels under different nozzle diameter/co-flow velocity configurations.

text: Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify models of the flame shapes under co-flow conditions.
doc_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment

doc_title: Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment

text: Introduction 1.1 Combustion in Microgravity Microgravity, i.e., apparent near weightlessness, is a unique environment for conducting combustion research.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Many flames are dramatically influenced by the near elimination of buoyant convection, where the resulting effects are often advantageous 1-2).
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: For example, it is possible to create spherically symmetric flames enabling one-dimensional analysis.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: More generally, the effective elimination of flicker yields quasi -steady flames.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Furthermore, the length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of their structure.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere than normal -gravity flames and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: For example, the long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free due to radiative heat loss.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Even neglecting soot, microgravity flames can be appropriate for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are importan t.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: It is also possible to study momentum -dominated flames at low velocities.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: And of course, microgravity is the appropriate environment for studies related to spacecraft fire safety.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Although microgravity combustion research has long been conducted in dr op facilities and research aircraft flying parabolic maneuvers, spacecraft like the International Space Station (ISS) offer significant advantages.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Drop durations, which are ~5 s or less in NASA facilities, are too short for soot to achieve quasi-steady conditions.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: The y are also too short to first establish a flame and then vary conditions such as the flow rate, for example, to investigate stability or extinction limits.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Meanwhile, low -momentum flames can be dramatically disturbed by the g-jitter present in aircraft testing, which is nominally ±0.02 g for a ~20 s duration.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: The jitter can be avoided by floating an experiment within the aircraft, but that reduces the test duration to mere seconds.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: As a result, space -based testing is often necessary to get microgravity conditions of sufficient duration and quality for combustion research.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: 1.2 Previous Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuels Conducted in Space Five different experiments burning gaseous fuels were conducted during space shuttle missions in 1997 and 2003 .
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: More specifically, in th e three investigations the fuel issued from a burner into an oxidizer atmosphere.
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: Each of the other two studies instead featured premixed flames in which a combustion vessel was filled with a mixture of the reactants .
doc_title: Recent Research on Flames of Gaseous Fuel Aboard the International Space Station

text: The primary objective is to gain fundamental understanding that can enable improved efficiency and reduced emissions in practical combustion processes on Earth, for example through the development and verification of models for chemical kinetics and transport processes in computational simulations.

text: Some specific goals are to improve our understanding of combustion at fuel lean conditions where both optimum performance and low emissions can be achieved, cool flame chemistry, flame stability and extinction limits, materials flammability, oxygen-enriched combustion which could enable practical carbon sequestration, soot control and reduction, and the use of electric fields for combustion control.

doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: For example, it is possible to create spherically symmetric flames en abling one-dimensional analysis.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: More generally, the effective elimination of flicker yields quasi-steady flames.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Furthermore, the length scales are increased in microgravity flames faci litating analysis of the flame structure.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere than normalgravity flames and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: For example, the long residence times in microgravity flames ca n lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Even neglect ing soot, microgravity flames can be appropriate for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: It is also possible to study momentum-dominated flames at low velocities.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: And of course, microgravity is the appropriate environment for studies related to spacecraft fire safety.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Although microgravity combustion research has been conducted in drop facilities and research aircraft flying parabolic maneuvers, spacecraft li ke the International Space Station (ISS) offer significant advantages.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Drop durations, which are ~5 s or less in NASA facilities, are too short for soot to achieve quasi-steady conditions.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The drop durations are also too short to first establish a flame and then vary its flow rate, for example, to investigate stability or extinction
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Meanwhile, low-momentum flames can be dr amatically disturbed by the g-jitter present in the aircraft testing, which is nominally ±0.02 g for a ~20 s duration.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The jitter can be avoided by floating an experiment within the aircraft, but that reduces the test duration to mere seconds.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: As a result, space-based testing is often necessary to get microgravity conditions of sufficient duration and quality for combustion research.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Given the many advantages of space-based com bustion research, five gas-fueled non-premixed flame experiments have thus far been conducted in space, where they are listed chronologically in Table 1.

text: Science The current ACME experiments are primarily focused on energy and environmental concerns, but there is a secondary emphasis (w ith the BRE experiment) on fire prevention, especially for spacecraft.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: The primary objective is to ga in fundamental understanding that can enable improved efficiency and reduced emissions in practical combustion processes on Earth, for example through the development a nd verification of models for chemical kinetics and transport processes in computational simulations.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: In addit ion to enhanced performance, improved modeling capability can lead to reductions in the ti me and cost for combustor design.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Some specific goals are to improve our understanding of combustion at fuel lean conditions where both optimum performance and low emissions can be achieved, soot control and reduction, oxygenenriched combustion which could enable practica l carbon sequestratio n, flame stability and extinction limits, the use of electric fields for combustion control, and materials flammability.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Unlike the other current ACME experiments, the Bur ning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is focused on spacecraft fire prevention.
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: More specifically, BRE’s objective is to improve our fundamental understanding of materia ls flammability, such as ex tinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the relevance of existing flammability
doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: A flat porous burner fed with gaseous fuel will simulate the burning of solid and li quid fuels, where measurements are made of the thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon which the vaporization of c ondensed-phase fuels is dependent.

text: A small number of gaseous fuels (including mixtures with inert gases) will be used to simulate the burning of fuels such as paper, plastic, and alcohol by matching properties such as the heats of combustion and gasification, the surface temperature, and smoke point.

doc_title: Gaseous Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station

text: Outside review ers concluded that the experiment “ has great prospects of improving our understa nding of nearly every practical combustion device.” The experiment will be conducted with a simple gas -jet flame, where an electric field will be generated by creating a hig h voltage (up to 10 kV) differ ential between the burner and a flat circular mesh above (i.e., downstream of) the burne r.
